# Who Are You, Really? Finding Identity Beyond the Highlight Reel

Hey, everyone. Before we start, I want to ask you something, and I want you to actually think about it for a second—not answer out loud, just sit with it: *Who are you?*

I'm guessing some of you went straight to your achievements. "I'm a soccer player" or "I'm someone who gets good grades." Others maybe thought about what you look like, or how you come across online. Some of you might have thought about your friend group or your family role. And honestly? All of those things are part of the picture. But I'm wondering if they're the *whole* picture, and I think that's worth exploring.

Because here's what I've noticed: there's this weird moment in your teenage years where the question "Who am I?" stops being abstract and becomes *urgent*. It matters because colleges are asking, because people are watching, because you're starting to make real choices about your future. And that urgency can turn the question into something stressful instead of something liberating.

So let's talk about that.

## The Pressure to Be a Finished Product

Instagram doesn't show you the failed test. TikTok doesn't show you the friendship drama or the panic attack before the big game. Your parents' friends don't ask about the stuff you're figuring out—they ask "What are you doing after graduation?" as if you're supposed to already know.

The pressure is real, and it's multifaceted. You're supposed to be:
- Successful (but not so successful that you seem arrogant)
- Authentic (but not so authentic that you make people uncomfortable)
- Ambitious (but not anxious about it)
- Attractive (but not vain)
- Interesting (but not trying too hard)

That's an impossible equation. And when you're trying to solve it, you end up performing your life rather than living it. You're curating an identity instead of discovering one.

The thing is, I get why this happens. Identity *feels* like something you need to nail down, to lock in place. You think: *If I can just figure out who I am, then everything else follows.* You'll know what to wear, what to say, what to want. You'll be coherent. You'll be someone.

But that's not actually how identity works.

## The Myth of the Fixed Self

Here's something that might actually be freeing: you're not supposed to be a finished product right now. Not even close.

I know that sounds like something a guidance counselor would say, but stay with me. The idea that you need to have yourself "figured out" is based on a misunderstanding of what identity actually is. It's not a destination. It's not something you arrive at and then stay. It's more like a direction you're moving in—something that evolves as you do.

Think about someone you really respect. A teacher, a family member, an athlete, an artist—someone whose identity seems solid. Here's the thing: they're probably still figuring stuff out. They're probably still surprised by themselves sometimes. They've just learned something crucial that I want to hand to you early: *your identity is not primarily about what you achieve or how you look. It's about what you value and how you treat people.*

That's not poetic fluff. That's actually practical.

When you ground your identity in values instead of achievements, something shifts. Achievement is unstable. You can lose a game. You can get a bad grade. Your body changes. Your Instagram followers fluctuate. But your values? Those are something you choose, and they're something you can come back to.

If you're a soccer player and you blow out your knee, who are you then? If you're the smart kid and you fail a class, what happens to your identity? These aren't hypothetical questions—they're things that happen to people, and the ones who weather them best aren't the ones who had a backup achievement ready. They're the ones who knew their identity was rooted in something deeper.

## What Actually Matters

So what does it look like to build an identity around values instead of externals?

It means asking different questions. Instead of "How do I look?" ask "How do I want to treat people?" Instead of "Am I successful?" ask "Am I becoming someone I respect?" Instead of "What should I want?" ask "What do I actually care about?"

These are harder questions. They don't have quick answers. But they're real.

Here's what I mean concretely: maybe you're someone who values honesty. That doesn't mean you have to be perfect or always say the right thing. It means when you mess up, you own it. It means you don't pretend to be someone you're not just to fit in. That's an identity. That's who you are. And it's something nobody can take away from you.

Or maybe you value kindness. That doesn't mean being a doormat. It means you're aware of how your words land on people. It means you're willing to stand up for someone who's being treated badly. It means you're interested in people, not just how they perceive you.

Or maybe you value curiosity. You ask questions. You're not afraid to say "I don't know." You're genuinely interested in how things work and why people do what they do. That's an identity that's going to serve you for the rest of your life, in ways that being "the popular kid" or "the athlete" never will.

## The Practical Part

Okay, so all of that is nice in theory. How do you actually *do* this?

Here's what I want you to try this week:

**First, identify one or two core values.** Not ten. Not a list. One or two things that actually matter to you. And I mean *actually*—not what you think should matter, but what genuinely does. Is it honesty? Creativity? Loyalty? Courage? Justice? Growth? Humor? Write it down.

**Second, notice where your identity is currently tied to externals.** This is just observation, not judgment. Where are you performing? Where are you curating? Where are you anxious about being "found out"? What would happen to your sense of self if that thing changed? Just notice it.

**Third, do one small thing this week that aligns with your values, even if it's inconvenient.** If you value honesty, say something true that's a little uncomfortable. If you value kindness, do something for someone when nobody's watching. If you value courage, try something that scares you a little. Make it real. Make it count.

The point isn't to be perfect. The point is to start building an identity from the inside out instead of the outside in.

## One More Thing

I want to say this clearly: you're not alone in feeling the pressure to have yourself figured out. Every single person in this room is probably feeling it. The people who seem most confident? They're probably still figuring it out too. They've just learned to be okay with the uncertainty.

And here's the secret nobody tells you: that's actually where the freedom is. When you stop trying to be a finished product, when you stop performing your life, when you let yourself be someone who's still becoming—that's when you're actually most yourself.

Your identity isn't something you need to perfect or defend. It's something you get to build, day by day, choice by choice, through how you show up and what you care about.

So this week, start there. Figure out what actually matters to you. Build from that. The rest will follow.

You've got this.

But here's also what's real: the people who navigate life with any kind of grace, who actually seem to like themselves, who aren't constantly anxious about being "found out"—they're the ones who've figured out that their value as a person isn't on the line every single day. They've built their identity on something deeper than whether they win or lose, whether they look a certain way, whether they're liked.

## The Practical Part

Okay, so all of that is nice in theory. How do you actually *do* this?

Here's what I want you to try this week:

**First, identify one or two core values.** Not ten. Not a list. One or two things that actually matter to you. And I mean *actually*—not what you think should matter, but what genuinely does. Is it honesty? Creativity? Loyalty? Courage? Justice? Growth? Humor? Independence? Something else entirely? Write it down. Just for you.

**Second, notice where your identity is currently tied to externals.** This is just observation, not judgment. Where are you performing? Where are you curating? Where are you anxious about being "found out"? What would happen to your sense of self if that thing changed? Just notice it. Don't shame yourself about it. This is how most of us are operating. You're not broken for doing this.

**Third, do one small thing this week that aligns with your values, even if it's inconvenient.** And I want to be specific here because "do something that aligns with your values" can sound vague.

If you value honesty, maybe that means telling a friend something you've been afraid to say. Not something mean—something true. Like "I don't actually agree with you about this" or "I'm struggling and I need help" or "I appreciate you more than I usually say."

If you value kindness, maybe that means doing something for someone when nobody will ever know. Not a big grand gesture. Maybe it's helping a younger sibling with homework without being asked. Maybe it's leaving a note for someone who's been having a hard time. Maybe it's listening to someone without planning what you're going to say next.

If you value courage, maybe that means trying something that genuinely scares you a little. Joining a club you've been nervous about. Asking a question in class even though you might sound stupid. Doing something that matters to you even though it might not impress anyone.

Make it real. Make it count. And here's the important part: **tell someone about it.** Tell a friend, tell a parent, tell someone in this group. Not to brag—to make it real. Identity isn't something that happens only in your head. It happens in relationship. It happens when you show up for people and when people see you showing up. So share it.

## One More Thing

I want to say this clearly: you're not alone in feeling the pressure to have yourself figured out. Every single person in this room is probably feeling it. The people who seem most confident? I promise you, they're still figuring it out too. They've just learned to be okay with the uncertainty.

And here's the secret nobody tells you: that's actually where the freedom is. When you stop trying to be a finished product, when you stop performing your life, when you let yourself be someone who's still becoming—that's when you actually start to become someone worth knowing. Not someone impressive. Someone real.

Your identity isn't something you need to perfect or defend. It's something you get to build, day by day, choice by choice, through how you show up and what you care about.

So this week, start there. Figure out what actually matters to you. Do one thing that proves it. Tell someone about it. And then do it again next week. And the week after that.

You don't have to have it all figured out. You just have to start moving in a direction that's actually yours.

Some of you might have thought about your friend group or your family role. And honestly? All of those things are part of the picture. But I'm wondering if they're the *whole* picture, and I think that's worth exploring.

Because here's what I've noticed: there's this weird moment in your teenage years where the question "Who am I?" stops being abstract and becomes *urgent*. It matters because colleges are asking, because people are watching, because you're starting to make real choices about your future. And that urgency can turn the question into something stressful instead of something liberating.

So let's talk about that.

## The Pressure to Be a Finished Product

Let me paint a picture you probably recognize. You're scrolling through Instagram and you see someone from school with this perfect photo—perfect lighting, perfect angle, perfect caption. No sign of the fifteen takes it took to get there. No mention of the anxiety before the photo shoot, or the insecurity about how they actually look. Just the highlight reel.

And then there's TikTok, where you're supposed to be constantly interesting, constantly creating, constantly *on*. There's the pressure to maintain streaks, to get tagged in the right photos, to have the right number of followers. There's the unspoken rule that if you're not performing your life online, you're not really living it.

But it goes deeper than social media. Your parents' friends don't ask about the stuff you're figuring out—they ask "What are you doing after graduation?" as if you're supposed to already know. Teachers want you to be ambitious but not anxious about it. Your peers expect you to be authentic, but not so authentic that you make them uncomfortable. You're supposed to be successful without seeming arrogant, attractive without being vain, interesting without trying too hard.

That's an impossible equation. And when you're trying to solve it, you end up performing your life rather than living it. You're curating an identity instead of discovering one.

The thing is, I get why this happens. Identity *feels* like something you need to nail down, to lock in place. You think: *If I can just figure out who I am, then everything else follows.* You'll know what to wear, what to say, what to want. You'll be coherent. You'll be someone.

But that's not actually how identity works.

## The Myth of the Fixed Self

Here's something that might actually be freeing: you're not supposed to be a finished product right now. Not even close.

I know that sounds like something a guidance counselor would say, but stay with me. The idea that you need to have yourself "figured out" is based on a misunderstanding of what identity actually is. It's not a destination. It's not something you arrive at and then stay. It's more like a direction you're moving in—something that evolves as you do.

Think about someone you really respect. A teacher, a family member, an athlete, an artist—someone whose identity seems solid and clear. Here's the thing: they're probably still figuring stuff out. They're probably still surprised by themselves sometimes. They've just learned something crucial that I want to hand to you early: *your identity is not primarily about what you achieve or how you look. It's about what you value and how you treat people.*

That's not poetic fluff. That's actually practical, and it changes everything.

When you ground your identity in values instead of achievements, something shifts. Achievement is unstable. You can lose a game. You can get a bad grade. Your body changes. Your Instagram followers fluctuate. A photo you thought was cool gets roasted in a group chat. But your values? Those are something you choose, and they're something you can come back to, even when everything else is falling apart.

If you're a soccer player and you blow out your knee, who are you then? If you're the smart kid and you fail a class, what happens to your identity? If you get a bad haircut or a photo of you goes viral for the wrong reasons, does your sense of self collapse? These aren't hypothetical questions—they're things that happen to people, and the ones who weather them best aren't the ones who had a backup achievement ready. They're the ones who knew their identity was rooted in something deeper.

## What Actually Matters

So what does it look like to build an identity around values instead of externals?

It means asking different questions. Instead of "How do I look?" ask "How do I want to treat people?" Instead of "Am I successful?" ask "Am I becoming someone I respect?" Instead of "What should I want?" ask "What do I actually care about?"

These are harder questions. They don't have quick answers. But they're real, and they lead somewhere.

Here's what I mean concretely: maybe you're someone who values honesty. That doesn't mean you have to be perfect or always say the right thing. It means when you mess up, you own it. It means you don't pretend to be someone you're not just to fit in. It means you're willing to say "I don't know" instead of pretending to have all the answers. That's an identity. That's who you are. And it's something nobody can take away from you.

Or maybe you value kindness. That doesn't mean being a doormat. It means you're aware of how your words land on people. It means you're willing to stand up for someone who's being treated badly, even if it costs you socially. It means you're interested in people, not just how they perceive you.

Or maybe you value curiosity. You ask questions. You're genuinely interested in how things work and why people do what they do. You don't need to have the "right" opinion—you're interested in understanding different perspectives. That's an identity that's going to serve you for the rest of your life, in ways that being "the popular kid" or "the athlete" never will.

When you know your core values, something else happens: you start to see your *purpose*. And I don't mean your future job or your five-year plan. I mean the reason you matter right now, in this moment. If you value justice, your purpose might be to speak up when something unfair is happening—whether you're in a classroom, a friend group, or a comment section. If you value creativity, your purpose might be to make things that didn't exist before, to help people see the world differently. If you value growth, your purpose might be to challenge yourself and help others do the same. Your purpose isn't something you'll discover in college or after graduation. It's something you're already living, every time you choose to act according to your values.

## The Practical Part

Okay, so all of that is nice in theory. How do you actually *do* this?

Here's what I want you to try this week:

**First, identify one or two core values.** Not ten. Not a list. One or two things that actually matter to you. And I mean *actually*—not what you think should matter, not what your parents want or what looks good on a college application, but what genuinely does. Is it honesty? Creativity? Loyalty? Courage? Justice? Growth? Humor? Kindness? Write it down somewhere you'll see it.

Where are you anxious about being "found out"? What would happen to your sense of self if that thing changed? Just notice it. You don't have to fix it all at once.

**Third, do one small thing this week that aligns with your values, even if it's inconvenient.** And here's where it gets real, because I want these examples to actually apply to your life:

If you value *integrity*, maybe this week you choose not to participate in a group chat where someone is being bullied, even if it feels awkward to stay silent. Or you admit that you didn't actually read the article before sharing it.

If you value *honesty*, maybe you tell a friend something true that's uncomfortable, or you own up to a mistake instead of making an excuse.

If you value *truth*, maybe you fact-check that viral post before sharing it, even though it would be easier not to.

If you value *courage*, maybe you try something that scares you a little—raise your hand in class when you're not sure of the answer, start a conversation with someone new, or say no to something you don't actually want to do.

If you value *kindness*, maybe you do something for someone when nobody's watching, or you reach out to someone who seems like they're struggling.

The point isn't to be perfect. The point isn't to prove anything to anyone. The point is to start building an identity from the inside out instead of the outside in. Make it real. Make it count.

## One More Thing

I want to say this clearly: you're not alone in feeling the pressure to have yourself figured out. Every single person in this room is probably feeling it. The people who seem most confident? They're probably still figuring it out too. They've just learned to be okay with the uncertainty.

And here's the secret nobody tells you: that's actually where the freedom is. When you stop trying to be a finished product, when you stop performing your life, when you let yourself be someone who's still becoming—that's when you're actually most yourself.

Your identity isn't something you need to perfect or defend. It's something you get to build, day by day, choice by choice, through how you show up and what you care about. And the beautiful part? That foundation—those values, that sense of purpose—that's something that stays with you. It's yours.

So this week, start there. Figure out what actually matters to you. Do one small thing that proves it to yourself. Build from that. The rest will follow.

You've got this.

# Who Are You When Nobody's Watching?

Hey, everyone. Before we start, I want to ask you something—and you don't have to answer out loud. Just think about it: Right now, at this moment, who are you?

I don't mean your name. I mean, if someone asked you to describe yourself, what would you say? Maybe you'd say "I'm a soccer player" or "I'm an artist" or "I'm a student at Lincoln High." Maybe you'd mention your GPA, your follower count, or what you're planning to study. Maybe you'd describe yourself by who your friends are or what you're known for.

Here's the thing I've noticed: most of us answer that question the same way. We describe ourselves by what we *do* or what we've *achieved*. And I want to talk about why that's happening, and why it matters.

---

## The Performance Trap

Let me tell you about someone. Her name is Maya—not a real person, but someone who could be any of us. Maya is 16. By most standards, she's crushing it. She's got a 3.8 GPA, she's on the volleyball team, she's got about 4,000 Instagram followers, and she's already thinking about which Ivy League school she wants to go to. On paper, Maya's life is impressive.

But here's what Maya told a counselor: "I don't actually know who I am without the achievements."

She said that when she's not doing something that looks good on a resume or gets likes online, she feels invisible. And when she's not getting straight A's or winning games, she feels like a failure. She's living in this constant state of performance—like she's always on stage, always being evaluated.

Does that resonate with anyone?

Because here's the reality of being your age right now: you're living in a time when everything you do is potentially visible. You can post a photo and get immediate feedback in the form of likes. You can see your GPA calculated down to the hundredth of a point. You can compare your achievements to literally thousands of other people your age. And everyone around you—parents, teachers, colleges, social media, your own brain—is sending the message that your value is tied to what you accomplish.

That's not new pressure. Every generation has felt pressure to succeed. But the *visibility* of it is new. And the *comparison* is new. And the *speed* of it is new.

So you're all operating under this assumption that your identity is something you have to *build*—through achievements, through the image you project, through the metrics that prove you're worth something. And that's exhausting. That's unsustainable. And honestly, that's a lie.

---

## The Thing About Deep Identity

I want to introduce you to a different way of thinking about who you are.

Imagine you lost everything tomorrow. Not in a dramatic way—just imagine your Instagram got deleted, your grades got erased, you had to quit your team. Imagine all the external markers of your identity just vanished. Who would you be then?

That question is actually important, because the answer points to what philosophers and psychologists call your "intrinsic identity"—the parts of you that aren't dependent on external validation or achievement.

Your intrinsic identity is made up of things like:

**Your values.** What actually matters to you? Not what you think should matter, not what looks good—what genuinely matters? Is it kindness? Creativity? Honesty? Justice? Adventure? Loyalty? These are the things you're drawn to, the things that feel true to who you are.

**Your character.** This is who you are when nobody's watching. It's how you treat people when it doesn't benefit you. It's whether you're honest when lying would be easier. It's whether you show up for people. Character is built through small choices, not big achievements.

**Your curiosity and creativity.** What makes you genuinely curious? What do you create just because you want to—not because it's for a grade or for social media? What problems do you want to solve? What stories do you want to tell?

**Your capacity for connection.** How do you make people feel? Can you listen? Can you be vulnerable? Can you make someone laugh or feel less alone? This is actually one of the most valuable things about you, and it's completely invisible on a resume.

**Your resilience and growth.** Not your success rate—your ability to fail, learn, and try again. Your willingness to change your mind. Your ability to sit with difficulty without falling apart.

Here's why this matters: all of those things are *yours*. They're not dependent on anyone else's opinion. They don't go away when you have a bad day or make a mistake. They're not in competition with anyone else's. And they actually form the foundation for genuine success and purpose, not the other way around.

---

## Purpose Isn't a Destination

Let me be real with you: a lot of people will tell you that you need to "find your purpose." It's usually framed like purpose is this thing you discover—like it's buried treasure and you just have to dig in the right place. And once you find it, you've got it figured out.

That's not quite how it works.

Purpose isn't a destination you arrive at. It's more like a direction you're moving in. It's what you're oriented toward. And it grows out of your actual identity—out of who you really are and what you actually care about.

Here's a practical way to think about it: your purpose is usually found at the intersection of three things:

**What you're good at.** Not what you think you should be good at, but what comes naturally to you or what you've developed skill in.

**What you care about.** What problems make you angry? What injustices bother you? What would you work on even if nobody paid you? What do you want to be part of?

**What the world needs.** This sounds big, but it's not. It could be that the world needs someone to make your little corner of it more beautiful. Someone to listen to the lonely kid at school. Someone to ask good questions. Someone to create something that makes people feel less alone.

When those three things overlap, you're in the neighborhood of purpose. And here's the beautiful thing: your purpose will probably evolve. It'll change as you learn more about yourself and the world. That's not failure. That's growth.

---

## This Week, Try This

I want to give you some concrete things you can actually do, starting this week:

**First: Have one conversation where you describe yourself without mentioning achievements.** Talk to a friend, a family member, a counselor—someone you trust. Tell them who you are based on your values, your character, what you care about. Notice how that feels different from your usual self-description.

**Second: Do one thing this week that's just for you.** Not for a grade. Not for social media. Not to impress anyone. Just because you want to. Create something, learn something, explore something. Notice how it feels to do something without an audience.

**Third: Ask someone you respect this question: "What do you think I'm actually good at?"** Not your grades or your achievements—what do they actually see in you? Sometimes other people see our real strengths more clearly than we do.

**Fourth: Get offline for one day.** Or even just one evening. Not as punishment—as an experiment. See who you are when you're not performing, not comparing, not curating. What do you actually want to do? What matters when there's no one watching?

---

## The Real Thing

Here's what I want you to know: you are not a project to be optimized. You're not a resume to be built. You're a person—complex and valuable and worth knowing, right now, as you are.

Your identity isn't something you have to earn. It's something you get to *discover* and *develop*. And it's not about being the best at anything. It's about being genuinely *you*—the you that's honest and curious and capable of caring about things. The you that tries and fails and tries again. The you that makes people feel seen.

That person is already enough. And that person is also capable of doing remarkable things—not because you're trying to prove something, but because you're moving toward what actually matters to you.

So this week, ask yourself: Who am I when nobody's watching? And then—be that person. In public too.

Not what would you lose. *Who would you be?*

Sit with that for a second, because I think it's a more uncomfortable question than it sounds.

---

Here's why I ask. I talk to a lot of students, and there's something I keep hearing underneath everything — underneath the jokes, underneath the confidence, underneath even the stuff that looks like not caring. It's this low hum of pressure. And the pressure sounds like a question that never quite goes away:

*Am I enough?*

Am I smart enough? Am I attractive enough? Am I talented enough, interesting enough, popular enough? Am I enough for my parents, my friends, the algorithm, the group chat, the university admissions portal, the person I like, the future I'm supposed to be building?

And here's what's wild — that question isn't new. People have always felt it. But what IS new is that we're now expected to answer it publicly, in real time, with metrics. You don't just wonder if you're enough. You can literally count the likes and watch the number tell you.

That changes something in your brain. It changes something in your soul.

---

A friend of mine once told me about this guy in her year — I'll call him Marcus. Marcus was, by every visible measure, crushing it. Good grades. Starting lineup on his football team. Funny. The kind of person who walks into a room and the energy shifts. His Instagram was exactly what you'd expect — wins, friends, confidence.

And one night, at something a lot like this, he stayed back after everyone else had left, and he said something I've never forgotten. He said: "I feel like I'm performing a version of myself that everyone likes, and I'm terrified that if I stop performing, there'll be nothing underneath."

Nothing underneath.

That's not a failure story. Marcus wasn't falling apart. He was succeeding — and still felt hollow. Because he'd built his entire identity on the outside, and nobody had ever told him there was supposed to be something on the inside holding it all up.

Marcus felt like there was nothing underneath the performance because he'd confused his **image** for his **identity**. And that's what I want to talk about tonight.

---

Your image is the curated version. It's the version you build for other people — the performance for your parents, the performance for your friends, the performance for the algorithm. It's the right angle, the right caption, the right answer in class, the right personality for the right group. And listen — I'm not going to stand here and tell you image doesn't matter at all, because we all navigate the world with some awareness of how we come across. That's human. That's fine.

But here's the problem: your image is fragile. It depends entirely on the audience. Change the room, and you have to change the performance. Lose the audience's approval, and the whole thing collapses. If your identity is your image, then you are only ever as secure as your last impression.

That's an exhausting way to live. And if we're honest, I think a lot of us are exhausted by it.

**Identity** is different. Identity is who you are when no one's watching, when no one's clapping, when the phone is off, when the performance stops. It's the deep, stable, quiet thing at the centre of you that doesn't need to be proved because it simply *is*.

And here's what I think matters most tonight: **you don't have to earn your identity. You have to discover it.**

---

There's a difference between those two ideas that will shape your entire life.

Failure becomes information, not identity. Other people's opinions become interesting but not authoritative. You're free to be honest about who you actually are, because who you actually are isn't a liability — it's the whole point.

You might just breathe. But practice being a person who doesn't need the noise to feel real.

It's the point.

And if that phone disappeared tomorrow? *You* would still be here. Not diminished. Not deleted. Still you — and that was always the thing that mattered.

Thanks for listening.

# You Are Not Your Highlight Reel

---

Picture this: you walk out of a game — or a rehearsal, or a shift at work, or just another long Wednesday — and your phone buzzes. A flood of notifications. Someone tagged you, someone liked the thing you posted, someone screenshotted something and sent it to a group chat you're not in. And for about thirty seconds, you feel this little lift. Like you matter. Like you're visible.

Then the buzz fades. And you're just you again, standing in a car park, with that familiar quiet question underneath everything:

*Do people actually know me — or just the version I showed them?*

Tonight I want us to sit with that question together. Not because I have some neat answer to hand you, but because I think it's one of the most important questions we can ask — and I think most of us are asking it more than we admit.

---

Here's what I keep noticing — in conversations with people your age, but honestly, in my own life too. There's this low hum of pressure that never quite switches off. And the pressure sounds like another question:

*Am I enough?*

Am I smart enough, attractive enough, talented enough, interesting enough? Am I enough for my parents, my friend group, the algorithm, the person I like, the future everyone keeps telling me I should be building?

That question isn't new. People your age have always felt it. But what *is* new is that you're the first generation that has to answer it publicly, in real time, with metrics. You don't just wonder if you're enough. You can literally count the likes and watch the number tell you. You can see exactly who viewed your story and who didn't. You can watch someone's follower count climb past yours and feel something shift in your chest that you can't quite name.

That changes something in us. Not just in our heads — somewhere deeper.

---

Let me tell you about someone I knew — I'll call him Marcus. By every visible measure, Marcus was crushing it. Good grades. Starting lineup on his football team. Funny, magnetic — the kind of person who walks into a room and the energy shifts. His Instagram looked exactly like you'd expect: wins, friends, confidence.

One night, at something a lot like this, the room had mostly emptied out. A few chairs were still scattered around, the lights were that weird half-dim they go when someone's already started locking up. Marcus was sitting on the edge of the stage, turning his phone over in his hands, and he said something I've never forgotten.

"I feel like I'm performing a version of myself that everyone likes, and I'm terrified that if I stop performing, there'll be nothing underneath."

*Nothing underneath.*

That's not a failure story. Marcus wasn't falling apart. He was succeeding — and still felt hollow. Because he'd built his entire sense of self on the outside, and nobody had ever helped him see that there was supposed to be something on the inside holding it all up.

I think a lot of us know that feeling, even if we'd never say it out loud. Maybe especially if we'd never say it out loud.

---

So here's what I want us to explore tonight: the difference between your **image** and your **identity**.

Your image is the curated version. It's the version you build for other people — the right angle, the right caption, the right personality for the right group. The way you talk in one friend group versus another. The version of your life that makes it onto the feed. And look, I'm not going to pretend image doesn't matter at all. We all navigate the world with some awareness of how we come across. That's human.

But here's the problem: your image is fragile. It depends entirely on the audience. Change the room, change the performance. Lose the audience's approval, and the whole thing wobbles. If your identity *is* your image, then you're only ever as secure as your last impression.

That's an exhausting way to live. And I think a lot of us are exhausted.

**Identity** is different. Identity is who you are when no one's watching, when no one's clapping, when the phone is off and the performance stops. It's the deep, stable, quiet thing at the centre of you that doesn't need to be proved because it simply *is*.

And here's the idea I want us to sit with: **what if identity isn't something we have to earn — but something we discover?**

---

That distinction — earning versus discovering — will shape everything.

If you have to *earn* your identity, you're always auditioning. Every exam is a referendum on your worth. Every rejection is evidence you're not enough. Every comparison — and we compare more than any generation in history, because the comparison machine lives in our pockets — every comparison becomes a verdict.

But if identity is something you *discover*, something already true about you, the whole game changes. You stop auditioning and start exploring. Failure becomes information, not a final sentence. Other people's opinions become interesting but not authoritative. You're free to be honest about who you actually are, because who you actually are isn't a liability — it's the whole point.

Now, I want to be honest: this isn't a one-time revelation. There isn't some magic moment where you "find yourself" and never struggle again. Discovering your identity is more like a practice you return to — messy, nonlinear, sometimes confusing. You'll get it wrong. You'll try on versions of yourself that don't fit. You'll have seasons where you feel completely lost. That's not failure. That's the process.

So what does that deeper identity actually look like? I think it involves a few things that are true about every person in this room, whether you feel them right now or not:

**You are not an accident.** You exist on purpose — not because you've done something to justify your existence, but because your existence doesn't require justification. You're not a product to be optimised. You're a person to be known.

**You are not your worst moment.** You're not defined by a mistake you can't take back, and you're not stuck there either. The rumour, the screenshot, the thing you said at 2am that still makes your stomach drop — those things happened. They don't define you. There is always more to your story.

**You are not your best moment, either.** This one's harder, because we love attaching ourselves to our peaks. But if your identity is your greatest achievement, what happens when someone achieves more? You are not your trophy, your grade, your follower count, or your acceptance letter. Those things might reflect something about you, but they are not *you*.

**You are capable of being deeply known — and deeply loved — and those two things don't have to cancel each other out.** Most of us believe, somewhere underneath, that if people really saw us — the real us, the uncertain, contradictory, still-figuring-it-out us — they'd back away. So we hide. We perform. We curate. But the deepest kind of love is the kind that sees clearly and stays. That kind of love exists — in real friendships, in family, in mentors, in faith communities, in the people who show up for you without needing you to be impressive first. Finding those people, and being that kind of person for someone else — that's some of the most important work you'll ever do.

A quick caveat: not every relationship in your life will be safe or healthy. Some won't be. Part of discovering your identity is also learning to recognise the people and spaces that reflect back a truer version of you — and having the courage to step back from the ones that don't. If you're not sure who those trustworthy people are, start with one adult you respect. A teacher, a coach, a counsellor, a youth leader. You don't have to figure this out alone.

---

Now — I promised practical stuff, and I don't want to leave us with just ideas. Ideas are great, but they don't change your Tuesday morning. So here are three things you can actually try this week:

**One: Audit your inputs.** Spend ten minutes scrolling through the accounts you follow and ask yourself two questions: *Does this make me more curious or more anxious? Does this help me become who I want to be, or does it make me feel like I'm falling behind?* You don't have to delete everything. Just notice. Then unfollow one account that consistently makes you feel like you're not enough. Just one. See what shifts.

**Two: Tell one person one true thing.** Not a dramatic confession. Just something honest you'd normally keep behind the performance. It could sound like: *"I'm actually struggling with this."* Or: *"I don't know what I want to do with my life, and that scares me."* Or even: *"I really value our friendship and I've never actually said that."* Pick someone you trust. Say something real. It'll cost you a little comfort, and it'll teach you that honesty doesn't make you weaker — it makes you more *you*.

**Three: Sit with the quiet.** At some point this week — even five minutes — put the phone in another room, turn off the noise, and just be. No productivity, no content, no performance. You might journal a single sentence about how you're actually doing. You might pray. You might just breathe and notice what comes up. It'll probably feel uncomfortable. That's okay. The discomfort is the sound of you meeting yourself without an audience — and that meeting matters.

*Who are you when you're not being watched?* That's the question underneath all three of these. And the answer isn't something you perform. It's something you practice.

---

I want to close with this.

We're living in a world that will try, every single day, to convince us that we are what we produce, what we look like, what we achieve, and what other people think of us. That world is loud. It's convincing. It's relentless.

But it's wrong.

You are deeper than your feed. You are more than your performance. You are not a brand to be managed — you are a person to be *lived*. And the most radical, countercultural thing any of us can do in a world that profits from our insecurity is to simply, stubbornly, quietly believe that who we are — the real, unfiltered, still-becoming version — is not just enough.

It's the point.

Thanks for being here tonight.

So I want to start with a question, and I want you to actually think about it — not just wait for me to give you the answer.

If you lost your phone tomorrow — like, gone forever, no backup — and with it, every photo, every post, every conversation, every playlist, every carefully curated version of yourself that exists online… who would you be?

Not what would you lose. *Who would you be?*

Sit with that for a second.

…

Because I think it's a more uncomfortable question than it sounds.

---

Here's why I ask. I talk to people your age a lot, and there's something I keep hearing underneath everything — underneath the jokes, underneath the confidence, underneath even the stuff that looks like not caring. It's this low hum of pressure. And the pressure sounds like a question that never quite goes away:

*Am I enough?*

Am I smart enough? Am I attractive enough? Am I talented enough, interesting enough, popular enough? Am I enough for my parents, my friends, the algorithm, the university admissions board, the person I like, the future I'm supposed to be building?

And here's what's wild — that question isn't new. People your age have always felt it. But what IS new is that you're the first generation that has to answer it publicly, in real time, with metrics. You don't just wonder if you're enough. You can literally count the likes and watch the number tell you.

That changes something in your brain. It changes something in your soul.

---

Let me tell you about a guy I knew — I'll call him Marcus. Marcus was, by every visible measure, crushing it. Good grades. Starting lineup on his football team. Funny. The kind of person who walks into a room and the energy shifts. His Instagram was exactly what you'd expect — wins, friends, confidence.

And one night, at something a lot like this, he stayed back after everyone else had left. And he said something I've never forgotten.

He said: "I feel like I'm performing a version of myself that everyone likes, and I'm terrified that if I stop performing, there'll be nothing underneath."

…

Nothing underneath.

That's not a failure story. Marcus wasn't falling apart. He was succeeding — and still felt hollow. Because he'd built his entire identity on the outside, and nobody had ever told him there was supposed to be something on the inside holding it all up.

---

Here's what I want to talk about tonight: the difference between your **image** and your **identity**.

Your image is the curated version. It's the version you build for other people. It's the right angle, the right caption, the right answer in class, the right personality for the right group. And listen — I'm not going to stand here and tell you image doesn't matter at all, because we all navigate the world with some awareness of how we come across. That's human. That's fine.

But here's the problem: your image is fragile. It depends entirely on the audience. Change the room, and you have to change the performance. Lose the audience's approval, and the whole thing collapses. If your identity is your image, then you are only ever as secure as your last impression.

That's an exhausting way to live. And I think a lot of you are exhausted.

**Identity** is different. Identity is who you are when no one's watching, when no one's clapping, when the phone is off, when the performance stops. It's the deep, stable, quiet thing at the centre of you that doesn't need to be proved because it simply *is*.

And the most important thing I'll say tonight is this: **you don't have to earn your identity. You have to discover it.**

---

There's a difference between those two ideas that will shape your entire life.

If you have to *earn* your identity, then you are always auditioning. Every test is a referendum on your worth. Every rejection is evidence that you're not enough. Every comparison — and your generation compares more than any generation in history, because the comparison machine lives in your pocket — every comparison becomes a verdict.

But if your identity is something you *discover*, something that's already true about you, then the whole game changes. You stop auditioning and start exploring. Failure becomes information, not identity. Other people's opinions become interesting but not authoritative. You're free to be honest about who you actually are, because who you actually are isn't a liability — it's the whole point.

So what does that deeper identity look like?

I think it comes down to a few things that are true about every person in this room, whether you feel them right now or not.

**You are not an accident.** You exist on purpose. Not because you've done something to justify your existence, but because your existence doesn't require justification. You are not a product to be optimised. You are a person to be known.

**You are not your worst moment.** You're not the thing you said that you can't take back. You're not the failure, the rejection, the screenshot, the rumour. Those things happened. They don't define you. There is always more to your story.

**You are not your best moment either.** This one's harder to hear, because we love attaching ourselves to our peaks. But if your identity is your greatest achievement, what happens when someone achieves more? You are not your trophy, your grade, your follower count, or your acceptance letter. Those things may reflect something about you, but they are not *you*.

**You are known and you are loved — and those two things don't cancel each other out.** This is the big one. Most of us believe, deep down, that if people really knew us — the real us, the messy, uncertain, contradictory, struggling us — they wouldn't stick around. So we hide. We perform. We curate. But the deepest kind of love is the kind that sees you clearly and stays. And that kind of love exists. Finding it — in real friendships, in family, in faith, in community — that's one of the most important things you'll ever do.

---

Now. I promised practical takeaways, and I don't want to leave you with just ideas. Ideas are great, but they don't change your Tuesday morning. So here are three things you can actually do this week.

**One: Audit your inputs.** Spend ten minutes — honestly, just ten — looking at the accounts you follow, the content you consume, and ask yourself: *Does this make me more myself, or less?* Does it make me more curious, more compassionate, more alive? Or does it make me more anxious, more comparative, more performative? You don't have to delete everything. Just notice. Awareness is the first step. Then unfollow one account that consistently makes you feel like you're not enough. Just one. See what happens.

**Two: Tell one person one true thing.** Not a dramatic confession. Not a crisis. Just one honest thing you normally wouldn't say. "I'm actually struggling with this." "I don't know what I want to do with my life, and that scares me." "I really value our friendship." Something real. Something that costs you a little bit of comfort. Because identity gets stronger every time you practice being honest, and it gets weaker every time you practice performing.

**Three: Sit with the quiet.** At some point this week — even just for five minutes — put the phone in another room, turn off the noise, and just… be. No productivity. No content. No performance. Just you. It will probably feel uncomfortable. That's okay. The discomfort is the sound of you meeting yourself without an audience, and that meeting is important. You might journal. You might pray. You might just breathe. But practice being a person who doesn't need the noise to feel real.

---

I want to close with this.

You are living in a world that will try, every single day, to tell you that you are what you produce, what you look like, what you achieve, and what other people think of you. And that world is loud. It's convincing. It's relentless.

But it's wrong.

You are deeper than your feed. You are more than your performance. You are not a brand to be managed — you are a person to be *lived*.

And the most radical, countercultural thing you can do in a world that profits from your insecurity is to simply, stubbornly, quietly believe that who you are — the real, unfiltered, still-becoming you — is not just enough.

It's the point.

…

Thanks for listening.

# You Are Not Your Highlight Reel

---

So let me start with a question. And I want you to actually think about this one — don't just let it bounce off you.

If I took your phone right now — your Instagram, your TikTok, your Snapchat, your texts, your search history, your notes app at 2am — would I know who you are?

You'd probably say yes. And also no. And you'd be right on both counts.

Here's what I mean. A couple of years ago, I was talking with a girl — she was about sixteen — and she told me something I haven't forgotten. She said, "I have three versions of myself. There's the version my parents see, the version my friends see, and the version I am when I'm alone in my room at night. And honestly? I don't know which one is the real me."

I don't think she's unusual. I think she's most of us.

---

We live in a world that is constantly asking you to define yourself. And not gently. Aggressively. Every app, every platform, every conversation at school is quietly — or not so quietly — asking: *Who are you? What's your thing? What makes you special? What's your brand?*

And the answers the world offers you are pretty narrow. You can define yourself by how you look. By your grades. By how many people follow you or like your posts. By whether you made the team, got the part, got invited. By who you're dating. By how funny or smart or talented or attractive other people think you are.

And here's the thing — none of those things are bad. Doing well in school isn't bad. Caring about how you look isn't bad. Having a presence online isn't bad. But when those things become the *foundation* of your identity — when your sense of who you are rises and falls with a grade, a comment, a like, a look in the mirror — you're building your life on something that will shift under your feet every single time.

You know this already. You've felt it. That feeling when you post something and it doesn't get the response you expected, and suddenly you feel small. That feeling when you ace an exam and for about forty-five minutes you feel great, and then someone else did better and now you feel average. That feeling when a friend group shifts and suddenly you're not sure where you belong, and it's like part of your identity just got deleted.

That's not a you problem. That's a *foundation* problem.

---

So if all of that is shaky ground, what isn't?

I want to suggest something to you, and I know it might sound simple at first, but stay with me — because I think it's actually the most radical thing you'll hear all week.

**You are not something you have to construct. You are someone you already are.**

Most of the anxiety around identity comes from this idea that you have to *build* yourself — that you're a blank canvas and the pressure is on you to become something impressive, something worthy, something enough. And if you don't? Then you've failed.

But what if that's the wrong starting point entirely?

What if who you are isn't something you earn? What if it's something you *discover*?

There's a difference between building an identity and uncovering one. Building is exhausting. It means performing, comparing, measuring. Uncovering is different. It means paying attention — to what moves you, to what breaks your heart, to what lights you up when nobody's watching, to the values you hold even when they cost you something.

Your identity isn't your stats. It's your substance. It's not what you *do*. It's what you carry inside you — your convictions, your compassion, the way you treat people when there's nothing in it for you.

And here's what I really believe: you are someone of inherent, non-negotiable worth. Not because of what you've achieved. Not because of what you look like. Not because of who follows you. But because you are a human being with a depth and a dignity that no algorithm can measure and no failure can erase.

That's not a participation trophy. That's the truth.

---

Now let me talk about purpose for a minute, because identity and purpose are connected. Once you start to settle into who you actually are — not who the internet says you should be — you start to ask a different question. Not "how do I get people to notice me?" but "what am I here to do?"

And I want to be honest with you: I don't think purpose is something most people figure out at sixteen. Or twenty. Or sometimes even forty. And that's okay. The pressure to have your life figured out right now is a lie. It's a lie sold to you by a culture that monetises your anxiety.

But here's what I *do* think you can do right now, today, this week: you can pay attention to what I call your "purpose clues."

Purpose clues are the moments when something resonates deep in your chest. When you help someone and it doesn't feel like obligation — it feels like *rightness*. When you're working on something and you lose track of time. When you see an injustice and something in you says, "That's not okay, and I want to do something about it." When you're in a conversation and you feel fully yourself — not performing, not filtering, just *present*.

Those moments are data. Collect them. They're telling you something.

Purpose isn't usually a lightning bolt. It's a trail of breadcrumbs. And you find it by walking, not by standing still and waiting for a sign.

---

So let me land this with some things you can actually do. Not abstract ideas. Real things. This week.

**One: Audit your mirrors.** What are you using to measure your worth right now? Be honest. Is it likes? Grades? A relationship? Your body? I'm not asking you to delete your apps or stop caring about school. I'm asking you to notice when those things start to *own* you — when a bad result or a quiet notification makes you feel like you're less. When you catch that happening, name it. Say to yourself, "That's a mirror, but it's not the truth."

**Two: Write down three things that are true about you that have nothing to do with achievement or appearance.** Not "I'm good at football." Not "people say I'm pretty." Deeper than that. Maybe it's "I'm the person my friends call when they're struggling." Maybe it's "I care about fairness." Maybe it's "I notice people who are left out." Put those somewhere you'll see them. Those are closer to the real you than anything on your profile.

**Three: Do one thing this week that's just for you.** Not for a grade. Not for content. Not to impress anyone. Something that feeds the version of you that exists when nobody's watching. Read something. Make something. Go for a walk without your phone. Sit with your own thoughts for twenty minutes. I know that sounds almost countercultural. That's because it is. And that's why it matters.

**Four: Ask someone you trust — a parent, a mentor, a friend who's honest with you — "What do you see in me that I might not see in myself?"** This takes guts. But other people often see our gifts and our substance more clearly than we do, because we're too busy comparing ourselves to everyone else to notice.

---

I want to close with this.

You are living in a world that is louder than any generation before you has ever had to deal with. The volume of opinions, images, expectations, comparisons — it's relentless. And I'm not going to stand here and pretend that's easy, because it's not.

But underneath all that noise, there is a you that is real. Not curated. Not filtered. Not performing. A you that has something to offer the world that nobody else can, because nobody else is you. Not in a cheesy, motivational-poster way. In a true way.

You don't have to have it all figured out. You don't have to be the best at anything. You don't have to earn your right to take up space in this world.

You just have to be willing to stop building a version of yourself for other people and start discovering the one that's already there.

That's the work. And it's worth it.

---

*Thanks for listening.*

Now imagine that every external measure — likes, grades, other people's opinions — is a magnet. Hold enough magnets up to a compass and the needle spins wildly. It can't find north. Not because north has disappeared, but because there's too much interference.

Now let me talk about purpose, because identity and purpose are connected. Once you start to settle into who you actually are — not who the internet says you should be — you start to ask a different question. Not "how do I get people to notice me?" but "what am I here to do?"

But here's what you *can* do right now: you can start collecting what I call your **purpose clues**. Think of them as breadcrumbs.

Purpose clues are those moments when something resonates deep in your chest. When you help someone and it doesn't feel like obligation — it feels like *rightness*. When you're working on something and you lose track of time. When you see an injustice and something in you says, *that's not okay, and I want to do something about it.* When you're in a conversation and you feel fully yourself — not performing, not filtering, just present.

Those moments are data. They're breadcrumbs on a trail, and your compass is pointing you toward them. Collect them. Write them down. They're telling you something about who you are and where you're headed.

Purpose isn't usually a lightning bolt. It's a trail you find by walking, not by standing still and waiting for a sign.

---

Not abstract ideas. Real things. Starting tomorrow.

Pick the two or three mirrors you check most often, and for each one, ask yourself two questions: *What event makes this feel like the truth about me?* and *What would still be true about me even if this mirror broke?* When you catch a bad result or a quiet notification making you feel like you're less, name it. Say to yourself: *That's a mirror, not the truth.*

**Two: Write down three things that are true about you that have nothing to do with achievement or appearance.** Not "I'm good at football." Not "people say I'm pretty." Deeper. Here are some prompts to get you started: *I notice when someone's being left out. I care about fairness. I'm the person my friends call when things fall apart. I feel things deeply and I'm not ashamed of that.* Put those three truths somewhere you'll see them — your lock screen, your mirror, a note in your pocket. Those are closer to the real you than anything on your profile.

**Three: Do one thing this week that's just for you.** Not for a grade. Not for content. Not to impress anyone. Something that feeds the version of you that exists when nobody's watching. Read something for pleasure. Make something with your hands. Go for a fifteen-minute walk without your phone. Sit with your own thoughts and see what surfaces. I know that sounds almost countercultural. It is. That's why it matters.

**Four: Ask someone you trust one question.** A parent, a mentor, a friend who's genuinely honest with you. Here's a script if you need one: *"Hey, I'm trying to understand myself beyond grades and appearances. What do you see in me that I might not see?"* This takes guts. But other people often see our substance more clearly than we do, because we're too busy comparing ourselves to notice.

And one more small thing: at the end of each day this week, take thirty seconds to ask yourself, *When did I feel most like myself today?* Just notice. That's a breadcrumb. Follow it.

---

Before I close — if any of this has stirred up something heavy, if you're in a place where you're not just questioning your identity but questioning whether you matter at all, please talk to someone. A parent, a counsellor, a teacher, a helpline. What you're carrying is real, and it deserves more than a talk in a room can give. You are not alone in that, and asking for help is one of the bravest things a person can do.

---

I want to leave you with this.

You are living in a world louder than any generation before you has had to navigate. The volume of opinions, images, expectations, comparisons — it's relentless. I'm not going to pretend that's easy.

But underneath all that noise, your compass is still there. Not curated. Not filtered. Not performing. Pointing toward a you that has something to offer the world that nobody else can — because nobody else is you. Not in a motivational-poster way. In a true way.

You don't have to have it all figured out. You don't have to be the best at anything. You don't have to earn your right to take up space.

You just have to be curious about who you're becoming — and willing to follow the breadcrumbs.

So here's your invitation. Say this to yourself — not out loud if that's weird, but somewhere inside: *I am more than what I show the world. And I'm learning who I am by what I find when I stop performing.*

Then do one thing this week that isn't for a grade or a post. See what happens.

That's the work. And it's worth it.

---

*Thanks for listening.*

# You Are Not Your Highlight Reel

---

So I want to start with a question, and I want you to actually think about it — not just wait politely until I move on.

If you lost your phone tomorrow — like, permanently, gone forever, no backup — and with it, every photo, every post, every conversation, every follower count… would you still know who you are?

Most of us would say yes. Obviously. Of course I'd still be me.

But I think if we're honest, something in that scenario makes us uneasy. And that unease is worth paying attention to.

---

## The Bio Problem

Here's something I've noticed. If you ask someone your age — or honestly, someone my age — "Who are you?", most people answer with a list. I'm a student. I'm a swimmer. I'm someone with 2,000 followers. I'm the funny one in my friend group. I'm someone who gets good grades. I'm someone who doesn't get good grades and has made that part of my personality too.

We build these little bios for ourselves, like we're writing an Instagram profile for our souls. And the problem isn't that any of those things are bad. Being a swimmer is great. Being funny is a gift. Working hard at school matters. The problem is what happens when you build your entire identity on things that can be taken away.

Because they can be. All of them.

You get injured, and suddenly you're not an athlete anymore. Your grades slip, and the "smart kid" label peels off. A friendship group shifts — the way they do, sometimes overnight, for reasons no one fully explains — and the role you played in it disappears. You post something you thought was brave or funny, and it gets three likes, and you feel like you shrank.

If who you are is only what you do, what you look like, or what other people reflect back at you, then your identity is essentially on loan. You don't own it. Other people do. Circumstances do.

And that is an exhausting way to live.

---

## The Pressure No One Talks About Enough

I don't think adults always understand the specific kind of pressure you're under. It's not just peer pressure in the old-fashioned sense — someone offering you a cigarette behind the gym. It's something more ambient than that. It's the pressure to perform a version of yourself — constantly, publicly, and convincingly.

You're supposed to have a personal brand. You're supposed to know what you want to do with your life at sixteen. You're supposed to look effortless while trying incredibly hard. You're supposed to have opinions, but not the wrong ones. You're supposed to be authentic — but only in a curated, aesthetically pleasing way.

That's not authenticity. That's a performance of authenticity, and it's more tiring than just being fake, because at least when you're being fake, you know it.

Here's what I want to say to you as clearly as I can: **you are not behind.** You are not failing at being yourself. The fact that you don't have it all figured out is not a sign that something is wrong with you. It's a sign that you're a human being in the middle of becoming, which is exactly what you should be.

---

## So Where Does Identity Actually Come From?

If it doesn't come from your achievements, your appearance, or your follower count, then where?

I think real identity — the kind that holds up when everything else shakes — comes from something deeper than what you do. It comes from what you value. What you love. What you're willing to be honest about. How you treat people when no one's recording it.

Let me put it differently. There's a version of you that exists when no one is watching. When you're not performing for a teacher, a coach, a crush, a camera. When you're just… you. Sitting with your own thoughts. Reacting to something that moves you. Choosing to be kind when it costs you something. Choosing to tell the truth when a lie would be easier.

That version of you is not less real than the public one. It might be the most real version there is.

Identity isn't something you build like a brand. It's something you discover — and it's discovered slowly, through experience, through failure, through the kind of quiet moments that never make it onto anyone's story.

You find out who you are when you stand up for someone and your voice shakes. You find out who you are when you sit with a friend who's hurting and you don't try to fix it, you just stay. You find out who you are when you admit you were wrong. You find out who you are in the choices that no one applauds.

---

## Purpose Isn't a Career Plan

While we're at it, let's talk about purpose, because I think it gets misunderstood too.

People will ask you, "What do you want to be when you grow up?" as if purpose is a job title. As if you need to pick a destination on a map and walk toward it in a straight line.

But purpose isn't a destination. It's a direction. It's not "I'm going to be a doctor" or "I'm going to be a filmmaker." It's more like: I care about justice. I'm drawn to beauty. I want to understand how things work. I come alive when I'm helping people. I notice things other people walk past.

Those instincts — the things that light you up, the things that break your heart, the things you can't stop thinking about — those are clues. You don't need to have them all decoded by the time you're eighteen. You just need to pay attention to them.

Purpose isn't about having a five-year plan. It's about being awake to your own life. It's about noticing what matters to you and having the courage to move toward it, even when it doesn't look impressive on paper.

Some of the most purposeful people I know couldn't have predicted where they ended up. They just kept following what was true, one decision at a time.

---

## Four Things to Try This Week

Okay. I don't want to leave you with just ideas. I want to give you something to actually do. So here are four small things — pick one, pick all four, I don't care — but try at least one before next week.

**1. Audit your inputs.**
Spend ten minutes scrolling through whoever you follow on social media, and ask yourself honestly: does this person make me want to be more myself, or does this person make me feel like I'm not enough? You're allowed to mute, unfollow, and curate what shapes your thinking. That's not being sensitive. That's being smart.

**2. Write down three things you value — not three things you're good at.**
There's a difference. You might be good at maths but value compassion. You might be average at sport but value courage. Your values are closer to your identity than your abilities are. Know what they are.

**3. Do one thing this week that no one will see.**
Write a note to someone. Help with something at home without being asked. Spend twenty minutes doing something you love with no intention of documenting it. Practice being someone who doesn't need an audience to exist.

**4. Ask someone you trust: "What do you see in me?"**
Not "Am I cool?" Not "Do people like me?" But genuinely — what do you see? Sometimes other people can name things in us that we can't see in ourselves yet. Let someone reflect you back — not a screen, a person.

---

## One Last Thing

You are living in a world that is constantly trying to turn you into a product — something to be optimised, branded, and measured by engagement. And I'm not saying that world is all bad. But I am saying it will not tell you who you are. It will only tell you who it wants you to be.

You are not your grades. You are not your body. You are not your worst moment or your best post. You are not the number next to your name on any platform.

You are a person — complex, unfinished, full of contradictions, and more interesting than any version of yourself you could curate.

The world doesn't need your highlight reel. It needs you — the real, stumbling, searching, brave version of you that's sitting in this room right now.

Don't rush to become someone. You already are someone.

Now go find out who.

---

## The Three Boxes

Here's what I see happening—and tell me if I'm wrong.

From the time you're about thirteen, the world starts handing you three boxes and asking you to climb inside one. Sometimes all three.

**Box one: What you achieve.** Your grades. Your sport. Your ranking. Your university prospects. The question adults love to ask—*"So what do you want to do when you grow up?"*—as if you're supposed to have a career trajectory mapped out while you're still figuring out how to do your own laundry. Achievement tells you that you are what you produce. That your worth is your output. **Box two: How you look.** This one is relentless. It's not just billboards and magazines anymore; it's filters that reshape your jaw in real time. It's the ugly-pretty cycle of trends that change every six months so you can never quite arrive. It's comparison at a speed and scale that no previous generation of teenagers has ever had to deal with. And I want to be honest about that—what you're navigating is genuinely harder than what I navigated at your age. The pressure is more constant, more visual, and more public.

**Box three: Your social presence.** Your follower count. Your likes. Who tagged you. Who didn't. The invisible algorithm of social belonging that runs twenty-four hours a day. This box tells you that you are who other people perceive you to be. That identity is a performance, and the audience gets to vote.

Now here's the thing about boxes: they're easy to measure. That's why we like them. Achievement gives you numbers. Appearance gives you mirrors. Social media gives you metrics. And when you're at a stage of life where everything feels uncertain—when your body is changing, your friendships are shifting, your future is a blank page—anything that feels measurable feels *safe*.

But those boxes are also fragile. They break. You get a bad result, and the achievement box collapses. You have a rough skin week, and the appearance box wobbles. Someone screenshots something you said, and the social box catches fire. If your identity lives in those boxes, then your identity is only ever as stable as your last win, your last photo, your last interaction.

That's an exhausting way to live. And I think a lot of you are already tired.

---

## The Deeper Thing

So what's the alternative?

I'm not going to stand here and pretend I have a neat formula. "Five steps to knowing who you really are!" That would be dishonest, and you'd see right through it.

But I will tell you something I wish someone had told me at your age.

**You are not a product to be optimised. You are a person to be known.**

There's a difference. A product is evaluated by its performance. A person is valued by their existence. A product becomes obsolete. A person has inherent dignity that doesn't expire, fluctuate, or depend on an audience.

Your identity—the real one, the one underneath the boxes—isn't something you build like a brand. It's something you *uncover*. It's already there. It's in the things you care about when nobody's watching. It's in the questions that keep you up at night. It's in the way you treat people who can't do anything for you. It's in the stuff that makes you laugh so hard you can't breathe—not the performative laugh, the real one. It's in your convictions, your curiosity, your kindness, your weird, specific, irreplaceable way of seeing the world.

That identity doesn't need a filter. It doesn't need validation. It doesn't need a thousand likes. It needs *attention*. Your attention. The patient, unglamorous work of getting to know yourself—not the version of yourself that performs well, but the version that exists when the performance stops.

And here's what I've learned, slowly and sometimes painfully: purpose flows from that kind of identity. Not the other way around. We think we need to find our *purpose* and then we'll know who we are. But it actually works in reverse. When you start to know who you are—what you value, what moves you, what you're willing to be uncomfortable for—purpose starts to show up. Not always as a grand calling. Sometimes just as a quiet sense of direction. A feeling of *yes, this matters. This is worth my time. This is worth my life.*

Purpose isn't a destination you arrive at. It's a direction you grow into. And it usually starts small. It starts with paying attention.

---

## This Week

Okay. I said I'd give you something practical, so here it is. Four things. Small ones. You could start tonight.

**One: Audit your inputs.** Not in a dramatic, delete-everything way. Just notice. For the next few days, pay attention to how you feel *after* you scroll, after you compare, after you consume. **Three: Do one thing this week that no one will see.** Write something you won't post. Help someone without documenting it. Spend an hour on something you love without any thought of whether it's impressive or productive. Practice being yourself without an audience. It will feel strange. That strangeness is important—it's the distance between who you are and who you perform, and it's worth closing.

**Four: Talk to someone who knows you.** Not your followers. Not your group chat. One person. A friend, a parent, a mentor, a sibling—someone who has seen you at your worst and still chose to stay. ---

I know some of you are sitting here thinking, *That's easy to say. You don't know what my school is like. You don't know what my home is like. You don't know what I'm dealing with.*

You're right. I don't.

But I know this: every person in this room is in the middle of becoming someone. And the pressure to become someone *impressive* is so loud that it can drown out the quieter, more important invitation—to become someone *real*.

The world doesn't need another curated highlight reel. It needs people who know who they are and have the courage to live from that place. People who are kind when it costs them something. People who are honest when it's uncomfortable. People who don't need applause to do the right thing.

You don't have to have it all figured out. You're not supposed to—not at fifteen, not at twenty-five, honestly not ever. But you can start paying attention. You can start asking better questions. You can start building an identity that doesn't collapse when the Wi-Fi goes out.

You are more than your grades. You are more than your face. You are more than your feed.

And the sooner you believe that, the sooner you'll be free to actually live.
