Here is the revised version of the talk. It incorporates the feedback by unifying the metaphors (Cursor/Mirror/Anchor), adding specific "micro-moments" of teen life to increase relatability, and softening the instructional tone to be more conversational and less prescriptive.

I have written this for a **general Christian youth group context**, as this is the most common setting for this prompt, but the language focuses on "Belovedness" and "Grace" in a way that is accessible to seekers or kids who aren't sure what they believe yet.

***

**Title:** The Cursor, The Mirror, and The Anchor
**Audience:** High School (14–18)
**Tone:** Conversational, vulnerable, encouraging
**Time:** Approx. 20–25 minutes

***

### I. The Blinking Cursor

I want to start with a specific feeling. You know the one.

It’s 11:30 PM. You’re lying in bed. The room is dark, but your face is lit up by that blue glow. You’ve just downloaded a new app, or maybe you’re updating a profile, and you get to that little text box.

*Bio.*

And there’s that little vertical line. The cursor. Blinking. On. Off. On. Off.

It’s waiting. You have 150 characters to explain your entire existence. What do you type?
Do you put your school? Your sport? "Varsity Soccer"?
Do you try to be funny? "Professional napper"?
Do you use a quote from a song that makes you seem deep, but not *too* deep, because you don’t want to look like you’re trying too hard?
Maybe you just put the flag of your country and a coffee cup emoji and call it a day.

It’s a tiny box on a screen, but for some reason, it makes your stomach drop. Why?

Because that blinking cursor is asking the biggest, scariest question a human being can ask: *Who are you?*

And the unspoken follow-up question is: *And do you matter?*

Tonight, I want to talk about that cursor. I want to talk about the exhausting hustle to build a version of ourselves that looks good to the world, and why that hustle is burning us out. And then, I want to offer you an anchor—a way to find out who you are that doesn’t depend on your grades, your mirror, or your notifications.

### II. The Mirror and The Traps

If we’re honest, most of us are trying to answer the "Who am I?" question by building a resume. We look for things that make us feel solid. Usually, we fall into one of three traps.

**Trap #1: The Performance Trap (I am what I achieve)**
This is the voice that says you are only as valuable as your last report card or your last game.

We live in a world that is obsessed with stats. We track our steps, we track our sleep, we track our followers. And somewhere along the way, it’s easy to start believing that *we* are the data.

I know some of you feel this in your chest every time you refresh the grade portal. You see an 'A' and you feel safe. You see a 'C' and you feel like the floor just fell out.

I knew a guy in high school—let’s call him Mike. Mike was a baseball phenomenon. Pitcher. It was his whole bio. It was how everyone introduced him. "This is Mike, the pitcher." Then, junior year, he tore his shoulder. Surgery, rehab, the works. He couldn't play. And I watched him go into a tailspin, not just because he missed the sport, but because he felt like he had ceased to exist. He had confused *what he did* with *who he was*.

The problem with anchoring your identity in achievement is simple: What happens when you fail? If you are the straight-A student, who are you when you bomb the final? If you’re the athlete, who are you when you’re injured?

**Trap #2: The Mirror Trap (I am how I look)**
This is the pressure to be an image. And look, I’m not going to give you the "looks don't matter" speech. In our world, they do. But it’s gotten messy.

None of the adults before you had to grow up with a high-definition camera in their pocket 24/7. You don’t just live your life; you have to curate it. You know that feeling when you open your camera app and it’s accidentally on the front-facing mode? It ruins your mood for twenty minutes.

There is massive pressure to have the right "aesthetic." To look effortless—even though we all know it took forty-five minutes, three outfit changes, and good lighting to look that "effortless."

The danger here is that your body becomes a billboard rather than a home. You start treating yourself like a product to be marketed. And just like the Performance Trap, this is fragile. What happens when you have a bad breakout? What happens when you don’t fit the trend? If your value is tied to the mirror, you will always be insecure, because there will always be someone with a better filter.

**Trap #3: The Approval Trap (I am what people say about me)**
This is the big one. In the old days, you only had to worry about what the 30 kids in your homeroom thought of you. Now, you have to worry about what 500 followers think.

We outsource our self-esteem to the crowd. You post something, put the phone down, and then pick it up forty seconds later. *Did it land? Did they like it?*

It’s a head game. When the numbers go up, you feel untouchable. When the numbers stay flat, or the group chat goes silent after you send a text, you feel like trash. You start wondering, *Am I annoying? Do they actually like me?*

### III. Drifting in the Storm

Here is the hard truth about those three traps: They are all based on things that change.

*   Your grades will fluctuate.
*   Your looks will change.
*   People’s opinions will shift.

If your identity is built on these things, you aren't anchored. You’re drifting. You will live in a constant state of low-grade anxiety, constantly hustling to keep the numbers up, constantly defending your spot.

I talk to so many of you, and the word I hear most often isn't "excited" or "hopeful." It’s "tired."

You are tired of the hustle. You are tired of the performance. You are tired of trying to be "enough."

So, what is the alternative?

### IV. The Anchor: Received Identity

The alternative is a shift in your mindset. It’s moving from an **Achieved Identity** to a **Received Identity**.

An *Achieved Identity* is one you have to earn. You build it, brick by brick, with your wit, your abs, and your GPA. It’s heavy. You have to carry it everywhere, and you’re terrified of dropping it.

A *Received Identity* is different. It is the belief that your value is not something you earn; it is something you already possess.

Now, I know what some of you are thinking. You’re thinking, *"Okay, that sounds nice, but if I stop trying to achieve, won’t I become a slacker? If I’m already ‘enough,’ why study? Why practice?"*

That is a valid fear. But here is the secret: Received Identity doesn’t kill your ambition. It heals it.

Think about a diamond. If you find a diamond in the mud, covered in dirt, is it valuable? Yes. Why? Does it *do* anything? No. It just sits there. It is valuable because of *what it is*, not because of what it does. Its value is inherent. The mud doesn't change the molecular structure of the gem.

In the Christian faith, we have a name for this. It’s called being a **Beloved Child of God**.

The core message of Jesus isn't "Do better and I'll love you." It is, "I love you, now go live like it."

When you understand that you are the diamond—that you are made in the image of the Creator, that you are known and loved before you ever score a goal or pass a test—it becomes your **Anchor**.

An anchor doesn’t stop the storm. The waves still crash. You will still fail tests. You will still get your heart broken. You will still have bad hair days. But an anchor keeps you from drifting out to sea.

When you are anchored in a Received Identity:
*   You can get a 'C' on a test and think, *"I need to study harder,"* instead of, *"I am a failure."*
*   You can see a bad photo of yourself and think, *"Not my best angle,"* instead of, *"I am ugly."*
*   You can strive for greatness, not to *prove* you matter, but because you’re free to enjoy the game.

### V. Reframing Purpose: The "Who" before the "What"

When you stop obsessing over the cursor—trying to type in the perfect description of yourself—you are finally free to look away from the screen and look at the world.

This changes how you find your purpose.

When you are insecure, you use your purpose to prove yourself. You use your future career to scream, "Look at me! I’m important!"

But when you are anchored, your purpose shifts. It stops being about *impressing* people and starts being about *blessing* people.

I want to challenge you to stop asking, "What do I want to be when I grow up?" That’s just a question about a job title.
Start asking, "What kind of person do I want to be?" and "What problem do I want to help solve?"

Purpose isn't a title. Purpose is contribution. And you don’t have to wait until you’re 25 to find it.
*   Maybe you’re the friend who actually listens when everyone else is just waiting for their turn to talk. That is a purpose.
*   Maybe you’re the guy who notices the kid sitting alone in the cafeteria and pulls up a chair. That is a purpose.
*   Maybe you’re an artist. Your purpose isn't to get famous; it’s to make something beautiful that brings joy to a stressed-out world.

Real purpose is found at the intersection of *what you love* and *what the world needs*.

### VI. Practical Takeaways

I don’t want you to just leave here with a nice idea. I want you to leave with some tools. Here are three ways to drop the anchor this week.

**1. The "Feed Audit"**
Take ten minutes tonight. Scroll through your "Following" list on Instagram or TikTok. Ask yourself one question for every account: *Does following this person make me feel capable and inspired, or does it make me feel inadequate and jealous?*
If an account makes you feel like you aren't enough—even if it’s a friend, even if it’s a celebrity—mute them. You don't have to unfollow if that causes drama, just mute. Protect your headspace. You cannot build a healthy identity if you are constantly feeding your brain evidence that you’re broken.

**2. The "Two Lists" Exercise**
If you are someone who stresses about achievement, try this. At the end of the week, make two lists.
*   **List A:** What I Did. (This is where you put your grades, your goals, your chores).
*   **List B:** Who I Was. (Did you help your little brother? Were you honest when it was hard? Were you a good friend?)
Look at List B. That is the list that actually defines you. Remind yourself that List A is just stuff you *did*. List B is who you *are*.

**3. The "Secret Service" Shift**
The quickest way to kill the ego and find purpose is to serve, but there’s a catch: You can’t tell anyone.
This week, do one thing for someone that cannot benefit you in any way.
*   Take out the trash without your parents asking (and don't mention it).
*   Send an encouraging DM to someone who seems down (and don't post a screenshot of how nice you are).
*   Clean up a mess you didn't make at school.
Notice how that feels. It feels good, not because you got a reward, but because you used your strength to help someone else. That is the spark of real purpose.

### Conclusion

Being a teenager right now is hard. The pressure to define yourself, to brand yourself, and to prove yourself is heavier than it has ever been.

But you do not have to play that game. You can step off the treadmill.

Next time you see that blinking cursor, and you feel that anxiety rising, take a breath. Remember the Anchor.

You are not your GPA. You are not your followers. You are not your varsity jacket or your lack of one.

You are a person of infinite worth. You are a diamond, even in the mud. You are loved.

That is who you are. Everything else is just details.

Thanks for listening.

It is a tiny, digital text box, but for many of us, it causes a massive amount of physical anxiety. Why? Because that blinking cursor is asking the biggest, scariest question a human being can ask: *Who are you?*

And the unspoken follow-up question is even heavier: *And do you matter?*

Now, I’m a bit older than you. When I was your age, we didn’t have the bio box. We had yearbooks and cafeteria tables. But I remember that exact same pressure. I remember walking into the lunchroom and scanning the room, trying to figure out where I fit. Was I the funny guy? The smart kid? The athlete? The invisible one? The technology has changed, but the panic hasn't. We are all desperate to define ourselves before someone else defines us.

Tonight, I want to talk about that blinking cursor. I want to talk about the exhausting hustle to build a version of ourselves that looks good to the world, and why that hustle is burning us out. And then, I want to offer you a way to break the cycle. A way to think about your identity and your purpose that doesn’t depend on how many likes you get, what your GPA is, or what you see in the mirror.

**II. The Three Traps of Modern Identity**

If we look closely at how we try to answer that question—*Who am I?*—most of us are building our identities on three specific things. I call them the Three Traps. They look solid from the outside, but they are actually incredibly fragile.

**Trap #1: I am what I achieve.**
This is the "Performance Trap." You know this voice. This is the internal monologue that says you are only as valuable as your last report card, your last goal, or your college acceptance letter.

We live in a culture that is absolutely obsessed with metrics. We measure everything. We track our steps, we track our sleep, we track our calories, we track our grades to the second decimal point. And somewhere along the way, we started believing that *we* are the data. We think we are the sum of our stats.

The problem with anchoring your identity in achievement is simple: What happens when you fail? And you *will* fail. If you are the "Straight-A Student," who are you when you get a C in Chemistry? If you are the "Star Athlete," who are you when you tear your ACL?

I knew a guy in high school named Mike. Mike was a baseball phenomenon. It wasn’t just a hobby; it was his bio. It was how everyone introduced him: "This is Mike, the pitcher." It was his ticket to college, his ticket to popularity, his ticket to worth. Then, junior year, he blew out his shoulder. I remember seeing him a few weeks after the surgery. He wasn't just bummed out that he couldn't play; he was in a tailspin of depression. He looked hollow. He hadn't just lost a sport; he felt like he had ceased to exist. He had confused *what he did* with *who he was*.

**Trap #2: I am how I look.**
This is the "Mirror Trap." Look, I’m not going to stand here and pretend appearance doesn’t matter in our society. It does. But we have taken it to a level of psychological warfare.

You are the first generation in history to carry a high-definition camera, a broadcasting studio, and a magazine editing suite in your pocket. You don’t just live your lives; you curate them. We edit. We filter. We pose.

There is a massive pressure to have the right "aesthetic." To look effortless—even though we all know it took forty-five minutes, three outfit changes, and thirty-seven takes to look that "effortless." The danger here is that your body becomes a billboard rather than a home. You start treating yourself like a product to be marketed rather than a person to be known.

And just like the Performance Trap, this is fragile. What happens when you have a bad breakout? What happens when you don’t fit the trend? If your value is tied to your appearance, you will always be insecure, because there will always be someone with a better filter, a better angle, or better genetics.

**Trap #3: I am what people say about me.**
This is the "Popularity Trap." In the old days, you only had to worry about what the 30 kids in your homeroom thought of you. Now, you have to worry about what 500 followers think, or strangers on the internet who don't even know your last name.

We have begun to outsource our self-esteem to the crowd. We post something and then check the phone five minutes later. Then ten minutes. *Did it land? Did they like it? Am I funny? Am I cool?* It’s a dopamine loop. When the numbers go up, we feel like gods. When the numbers go down, or when someone leaves a snarky comment, we feel like trash. We let an algorithm determine our worth.

**III. The House Built on Sand**

Here is the hard truth about those three traps: They are all based on things that can be taken away.

Achievement can be lost through injury or failure. Appearance fades or changes. Popularity is fickle—people love you one day and cancel you the next.

If your identity is built on these things, you are building a house on sand. You will live in a constant state of low-grade anxiety, constantly defending your turf, constantly hustling to keep the numbers up. It is exhausting.

I talk to so many of you, and when I ask how you’re doing, the word I hear most often isn't "excited" or "hopeful." It’s "tired." You are tired of the hustle. You are tired of the performance. You are tired of trying to be someone worth loving.

So, what is the alternative? How do we stop the cursor from blinking?

**IV. Received Identity vs. Achieved Identity**

The alternative is a shift in your mindset. It’s moving from an **Achieved Identity** to a **Received Identity**.

An *Achieved Identity* is one you have to earn. You have to build it, brick by brick, with your grades, your abs, and your wit. It’s heavy. You have to carry it everywhere, and if you drop it, it shatters.

A *Received Identity* is different. It is the belief that your value is not something you earn; it is something you already possess. It is given to you.

Think about a diamond. Imagine I went into the backyard, dug a hole, and found a raw diamond. It’s covered in mud. It’s dirty. It’s not shiny. Now, ask yourself: Is it valuable?

Yes.

Why? Does it *do* anything? No. Is it performing? No. It’s just sitting there in the dirt. It is valuable because of *what it is*, not because of what it does. Its value is inherent. It’s built-in. If I wash the mud off, I haven’t made the diamond more valuable; I’ve just revealed the value that was already there.

You need to understand that your value as a human being is inherent. You are the diamond. The grades, the sports, the likes—that’s just the polish. But the value is in the stone.

*(Theological Anchor)*: In the Christian faith, we believe this is because you are made in the image of God. You are valuable because the Creator of the universe decided the world needed one of *you*. He didn't create you to be a product; He created you to be a person. Your identity isn't "High Achiever" or "Influencer," it is "Beloved Child." You don't have to earn that. You just have to receive it.

When you ground your identity in who you *are* (Received) rather than what you *do* (Achieved), the pressure releases. You can still play sports, but you don’t have to win to be worthy. You can still post on Instagram, but you don’t need the likes to feel seen. You can strive for good grades, but a 'C' doesn't mean you are a failure of a person.

You are the Diamond, not the mud.

**V. Reframing Purpose: The "Who" before the "What"**

Now, I know what you’re thinking. "Okay, that sounds nice, very poetic. But I still have to apply to college. I still need a job. I still need a purpose."

Absolutely. But here is the secret: You will never find your true purpose if you are looking for it to save you.

When you are insecure about your identity, you use your purpose—your career, your hobbies—to prove you matter. You use your future job to scream at the world, "Look at me! I’m important!"

But when your identity is secure—when you know you are valuable regardless of what you do—your purpose changes. It stops being about *impressing* people and starts being about *blessing* people.

I want you to stop asking, "What do I want to be when I grow up?" That question is about a job title. It’s about a paycheck.
Start asking, "What kind of person do I want to be?" and "What problem do I want to help solve?"

Purpose isn't a title. Purpose is contribution.

When you aren't staring in the mirror obsessing over your flaws, you are free to look out the window and see the needs of the world.
*   Maybe you’re great at listening. Your purpose right now isn't to be a therapist; it's to be the friend who actually puts their phone down and listens when everyone else is talking.
*   Maybe you’re great at math. Your purpose isn't just to get an A; it’s to notice the kid next to you who is drowning in calculus and offer to help.
*   Maybe you’re an artist. Your purpose isn't to get famous; it’s to make something beautiful that brings a little bit of joy to a dark world.

Real purpose is found at the intersection of *what you love* and *what the world needs*. And the best news? You can start living that right now. You don’t have to wait until you’re 25. You don't have to wait until you have the degree. You can live that purpose in the hallway tomorrow morning.

**VI. Practical Takeaways**

I don’t want you to just leave here with a nice feeling that fades by the time you get to the car. I want you to leave with some tools. Here are three things you can do this week to shift from an Achieved Identity to a Received Identity.

**1. The Social Media Audit**
I want you to take ten minutes tonight before you go to sleep. Open your phone and scroll through your "Following" list. Ask yourself one specific question for every account: *Does following this person make me feel inspired and capable, or does it make me feel inadequate and jealous?*
If an account makes you feel like you aren't enough—even if it’s a friend, even if it’s a celebrity, even if it's an "inspirational" account—mute them or unfollow them. Be ruthless. Protect your headspace. You cannot build a healthy identity if you are constantly feeding your brain images that tell you you’re broken.

**2. Separate Your "Do" from Your "Who"**
Next time you fail a test, miss a goal, or get rejected (because it will happen), I want you to physically say this out loud. Do it in your room, in your car, wherever. Say: *"That is what I did. That is not who I am."*
Create a mental gap between your performance and your personhood. Failure is an event, not a person. Don't let the failure stick to your identity.

**3. The Service Shift**
The quickest way to kill the ego and find purpose is to serve. This week, do one thing for someone that cannot benefit you in any way. And here is the catch: You cannot tell anyone. No posting it on your story. No humble-bragging about it.
Take out the trash without being asked. Help a younger sibling with homework. Sit with the kid who sits alone at lunch.
Notice how that feels. It feels good, not because you got a reward, but because you used your strength to help someone else. That is the spark of real purpose.

**Conclusion**

Being a teenager right now is hard. The pressure to define yourself, to brand yourself, and to prove yourself is heavier than it has ever been.

But I want you to hear this: You do not have to play that game. You can step off the treadmill.

If you are tired of the hustle, if you are tired of trying to curate a life that looks perfect, you can stop. You can drop the act.

You are not your GPA. You are not your followers. You are not your skin clearing up or breaking out. You are not your varsity jacket or your lack of one.

You are a person of infinite worth. That is your anchor. And once you are anchored, you can weather any storm, and you can set sail for a life that isn't just about looking good, but about doing good.

Thanks for listening.

If your identity is built on achievement, appearance, or approval, you are building a house on sand. You will live in a constant state of low-grade anxiety, constantly defending your turf, constantly hustling to keep the numbers up.

It is exhausting.

A *Received Identity* is different. It is the belief that your value is not something you earn; it is something you already possess.

It is valuable because of *what it is*, not because of what it does. Its value is inherent. It’s built-in. It doesn't need to perform to be worth something.

*(Note: If this is a faith-based group, insert this theological anchor here: "In the Christian faith, we believe this is because you are made in the image of God. You are not your GPA. You are not your followers. You are not your skin clearing up or breaking out. You are not your varsity jacket or your lack of one.

**Title:** The un-Selfie: Finding Out Who You Are When the Screen goes Dark

**(Speaker walks out, maybe holding a phone, looking at it casually before putting it away in a back pocket. No podium if possible. Just open, honest body language.)**

Hey everyone.

I want to start tonight with a question that sounds simple, but is actually terrifying. It’s a question you face every time you download a new app, join a new team, or walk into a party where you only know one person.

Here it is: **"Tell me a little bit about yourself."**

Or, if we’re talking online: **"Write your Bio."**

It’s just a blank text box, right? 150 characters. But suddenly, your thumbs freeze. You stare at the blinking cursor. And you start doing this mental calculus: *Okay, do I put my school? My graduation year? Do I put the sport I play? Do I try to be funny and sarcastic so I seem chill? Do I put a quote so I seem deep?*

We panic because that little blank box is asking us the biggest question in the universe: **Who are you?**

And the reason it’s stressful is that most of us, deep down, feel like we have to *construct* an answer that is impressive enough to justify our existence. We feel like we are the marketing managers of our own lives. We have to curate the brand called "Me."

Tonight, I want to talk about that pressure. I want to talk about why it’s exhausting us, and I want to suggest that maybe—just maybe—we are going about this whole "Identity" thing backwards.

### The Three Traps of Identity

If we’re honest, most of us try to build our identity on three things. These are the "Big Three" foundations. They look strong, but they are actually incredibly fragile.

**Trap #1: I am what I achieve.**
This is the performance trap. In this mindset, you are only as valuable as your last report card, your last game, or your current GPA. If you’re the "smart kid," getting a B- feels like a death sentence. If you’re the "athlete," getting injured feels like losing your soul.
The problem with building your identity on achievement is that you are only ever as good as your *next* success. It’s a treadmill that never stops. You can never rest, because if you stop achieving, you stop mattering.

**Trap #2: I am how I appear.**
We all know this one. This is the mirror, the filter, the fit check. It’s the belief that if I can just look a certain way—if I can just get my body, my hair, or my style to match what I see on my "For You" page—then I’ll be happy. Then I’ll be "someone."
But we know the game is rigged. The beauty standards shift every six months. And even if you achieve the "perfect" look, you live in constant fear of losing it. It’s a prison of comparison.

**Trap #3: I am how I am received.**
This is the scariest one. This is social currency. It’s likes, views, comments, and invites. It’s the terrifying gap between sending a message and seeing the word "Read."
When we build our identity here, we hand the keys to our happiness over to other people. We let the crowd decide if we matter today. If the photo gets 200 likes, I’m valuable. If it gets 12, I’m embarrassed. I’ll delete it. I’ll delete *me*.

Do you feel the weight of that? It’s heavy. It’s exhausting. It’s like carrying a backpack full of bricks everywhere you go. And the worst part is, we think this is normal. We think this is just how life works.

We think identity is something we have to **Achieve**. We think we have to go out into the jungle of high school, kill a bear, drag it back, and say, "Look! I did a thing! I am somebody!"

But what if we’re wrong?

### The Shift: From Achieved to Received

I want to offer you a different vision. It’s a vision that has been around for thousands of years, but in our digital age, it feels radical.

What if your identity isn’t something you **Achieve**? What if it’s something you **Receive**?

Imagine a painting. Let’s say, a masterpiece hanging in a museum. A Van Gogh. Why is that painting valuable?
Is it valuable because the paint is working really hard to stay on the canvas?
Is it valuable because the canvas is stressing out about whether the other paintings like it?
No.

It is valuable for two reasons:
1. Because of who painted it (The Artist).
2. Because of what someone is willing to pay for it.

The painting doesn’t have to *do* anything to be worth millions. It just has to *be*. Its value is intrinsic. It was given value the moment the artist finished it and signed their name in the corner.

This is the shift I want you to make tonight.

You are not your grades. You are not your Instagram following. You are not your acne, your anxiety, or your varsity jacket. Those are things you *have* or things you *do*. They are not who you *are*.

You are a creation. You are designed. Whether you are religious or not, there is a fundamental truth here: **Human value is inherent, not earned.**

If you are a person of faith, you believe that the God of the universe knit you together, knows the number of hairs on your head, and says, "You are mine." That is an anchor.
If you build your life on that, you become unshakeable.

Think about the difference:
*   **The "Achieved Identity" person says:** "I messed up on that test. I am a failure."
*   **The "Received Identity" person says:** "I messed up on that test. I am a valuable person who had a bad day. I’ll try again."

Do you see the freedom in that? When your identity is grounded in something deeper than your performance, you can fail without being destroyed. You can be rejected by a crush without losing your worth. You can post a photo that nobody likes, and you don’t care, because your value wasn’t in the "likes" to begin with.

### So, What About Purpose?

Now, you might be thinking, "Okay, that sounds nice and fuzzy. But if I don't have to prove myself, why do anything? What’s my purpose?"

This is the coolest part.

When you are trying to *earn* your identity, your purpose is always selfish. You do things to get attention, to get into college, to impress people. You are the center of your own universe, and it’s lonely there.

But when you *accept* your identity as a gift—when you realize you are already valuable, already loved, already enough—your purpose flips.

You stop working *for* approval, and you start working *from* approval.

You don't play soccer to prove you’re a winner; you play because you love the game and the joy of movement.
You don't study to avoid being called stupid; you study because the world is fascinating and you want to understand it.
You don't help your friend to look like a "good person"; you help them because you actually care about them.

Your purpose shifts from **"Look at me"** to **"How can I help you?"**

Real purpose isn't about becoming a celebrity or an influencer. Real purpose is finding a way to use your specific gifts—your humor, your listening skills, your strength, your creativity—to make the world slightly less broken for the people around you.

### Practical Takeaways

Okay, this is heavy stuff. How do we actually live this out on a Tuesday morning when you’re tired and you don't want to go to school?

Here are three challenges for you this week.

**1. The "Feed" Audit.**
Tonight, before you go to bed, look at your social media feed. I want you to unfollow or mute at least three accounts. Which ones? The ones that make you feel small. The ones that make you feel like you need to buy something or change your body to be happy.
Curate your input. If you fill your mind with garbage that tells you you’re not enough, you’re going to believe it. Protect your headspace.

**2. The "I Am" Rewrite.**
We all talk to ourselves. And usually, we are really mean. We say things to ourselves we would never say to a friend. "You're so awkward," "You're ugly," "You're dumb."
Catch yourself doing it. And when you do, flip the script.
Instead of "I have to get an A to be smart," tell yourself, "I am a hard worker, regardless of the grade."
Instead of "I need them to like me," tell yourself, "I am worthy of love, even if this person doesn't see it."
It feels cheesy at first. Do it anyway. Rewrite the narrative.

**3. The Service Shift.**
The quickest way to kill the anxiety of "Who am I?" is to focus on "How can I help?"
If you feel lonely or insecure this week, do one thing for someone else where you get zero credit. Take out the trash without being asked. Text a friend just to encourage them, not to talk about yourself. Sit with the kid who is sitting alone.
When you serve others, you remember that you have something to give. And if you have something to give, you have value.

### Closing

I want to close with this image.

Imagine you are holding a cup.
If you are running around trying to catch raindrops to fill your cup—trying to catch every compliment, every achievement, every "like"—you are going to be exhausted. You’ll be running forever, and the cup will never be full enough.

But there is a faucet. A source of water that is constant. That is the truth of who you are. You are created. You are known. You are loved.

Put your cup under *that* faucet. Let it fill up. And once it’s full, it will overflow. And that overflow? That’s your purpose. That’s the good stuff you spill out onto the world.

Stop hustling for your worth. You already have it.

Thanks for listening.

This is the scariest one. This is social currency. It’s likes, views, comments, and invites. It’s the terrifying gap between sending a message and seeing the word "Read" with no reply.
When we build our identity here, we hand the keys to our happiness over to other people. We let the crowd decide if we matter today. If the photo gets 200 likes, I’m valuable. If it gets 12, I’m embarrassed. I’ll delete it. And in a way, I’m deleting *me*.

I also want to acknowledge a nuance here. For some of you, this isn't just about Instagram or grades. It’s about family. It’s about culture. You might feel the weight of your parents' sacrifices on your shoulders, feeling like you *have* to be a doctor or an engineer to make their struggle worth it. I want to offer you a different vision. It’s a vision that has been around for thousands of years, but in our digital age, it feels radical.

Is it valuable because the paint is working really hard to stay on the canvas?

It is valuable for two reasons:
1. Because of who painted it (The Artist).
2. Because of the price someone was willing to pay for it.

*   You don't study to avoid being called stupid; you study because the world is fascinating and you want to understand it.

*   Sit with the kid who is sitting alone at lunch (even if you just say hi).

If you are running around trying to catch raindrops to fill your cup—trying to catch every compliment, every achievement, every "like"—you are going to be exhausted. You’ll be running forever, dodging storms, hoping for a drizzle. The cup will never be full enough, and you'll always be thirsty.

Put your cup under *that* faucet. Let it fill up. And once it’s full, it will overflow. And that overflow? That’s your purpose. That’s the good stuff you spill out onto the world.

Thanks for listening.

Tonight, I want to talk about the exhaustion of living that way. And I want to suggest that maybe—just maybe—we are going about this whole "Identity" thing backwards. I want to talk about the "Un-Selfie."

### The Three Traps of the "Selfie" Identity

If we’re honest, most of us try to build our identity on three foundations. These are the "Big Three." They look strong, but they’re actually incredibly fragile.

**Trap #1: I am what I achieve.**
This is the performance trap. In this mindset, you are only as valuable as your last report card, your last game, or your current GPA.
We all know the feeling. It’s the grind. If you’re the "smart kid," getting a B- doesn't just feel like a bad grade; it feels like an identity crisis. If you’re the "athlete," getting injured feels like losing your soul.
The problem with building your identity on achievement is that you are only ever as good as your *next* success. It’s a treadmill that never stops. You can never really rest. Even when you win, you don't feel joy—you just feel relief. And then the pressure starts all over again for the next thing.

**Trap #2: I am how I appear.**
We all know this one. This is the mirror, the filter, the fit check. It’s the belief that if I can just look a certain way—if I can just get my body, my hair, or my style to match what I see on my "For You" page—then I’ll be happy. Then I’ll be "someone."
But we know the game is rigged. The beauty standards shift every six months. One minute it's skinny jeans, the next it's baggy. One minute it's about being thin, the next it's about being "thick." Even if you achieve the "perfect" look today, you live in constant fear of losing it. It’s a prison of comparison, and the warden is an algorithm designed to make you feel like you’re missing something.

**Trap #3: I am how I am received.**
This is the scariest one. This is social currency. It’s likes, views, comments, and invites. It’s the terrifying gap between sending a vulnerable message and seeing the word "Read"... and then nothing. Just the silence.
When we build our identity here, we hand the keys to our happiness over to other people. We let the crowd decide if we matter today. If the photo gets 200 likes, I’m valuable. If it gets 12, I’m embarrassed. I’ll delete it. And in a way, I feel like I’m deleting *me*.

Do you feel the weight of that? It’s heavy. It’s exhausting. It’s like carrying a backpack full of bricks everywhere you go. And the worst part is, we think this is just how life works.

We think identity is something we have to **Achieve**. We think we have to go out into the world, hunt down some success, drag it back to the cave, and say, "Look! I did a thing! I am somebody!"

But what if we’re wrong?

### The Shift: From Achieved to Received

I want to offer you a different vision. It’s the "Un-Selfie." It’s what happens when you stop trying to curate the image and start understanding the reality.

What if your identity isn’t something you **Achieve**? What if it’s something you **Receive**?

Imagine a painting. Let’s say, a masterpiece hanging in a museum. A Van Gogh.
Why is that painting valuable?
Is it valuable because the paint is working really hard to stay on the canvas?
Is it valuable because the canvas is stressing out about whether the other paintings think it’s cool?
No.

It is valuable for two reasons:
1. Because of who painted it (The Artist).
2. Because of the price someone was willing to pay for it.

The painting doesn’t have to *do* anything to be worth millions. It just has to *be*. Its value is intrinsic. It was given value the moment the artist finished it and signed their name in the corner.

This is the shift I want you to make tonight.

You are not your grades. You are not your Instagram following. You are not your acne, your anxiety, or your varsity jacket. Those are things you *have* or things you *do*. They are not who you *are*.

You are a creation. You are designed. Whether you’ve grown up in church or you’re just checking this out for the first time, there is a fundamental truth here: **Human value is inherent, not earned.**

If you are a believer, this is the core of the Gospel. It’s the belief that the God of the universe knit you together, knows the number of hairs on your head, and says, "You are mine." That is an anchor.
If you build your life on that, you become unshakeable.

Think about the difference in how you talk to yourself:
*   **The "Achieved Identity" person says:** "I messed up on that test. I am a failure."
*   **The "Received Identity" person says:** "I messed up on that test. I am a valuable person who had a bad day. I’ll try again."

Do you see the freedom in that? When your identity is grounded in something deeper than your performance, you can fail without being destroyed. You can be rejected by a crush without losing your worth. You can post a photo that nobody likes, and you honestly don’t care, because your value wasn’t in the "likes" to begin with.

### So, What About Purpose?

Now, I know what some of you are thinking. "Okay, that sounds nice. But if I don't have to prove myself, why do anything? Does this mean I just sit on the couch playing video games because I'm 'inherently valuable'?"

No. Here’s where it gets interesting.

When you are trying to *earn* your identity, your purpose is always selfish. You do things to get attention, to get into college, to impress people. You are the center of your own universe, and honestly, it’s lonely there. That’s the "Selfie" life—everything is framed around you.

But when you *accept* your identity as a gift—when you realize you are already valuable, already loved, already enough—your purpose flips.

You stop working *for* approval, and you start working *from* approval.

*   **Take sports.** You don't play soccer just to prove you’re a winner or to avoid getting yelled at by the coach. You play because the feeling of a perfect cross feels like flying, and you love your team. You play with joy, not fear.
*   **Take school.** You don't study just to avoid being called stupid. You study because the world is weird and fascinating and you actually want to understand how it works.
*   **Take friendship.** You don't help your friend just to look like a "good person" or to make sure they owe you a favor later. You help them because you actually care about them.

Your purpose shifts from **"Look at me"** to **"How can I help you?"**

Real purpose isn't about becoming an influencer. Real purpose is finding a way to use your specific gifts—your humor, your listening skills, your strength, your creativity—to make the world slightly less broken for the people around you.

### Practical Takeaways

Okay, this is heavy stuff. How do we actually live this out on a Tuesday morning when you’re tired, you have a math test, and you feel like garbage?

Here are three challenges for you this week.

**1. The "Feed" Audit.**
Tonight, before you go to bed, look at your social media feed. I want you to unfollow or mute at least three accounts. Which ones? The ones that make you feel small. The ones that make you feel like you need to buy something, change your body, or be someone else to be happy.
Curate your input. If you fill your mind with content that tells you you’re not enough, you’re going to believe it. Protect your headspace.

**2. The "I Am" Rewrite.**
We all talk to ourselves. And usually, we are really mean. We say things to ourselves we would never say to a friend.
*   "You're so awkward."
*   "You're ugly."
*   "You should have kept your mouth shut."

Catch yourself doing it. And when you do, flip the script.
*   Instead of "I have to get an A to be smart," tell yourself, "I am a hard worker, regardless of the grade."
*   Instead of "I need them to like me," tell yourself, "I am worthy of love, even if this person doesn't see it."
*   Instead of "I’m so awkward, I shouldn’t have come," tell yourself, "I’m brave for showing up, and I’m going to focus on listening to others."

It might feel weird at first. Do it anyway. You have to rewrite the narrative in your head before you can change how you live.

**3. The Service Shift.**
The quickest way to kill the anxiety of "Who am I?" is to focus on "How can I help?"
If you feel lonely or insecure this week, do one thing for someone else where you get **zero credit**.
*   Take out the trash at home without being asked (and don't mention it).
*   Text a friend just to encourage them, not to talk about yourself.
*   Sit with the kid who is sitting alone at lunch.

When you serve others in secret, you break the cycle of performing for applause. You remember that you have something to give. And if you have something to give, you have value.

### Closing

I want to close with this image.

Imagine you are holding a cup.
The "Selfie" life is running around trying to catch raindrops to fill your cup—trying to catch every compliment, every achievement, every "like." You are running constantly, terrified of spilling a drop, but the sun keeps drying it up. You’re exhausted, and the cup is never full enough.

But there is a faucet. A source of water that is constant. That is the truth of who you are. You are created. You are known. You are loved.

Put your cup under *that* faucet. Let it fill up. And once it’s full, it will naturally overflow. And that overflow? That’s your purpose. That’s the good stuff you spill out onto the world.

Stop hustling for your worth. You already have it.

Thanks for listening.

**Title:** The Bio, The Brand, and The Truth About Who You Are
**Audience:** Youth Group (Ages 14-18)
**Tone:** Conversational, authentic, encouraging
**Time:** Approx. 15-20 minutes

***

**(The Setup: Walk out, maybe holding a phone, looking at it casually before looking up.)**

Hey everyone.

I want to start tonight by talking about one of the most stressful things you can do in the modern world. It’s not taking the SATs. It’s not parallel parking while your dad yells at you from the passenger seat.

It is the absolute nightmare of writing your Instagram or TikTok bio.

Think about it. You have a tiny little box, maybe 150 characters, and in that space, you are expected to summarize your entire existence. You stare at that blinking cursor and think: *Who am I?*

So, we default to the labels, right?
*Varsity Soccer. Class of ’26. Coffee Addict.*
Maybe you put a flag of where you’re from. Maybe a Bible verse to show you’re spiritual, but a link to your Spotify so people know you have good taste.

We laugh about it, but there is something actually kind of heavy about that blinking cursor. Because it’s asking you to package yourself. It’s asking you to turn your life into a brand. And whether we admit it or not, most of us are walking around with this low-level anxiety that if we don’t curate the perfect identity—if we don’t post the right highlights, get the right grades, or wear the right things—then we don’t really matter.

Tonight, I want to talk about that pressure. The pressure to *perform* your identity. And I want to suggest that maybe, just maybe, we are going about this whole "finding yourself" thing completely backward.

**(Section 1: The House of Mirrors)**

Let’s be honest about the water we’re swimming in. You guys are the first generation to grow up with a scoreboard attached to your social life.

When I was younger, if I had a bad hair day or said something awkward, maybe five people saw it. Today, everything is documented. Everything is measurable. You know exactly how many people "liked" your last post. You know exactly where you rank in your class GPA. You know exactly who viewed your story and who ignored it.

We live in what I call the "Performance Trap."

The Performance Trap tells you a simple lie: **You are what you achieve.**

It says your identity is something you have to build, brick by brick.
*   If you make the team, you’re an Athlete.
*   If you get the A, you’re Smart.
*   If you get the laugh, you’re Funny.
*   If you get the date, you’re Desirable.

But here is the dangerous flip side that keeps us up at night:
*   If you get injured, who are you?
*   If you fail the test, are you stupid?
*   If no one laughs, or if you get dumped, or if the likes don’t come in... do you cease to exist?

I talk to so many of you who feel exhausted. And it’s a specific kind of exhaustion. It’s not just from lack of sleep; it’s soul-exhaustion. It’s the exhaustion of an actor who has been on stage for 16 years and never gets to go backstage. You feel like you always have to be "on." You have to be the chill one, or the successful one, or the chaotic one.

You become a curator of your own life. You take 50 photos to post one, just to make it look like you weren't trying. It’s ironic, isn't it? We work so hard to look effortless.

And the tragedy is that eventually, you start to wonder if people like *you*, or if they just like the avatar you’ve created. If I stopped performing, would anyone stay?

**(Section 2: The Shift – Achieved vs. Received)**

I want to offer you a different way to view the world. A vision of identity that doesn't depend on how well you perform this week.

There are two ways to get an identity. The first is **Achieved Identity**. That’s what we just talked about. It’s earning your worth. It’s fragile, it’s stressful, and it’s never enough. As soon as you reach a goal, the goalpost moves. You get the A? Great, now you need an A in the next class. You get 100 likes? Now you need 200. It’s a treadmill that never stops.

The second way is **Received Identity**.

Think about a newborn baby. When a baby is born, they are completely useless. Seriously. They don’t contribute to the economy, they have terrible conversation skills, they wake you up at 3 a.m., and they make a mess. They have achieved *nothing*.

And yet... look at the parents. They are obsessed. They look at that baby with total, overwhelming love. They would die for that baby.

Why? The baby hasn't "earned" it. The baby has value simply because of *who it is*. It is a child of the family. Its identity is received, not achieved.

This is the core truth I want you to hear tonight: **Your value is not a wage you earn; it is a gift you receive.**

You are not a human *doing*; you are a human *being*.

If you have a faith background, you know this is where God comes in. The story of the Bible isn't about people being awesome so God will love them. It’s about God loving people who are messy, broken, and insecure, and giving them a status they didn't earn. You are made in the image of God. That is your bio. That is your label. And unlike "Varsity Athlete" or "Honor Student," that label cannot be lost. It cannot be injured. It cannot be rejected.

Imagine the freedom of walking into school tomorrow morning knowing, deep in your bones, *“I have nothing to prove.”*

Imagine walking into the cafeteria not needing to be the funniest or the loudest to justify your space. You are already valuable. The pressure is off. You can just... be.

**(Section 3: What About Purpose?)**

Now, I know what the skeptical side of your brain is thinking.
*"Okay, that sounds nice and soft. But if I don't have to achieve anything to be valuable, won't I just become lazy? If I’m already ‘enough,’ why should I do anything with my life?"*

This brings us to **Purpose**.

When your identity is based on achievement, your purpose is **Self-Preservation**. You do things to make yourself look good. You study to get the grade to get the status. You post to get the validation. It’s all inward. It’s all about feeding the hungry ego.

But when your identity is *Received*—when you know you are already loved and secure—your purpose shifts. You stop working *for* your value, and you start working *from* your value.

See the difference?

If I know I’m secure, I don’t have to use my life to prove I matter. I can use my life to help other people.

Real purpose isn't about becoming famous or rich. It’s about finding the place where your specific joy meets the world’s specific need.

*   Maybe you’re great at listening. Your purpose isn't to be a "Professional Therapist" one day; your purpose is to be the friend who actually puts their phone down and listens when someone is hurting *today*.
*   Maybe you’re great at math. Your purpose isn't just to get an A; it’s to help the guy next to you who is drowning in calculus.
*   Maybe you’re funny. Your purpose isn't to be the class clown for attention; it’s to bring lightness to a room that feels heavy.

When you aren't obsessed with how you look, you can finally see the people around you. You become dangerous in the best way possible. You become a person who can love others without needing anything back from them. That is a superpower in high school.

**(Section 4: Practical Takeaways)**

So, how do we actually do this? Because it’s easy to nod your head in this room, but it’s hard to live it out when you open TikTok on the ride home.

Here are three challenges for you this week.

**1. The "Input" Fast.**
Comparison is the thief of joy, and social media is the factory of comparison. I want you to try something radical. For the first 30 minutes of your day and the last 30 minutes of your day, keep your phone in a different room.
When you wake up, let your first thought be about who you are, not what everyone else is doing. Don't let an algorithm tell you how to feel before you’ve even brushed your teeth. Reclaim your headspace.

**2. Change the "So, how was it?" Conversation.**
We reinforce the performance trap by how we talk to each other. When your friend plays a game or takes a test, what’s the first thing we ask? "Did you win?" "What did you get?"
Try changing the question. Ask: "Did you have fun?" "What was the hardest part?" "I love watching you play."
Affirm your friends for who they are, not just how they performed. Be the one person in their life who doesn't demand a stat sheet.

**3. Do one thing "off the record."**
This week, do something kind or creative that you do *not* post about.
Paint something and don't show it to anyone. Go help your neighbor with their groceries and don't tell your youth leader. Write a poem and burn it.
Train your soul to realize that things have value even if no one "likes" them. Practice doing things just for the joy of it, not for the audience.

**(Conclusion)**

I want to close with this.

There is a Japanese art form called *Kintsugi*. When a precious bowl is broken, they don’t throw it away. Instead, they glue the pieces back together using gold lacquer. The result is that the bowl is actually more beautiful *because* of its brokenness. The cracks become the design.

Some of you feel like you have to present a flawless, unbroken version of yourself to the world. You’re terrified of the cracks. You’re terrified of your anxiety, your doubts, your mistakes.

But a curated, plastic, perfect life is boring. And it’s not real.

The most beautiful people I know are not the ones with the perfect bios. They are the ones who are honest about their cracks, who know they don't have it all together, but who know they are loved anyway.

You don't need a better bio. You don't need a rebrand. You just need to drop the heavy weight of trying to be your own god, your own PR agent, and your own savior.

You are loved. You are known. You have a purpose that is bigger than your stats.

So this week, take a deep breath. stop performing, and start living.

Thanks, guys.

It’s that little blinking cursor in the text box that says: *“Bio.”* Or the teacher who says, *“Let’s go around the room and tell us a little bit about yourself.”*

Does anyone else feel your heart rate spike when that happens? It’s such a simple request, right? Just tell us who you are. But suddenly, your mind goes blank. You start thinking, *Okay, what’s the cool answer? What’s the smart answer? Do I list my hobbies? Do I make a joke so I seem chill? Do I list my achievements so I seem impressive?*

We try to summarize our entire existence into 150 characters or a 30-second soundbite. And usually, we end up listing *what we do*. I’m a soccer player. I’m a gamer. I’m a straight-A student. I’m the funny one.

We treat our identity like it’s an avatar in a video game. You know the screen where you build your character? You pick the outfit, you pick the skills, you adjust the stats. You curate this version of yourself that you’re going to send out into the world to do battle.

But here is the problem, and it’s the main thing I want us to wrestle with tonight: **There is a massive difference between building an identity and actually having one.**

We are living in a time where the pressure to *build* a brand—even if you aren’t an influencer—is heavier than it has ever been in human history. You are the first generation that has to grow up with a digital scoreboard attached to your social life.

So, let’s talk about the pressure. Let’s be honest about the weight in the room.

Most of us are building our identity on three very shaky pillars.

**The first pillar is Performance.**
This is the "I am what I achieve" trap. This is the pressure that says you are only as valuable as your last report card, your last game, or your college acceptance letter. It’s the terrifying feeling that if you stop hustling, you disappear.
I know how much pressure you guys are under. The world tells you that if you don’t have it all figured out by age 16, you’re already behind. So, we work hard. We grind. But the problem with basing your identity on what you *do* is that eventually, you will fail. It’s not a matter of *if*, but *when*. You’ll bomb a test. You’ll get injured and can’t play. You won’t get the part in the play.
If your identity is "The Smart Kid," who are you when you get a C? If your identity is "The Athlete," who are you when you’re on the bench? If your worth is tied to your winning, then losing doesn’t just feel like a bad day—it feels like a death. It feels like you cease to exist.

**The second pillar is Appearance.**
This is the "I am how I look" trap. And look, I’m not just talking about vanity. I’m talking about the need to fit the aesthetic. We curate our photos, we check the angles, we use the filters. We want to be seen, but we’re terrified of being *truly* seen. We want people to see the highlight reel, not the behind-the-scenes footage where we’re tired, anxious, or breaking out.
The danger here is that you become a product. You start marketing yourself. And when you treat yourself like a product, you start wondering about your market value. *Do people like me? Is this version of me trending?* It is exhausting to live your life on a stage.

**The third pillar is Popularity (or The Algorithm).**
This is the "I am who others say I am" trap. It used to be that popularity was just about who you sat with at lunch. Now, it’s quantified. It’s data. If you post something and it gets 4 likes in an hour, you feel a physical drop in your stomach. You think, *“Was it stupid? Should I delete it? Do they hate me?”*
We outsource our self-esteem to the opinions of strangers or people we barely know. We let the algorithm decide if we matter today.

Here is the reality check: **Performance, Appearance, and Popularity are terrible places to build a house.** They are shifting sand. One bad day, one mean comment, one failure, and the whole house comes down.

If you are constantly exhausted, constantly anxious, and constantly feeling like you have to "perform" your personality, it’s because you are doing a job you were never meant to do. You are trying to *manufacture* your own worthiness.

So, what is the alternative? If we aren’t the sum of our grades, our looks, or our likes, then who are we?

I want to offer you a different vision. It’s the difference between an **Achieved Identity** and a **Received Identity**.

An Achieved Identity is one you have to earn. You have to wake up every morning and fight for it. It’s fragile. It’s stressful. It’s lonely.

A Received Identity is one that is given to you. It is a gift. It is solid. It is an anchor.

The deepest truth about you—the thing that is true about you at 3:00 AM when you’re staring at the ceiling and you’ve failed a test and you feel alone—is this: **You are intrinsic.** Your value is built-in. It is not something you negotiate; it is something you possess simply because you exist.

If we look at this through a spiritual lens, we see that the Creator doesn’t make "extras" or background characters. You are designed with intent. You are loved not because of what you bring to the table, but because you *are* at the table.

Think about a newborn baby. What has a baby achieved? Nothing. They don’t have a job. They have zero followers. They can’t even hold their own head up. They are, by society’s standards, completely unproductive. And yet, how do the parents look at that baby? With absolute, overwhelming, crushing love. The baby is valuable simply because it *is*.

You don’t lose that value just because you got older. You don’t lose that value because you made a mistake. You don’t lose that value because someone broke up with you.

When you shift from trying to build an identity to accepting a received identity, the pressure valve releases. You can take a deep breath. You can realize, *“I don’t have to be the best in the room to have a right to be in the room.”*

This changes everything about **Purpose**.

A lot of you are stressed about purpose because you think purpose means "A Career." You think finding your purpose means deciding right now if you’re going to be a lawyer or a graphic designer.

That’s not purpose. That’s just a job.

**Identity is who you are. Purpose is what you pour out.**

When you know you are valuable, loved, and secure, you stop trying to use the world to fill you up, and you start looking for ways to fill the world up.

If your identity is "I need to be important," your purpose will be selfish. You’ll use people to get ahead.
But if your identity is "I am loved and I have enough," your purpose becomes about service.

Your purpose right now, at 15 or 16 or 17, isn’t to decide your 40-year career path. Your purpose is to bring your unique flavor of light into the dark corners of your school, your home, and your friend group.

Maybe your purpose this week is to be the one person who actually listens when a friend is talking, instead of looking at your phone.
Maybe your purpose is to create art that makes people feel less alone.
Maybe your purpose is to stand up for the kid who is getting roasted in the group chat.

Purpose isn't a destination you arrive at. It’s the way you walk down the street. It’s the way you treat the cashier. It’s the way you treat yourself when you fail.

So, how do we actually do this? Because it sounds nice in a speech, but tomorrow morning you’re going to wake up and check your notifications and the pressure is going to come rushing back.

Here are three practical things I want to challenge you to try this week.

**1. The "Audit" (Curate your inputs)**
I want you to look at your social media feed with a critical eye. Scroll through the first ten posts. After each one, ask yourself: *How does this make me feel?*
Does this account make me feel inspired and happy? Or does it make me feel jealous, inadequate, or anxious?
If an account constantly makes you feel like you aren’t enough, **unfollow it.** You are not obligated to consume content that poisons your spirit. Protect your headspace. Curate a feed that reminds you of your received identity, not one that demands you achieve a fake one.

**2. The "Who," Not "What" Conversation**
This week, catch yourself when you’re talking to your friends. We usually ask, *“What did you get on the test?”* or *“Did you win the game?”*
Try to ask questions that get to the human, not the human *doing*.
Ask: *“What’s making you happy right now?”*
Ask: *“How are you actually holding up this week?”*
Ask: *“What was the best part of your day?”*
When you change the questions, you change the culture. You signal to your friends that you care about *them*, not just their stats. Be the friend who makes it safe to be real.

**3. The Anchor Moment**
Find five minutes a day—maybe right when you wake up, or right before you sleep—to disconnect from the "Avatar." Put the phone in another room.
Just sit in the quiet. It will feel weird at first. You might feel bored. That’s okay.
In that silence, remind yourself of the truth. Say it out loud if you have to. *“I am not what I do. I am not what I look like. I am loved. I am here on purpose.”*
You need to anchor yourself in the truth before the world tries to blow you away.

Look, I’m not saying this is easy. I’m an adult, and I still struggle with this. I still check my phone hoping for validation. I still feel bad when I fail. It’s a journey.

But I want you to know that you are already enough. You don’t have to hustle for your worthiness. You don’t have to edit yourself to be lovable. The mask can come down.

You are not a brand. You are not a profile. You are not a GPA.

You are a complex, messy, wonderful, infinite human being. You are loved. And the world needs *that* version of you—the real one—not the polished avatar.

So this week, let’s try to be a little less impressive, and a little more real.

Thanks, guys.

**Title: The Resume vs. The Reality: Finding Who You Are When the Phone is Off**

**[Opening]**

I want to start by asking a question, and I want you to be honest with yourself—you don’t have to raise your hand. How many of you have ever typed out a caption for a post, deleted it, typed a new one, deleted that, asked a friend what you should say, and then eventually just posted an emoji because it felt safer?

Or here’s another one: Have you ever met someone new—maybe at a party, or a new team tryout—and they ask that dreaded question: "So, tell me about yourself."

And suddenly, your mind goes blank. You start listing things like you’re reading off a cereal box. "Uh, I’m 16. I play soccer. I like… music?" And you walk away feeling like you just gave the most boring presentation in history.

We laugh about it, but there is a specific kind of anxiety that comes with those moments. It’s the anxiety of definition. It’s the pressure to take the complex, messy, weird, interesting human being that you are and compress it into a bio line.

We live in a world that is obsessed with "personal branding." Even if you aren’t an influencer, you are taught to think like one. You are taught that your identity is something you have to build, brick by brick, post by post, grade by grade.

And that is exhausting.

Tonight, I want to talk about that exhaustion. I want to talk about the heavy backpack of expectations you’re carrying, and I want to talk about a different way to live—a way where you don’t have to constantly prove that you matter.

**[The Performance Trap]**

Let’s look at the three main ways we try to build our identity today. I call this the "Performance Trap."

**1. The Achievement Trap:**
This is the voice that says, "I am what I accomplish."
You know this voice. It’s the one that screams at you when you get a bad grade. It’s the knot in your stomach before a big game. If you are the "smart kid," who are you if you fail a test? If you are the "athlete," who are you if you tear your ACL?
When we tie our identity to our achievements, we are only as good as our last success. That is a terrifying way to live, because it means your value is constantly on the line. You can never rest. You’re only "worthy" when you’re winning.

**2. The Appearance Trap:**
This is the voice that says, "I am how I look," or "I am how people perceive me."
We all know the photos we see online are curated. We know about the filters, the lighting, the angles. We know nobody’s life is actually that aesthetic. But knowing it doesn’t stop us from feeling it.
When you scroll through TikTok or Instagram, you aren’t just looking at pictures; you’re comparing your "behind-the-scenes" footage with everyone else’s "highlight reel." You compare your messy room, your acne, and your awkward family dinner to their vacation photos and perfect skin.
The Appearance Trap tells you that if you aren’t being admired, you don’t exist. It turns your life into a performance for an audience that, frankly, is too busy worrying about their own performance to really care about yours.

**3. The Association Trap:**
This says, "I am who I hang out with."
This is the pressure to be in the right group, to have the right boyfriend or girlfriend, to be tagged in the right stories. It’s the fear of missing out (FOMO), not just because you missed the fun, but because you missed the *status* of being there.

Here is the hard truth about the Performance Trap: It works… until it doesn’t.
You might get the grades. You might get the likes. You might make the team. But the problem with building your identity on these things is that they are external. They are outside of you. And anything that can be given to you can be taken away.

If your identity is a house, building it on achievement or appearance is like building on sand. The moment a storm comes—a breakup, a failure, a bad season—the house collapses, and you’re left standing in the rubble asking, "Who am I now?"

**[A Deeper Vision: Given vs. Earned]**

So, if we aren’t our grades, our looks, or our follower count, then what are we?

I want to offer you a shift in perspective. It’s the difference between an **Earned Identity** and a **Given Identity**.

An Earned Identity is what we just talked about. It’s a resume. It’s you saying, "I matter because I did X, Y, and Z." It is fragile, and it is heavy.

A Given Identity is totally different. It is the belief that your value is inherent. It is not something you achieve; it is something you possess simply because you exist.

Think about a newborn baby. When a baby is born, they haven’t done anything. They haven’t scored a goal, they haven’t passed a math test, they have zero followers. All they do is cry, eat, and sleep. And yet, they are infinitely valuable. Their parents would die for them. They are loved not for what they *do*, but for who they *are*.

Somewhere along the line, between being a baby and being a teenager, we convince ourselves that we lost that value. We convince ourselves that we have to start paying rent for our existence.

But the deeper truth—the truth that anchors the healthiest, strongest people I know—is that you are still that valuable. You are a unique, unrepeatable human being. You have a combination of thoughts, fingerprints, laughter, and perspective that has never existed before in the history of the universe and will never exist again.

Your identity is not a project to be completed. It is a reality to be discovered.

When you realize that your worth is settled—that you don’t have to hustle for it—it changes everything. It takes the pressure off. You can study hard because you’re curious, not because you’re terrified of failing. You can play sports because you love the game, not because you need the applause. You can post a photo because it’s a fun memory, not because you need validation.

**[From Identity to Purpose]**

This leads us to the second part of our topic: **Purpose**.

A lot of young people ask, "What is my purpose?" as if purpose is a hidden treasure map they have to find. They think purpose is a job title. "My purpose is to be a doctor" or "My purpose is to be an engineer."

But purpose isn’t a job title. Purpose is the natural output of a secure identity.

There is a famous quote by a philosopher named Howard Thurman. He said:
*"Don't ask what the world needs. Ask what makes you come alive, and go do it. Because what the world needs is people who have come alive."*

When you are stuck in the Performance Trap, you are asking, "What does the world want from me so they will clap?"
When you are grounded in a Given Identity, you ask, "What do I have to give?"

Your purpose right now, at 15 or 17 years old, isn't to decide what you’re going to do for the next 50 years. Your purpose is to figure out what makes you come alive and how you can use that to help the people around you.

Maybe you are a great listener. Your purpose this week is to be the friend who actually listens when everyone else is talking.
Maybe you are great at organizing things. Your purpose is to bring order to chaos in your student council or your family kitchen.
Maybe you are funny. Your purpose is to bring lightness to a heavy situation.

Purpose is not about being famous; it’s about being effective. It’s about leaving people better than you found them.

**[Practical Takeaways]**

I don’t want you to just leave here with a nice feeling. I want you to try something different this week. Here are three practical ways to shift from an Earned Identity to a Given Identity.

**1. The "Input" Audit.**
For the next week, pay attention to the voices you are letting into your head. If there are accounts on Instagram or TikTok that make you feel ugly, poor, or inadequate every time you see them—unfollow them. Seriously. Mute them. You are in charge of your feed.
Fill your mind with things that remind you of reality, not things that demand you perform. If you constantly consume content that tells you you’re not enough, you will believe it. Protect your headspace.

**2. Practice "Self-Forgetfulness."**
This sounds weird, but stay with me. The best moments of your life are usually the ones where you aren’t thinking about yourself at all. You’re lost in a movie, you’re laughing with friends, you’re in the "zone" in a sport.
Anxiety lives in the mirror. It lives in self-obsession.
This week, try to do one thing every day that gets you out of your own head. Help your parents without being asked. Volunteer. Tutor a younger kid. When you focus on serving someone else, the pressure to "be someone" disappears, and you find yourself just being *human*.

**3. Change Your "I Am" Statements.**
Catch yourself when you say things like, "I am such a failure" or "I am awkward."
Replace them with the truth.
Instead of "I am a failure," try "I am a person who failed a test, and I can learn from it."
Instead of "I am awkward," try "I am learning how to navigate social situations, and that’s okay."
Separate your *actions* from your *identity*. You might have *done* something dumb, but that doesn’t make *you* dumb.

**[Conclusion]**

I want to close with this image.

Imagine you are holding a cup. If you squeeze the cup tight, trying to hold it together, your hand will eventually cramp. You’ll get tired. You’ll drop it. That is the Earned Identity—constantly squeezing, constantly striving.

Now imagine holding your hand open, palm up. The cup rests there. You aren’t squeezing; you’re receiving.

You don’t have to build a brand. You don’t have to prove to this room, or to your school, or to the internet, that you matter. You matter because you are here. You matter because there is a spark in you that is entirely your own.

The world is going to try very hard to turn you into a product. Don’t let it. Be a person. Be messy, be real, be kind, and rest in the fact that you are enough, exactly as you are.

Thanks for listening.
