**Title: The Avatar vs. The Anchor**
**Audience:** Youth Group (Ages 14-18)
**Tone:** Conversational, vulnerable, encouraging

***

**[The Opening]**

I want to start by asking you a question that sounds simple, but is actually kind of terrifying. How long does it take you to write an Instagram bio? Or a TikTok profile?

You know that moment. You click "Edit Profile." You see that blinking cursor. And suddenly, you feel this weird pressure to summarize your entire existence in 150 characters. You think: *Do I put my school? My sport? Do I try to be funny? Do I use an obscure quote so I seem mysterious? Do I put a flag? A ring emoji?*

It feels like a small thing, but it’s actually a heavy weight. Because that little box is asking you: "Who are you?"

And not just "Who are you?" but "Who are you in a way that makes you worth following?"

We live in a weird time. For most of human history, you were just… you. You were John the baker’s son, or Sarah who lived by the river. You didn't have to manage a brand. But today, every single one of you is essentially the CEO of a small marketing firm called "Me, Incorporated." You have to handle the PR, the photography, the captions, and the public image. You have to prove, every single day, that you are interesting, successful, and happy.

And honestly? It is exhausting.

I’m looking around this room, and I see a lot of talent. I see athletes, musicians, gamers, scholars. But I also sense a lot of anxiety. Because when you are in charge of creating your own identity, you are constantly terrified that the "you" you’ve built might collapse.

So tonight, I want to talk about that pressure. I want to talk about the trap of the "Curated Self," and then I want to offer you a different way to live—a way that doesn't require you to hustle for your worth. We’re going to talk about Identity and Purpose.

**[The Problem: The Three-Legged Stool]**

Let’s be honest about how most of us try to build our identity. We usually build it on a three-legged stool.

**Leg 1 is Achievement.**
This is the "Report Card" identity. You are your grades. You are your stats on the field. You are your college acceptance letter. When you succeed, you feel like a god. But the second you fail—you fail a test, you get cut from the team, you get rejected—you don't just feel like you made a mistake. You feel like *you* are a mistake.

**Leg 2 is Appearance.**
This isn't just about being good-looking. It’s about the aesthetic. It’s about looking like you have it all together. It’s the photos where the lighting is perfect, and the mess of your actual bedroom is cropped out of the frame. It’s the pressure to look effortless, even though it took you forty-five minutes to get ready.

**Leg 3 is Approval.**
This is the metrics. Likes, views, comments, shares. We treat people like mirrors. We walk around asking, "Do you like me? Am I okay?" And if the notifications are buzzing, we feel alive. If the phone is silent, we feel invisible.

Here is the danger of the three-legged stool: It is incredibly fragile.

If your identity is "I am the smart kid," who are you when you get to college and you’re just average?
If your identity is "I am the athlete," who are you when you blow out your knee?
If your identity is "I have a boyfriend/girlfriend," who are you when they break up with you?

If your identity is based on things that can be taken away, you will always live in fear. You will always be defensive. You’ll be like a frantic construction worker, constantly trying to patch the cracks in the wall so nobody sees the real you inside.

**[The Pivot: Achieved vs. Received]**

I want to suggest that there is a better way to handle the question "Who am I?"

There are two types of identity: **Achieved Identity** and **Received Identity.**

Achieved Identity is what we just talked about. It’s a ladder. You climb it. You hustle. You earn it. It’s based on what you *do*. And it’s tiring because you can never stop doing it. You’re only as good as your last game, your last post, your last grade.

Received Identity is different. It’s an anchor. It’s not something you achieve; it’s something you are given. It’s based on who you *are*.

Imagine a newborn baby. What has that baby achieved? Nothing. They can’t walk, they can’t talk, they don't have a GPA, and they have zero Instagram followers. They just eat, sleep, and cry. And yet, the parents look at that baby and say, "I love you more than life itself. I would die for you."

Why? The baby hasn't earned it. The baby has value simply because it *exists*. It belongs to the family. Its worth is inherent, not earned.

As you get older, the world tries to beat that out of you. The world tells you, "No, no, you only matter if you produce something."

But the deepest truth—the spiritual truth—is that you are still that child. You have value that has nothing to do with your performance. You are a created being. You are designed. You are here on purpose.

When you ground your identity in the fact that you are loved *before* you achieve anything, it changes everything.

It means you can get a bad grade and still be valuable.
It means you can have a bad hair day and still be worthy.
It means you can be single, or awkward, or unsure of your future, and still be complete.

You don't have to invent yourself. You just have to be yourself.

**[The Shift to Purpose]**

Now, you might be thinking, "Okay, that sounds nice, but if I don't have to prove myself, what am I supposed to do with my life? Just sit on the couch?"

No. Actually, this is where it gets exciting. This is where we move from Identity to Purpose.

When your identity is insecure—when you’re trying to prove you’re cool or smart—you are self-obsessed. You have to be. You’re constantly checking the mirror. You walk into a room and think, "What do these people think of me?"

But when your identity is secure—when you know you are loved and valuable regardless of what happens—you can finally stop looking at yourself. You can put the mirror down and look out the window.

You stop asking, "What do people think of me?" and you start asking, "How can I help these people?"

That is the definition of Purpose.

There is a lie that says "Purpose" means being famous. We think having a purpose means standing on a stage with a microphone, or being an influencer with a blue checkmark, or starting a billion-dollar company.

Real purpose is much quieter, and much more powerful. Real purpose is using your unique design to make the world around you slightly less broken.

If you are a good listener, your purpose might be to be the safe harbor for friends who are struggling with mental health.
If you are an athlete, your purpose isn't just to score points; it’s to change the culture of your locker room to be less toxic and more inclusive.
If you are creative, your purpose is to make things that bring beauty into a cynical world.

Do you see the difference?
*Insecure Identity says:* "I will do this so people will look at me."
*Secure Purpose says:* "I will do this because I have something to give."

You are not a product to be sold. You are a gift to be given.

**[Practical Takeaways]**

So, how do we actually live this out? Because tomorrow morning, you’re going to wake up, pick up your phone, and the pressure is going to come rushing back.

Here are three practical things you can do this week to shift from the Avatar to the Anchor.

**1. The "Why" Audit.**
This week, pay attention to *why* you are doing things. When you post something, ask yourself: "Am I sharing this to bring joy, or am I fishing for compliments?" When you study, ask: "Am I learning because I’m curious, or am I terrified of being average?"
You don't have to stop achieving. Just stop trusting achievement to save you. Do the work because you love it, not because you need it to prove you exist.

**2. The Ruthless Unfollow.**
Your feed is your mental diet. If you follow accounts that make you feel ugly, poor, or boring, unfollow them. Seriously. You are voluntarily letting someone make you feel small.
If an account triggers that voice in your head that says, "You aren't enough," hit unfollow. Protect your headspace. Curate a feed that inspires you to look out at the world, not down at yourself.

**3. The Service Shift.**
The fastest way to kill insecurity is service. If you are feeling down about yourself, feeling like a loser, or feeling lonely—go help someone else. It sounds counterintuitive, but it works every time.
Text a friend who is having a hard time. Help your parents without being asked. Volunteer. When you serve, you remind yourself that you have power and agency. You remind yourself that you are effective. You stop being the victim of your own thoughts and become the agent of someone else’s joy.

**[Conclusion]**

I want to close with this.

There is a version of you that the world wants. That version is polished, filtered, straight-A’s, varsity captain, never sad, never messy. That version is an Avatar. It’s not real.

Then there is the real you. The you that sometimes wakes up with bad breath. The you that has doubts. The you that is weird and has niche interests. The you that fails sometimes.

I want you to know that the real you is the one that matters. The real you is the one that is loved.

You do not have to hustle for your worthiness. It is already yours. Your seat at the table is reserved, and you didn't have to buy the ticket.

So this week, take a deep breath. Drop the heavy weight of trying to be a brand. Be a person. Be a friend. Be messy. Be real.

Because the world doesn't need another perfect profile. It needs *you*.

Thanks, guys.

Hey everyone. Thanks for being here.

I want to start with something that sounds simple but is actually one of the most stressful things we do in the modern world. Tonight, I want to talk about that pressure. I want to talk about Identity and Purpose. Because if we’re honest, most of us feel like we’re constantly auditioning for our own lives. We feel like we have to build a brand, maintain a streak, and prove that we matter.

If you look at the world around us—school, TikTok, college applications, sports teams—they all preach the same message. They tell you that your identity is something you **achieve**. It’s something you build, brick by brick.

Usually, this falls into three traps. See if you recognize any of these in your own head.

**Trap #1: I am my Performance.**
This is the "Report Card" identity. You are your grades. You are your stats on the field. You are your trophies. If you get an A, you are a genius and a success. If you fail a test, you aren’t just a person who failed a test; you *are* a failure.
The problem with this? You’re only as good as your last game. You’re only as worthy as your last semester. It’s a treadmill that never stops. If your identity is "I’m the smart kid," what happens when you get to college and you’re suddenly average? If your identity is "I’m the athlete," who are you when you tear your ACL?

**Trap #2: I am my Appearance.**
This is the "Mirror" identity. I am my body. I am my style. I am how attractive people find me. This is the loudest one on social media, obviously. We curate these avatars of ourselves—filtering out the blemishes, posing at the right angles.
But we all know the truth: The avatar isn't real. It’s a highlight reel. And maintaining it is exhausting. You become a PR manager for your own life, constantly spinning the story to make sure you look happy, cool, and flawless.

**Trap #3: I am my Audience.**
This is the "Data" identity. I am who people say I am. I am my follower count. I am the number of likes I get within the first ten minutes of posting. If people include me, I have value. If I get left on read, or left out of the group chat, my value drops to zero.
This is the most dangerous one, because it puts the keys to your happiness in other people’s pockets. You are giving everyone else the power to determine your worth.

**The Collapse of the House of Cards**

Here is the hard truth about building your identity on performance, appearance, or popularity: **It is incredibly fragile.**

It’s like building a house of cards. It might look impressive from a distance. It might stand tall for a while. But the moment the wind blows—the moment you get dumped, the moment you fail the class, the moment someone spreads a rumor about you—the whole thing collapses.

And when it collapses, it hurts. Not just a little bit. It devastates us. Because we didn't just lose a game or a boyfriend; we lost our sense of *self*. We don't know who we are without that external validation.

I think a lot of the anxiety your generation is facing—and let’s be real, it’s at epidemic levels—comes from this. You are carrying the crushing weight of having to constantly invent and sustain your own worth. You wake up every morning effectively having to "earn" your right to exist.

That is too heavy a burden for anyone to carry. You were not made to carry it.

**The Pivot: Achieved vs. Received**

So, what is the alternative? If we don’t build our identity, where does it come from?

I want to offer you a different vision. It’s a vision that has been around for thousands of years, but it’s radical in 2024.

True identity is not **achieved**; it is **received**.

Think about an anchor. An anchor is useless if you throw it inside the boat. If you hook the anchor onto the captain’s chair, the boat is still going to drift in the storm. An anchor only works if it hooks into something *outside* the boat—something deeper, something unshakeable, something like the ocean floor.

Your identity is the same. You cannot anchor yourself to yourself. You cannot anchor your worth to your feelings, because feelings change like the weather. You need to anchor your identity in something outside of you that doesn't change.

For those of us of faith, we believe that "something" is the Creator. The One who made you.

The core message of a spiritual worldview is that your value is not a wage you earn; it is a gift you are given.

Think about a newborn baby. When a baby is born, they haven’t done anything. They haven’t scored a goal, they don’t have a GPA, they have zero followers, and honestly, they look kind of like wrinkled aliens. But their parents look at them with absolute, overwhelming love. That baby has infinite worth *just because they exist*. They are loved simply because they are children of their parents.

That is **Received Identity**.

It says: *You are valuable because you are here. You are valuable because you are known and loved by God. You are valuable not because of what you do, but because of who you are.*

**How This Changes Your Purpose**

Now, you might be thinking, "Okay, that sounds nice and poetic, but I still have to get into college. I still want to win the game. Does this mean I just stop trying?"

Absolutely not. In fact, this is the secret to finding your **Purpose**.

When you know who you are—when you know your value is secure and can't be taken away—you are finally free to really live.

If you are playing soccer to *prove* you are valuable, you will play with fear. You’ll be terrified of making a mistake. You’ll be jealous of your teammates.
But if you play soccer knowing you are *already* valuable, you play with freedom. You play for the joy of the game. You play harder, actually, because you aren't paralyzed by the fear of failure.

If you help people because you want them to think you’re a "good person," that’s actually selfish. You’re using them to boost your ego.
But if you help people because you know you are loved and you want to overflow that love to others, that is true service. That is real purpose.

**Purpose isn't about becoming a celebrity. Purpose is using your unique skills, personality, and energy to make the world around you brighter, knowing that you don't need the credit to survive.**

You stop working *for* your identity, and you start working *from* your identity.

**Practical Takeaways**

So, how do we actually do this? How do we stop the "hustle" and start living from a place of security? This isn't a switch you flip; it's a habit you build. Here are three things I want to challenge you to do this week.

**1. The Social Media Audit**
I want you to take ten minutes tonight and look at your feed. Pay attention to your body and your emotions as you scroll. When you look at certain accounts, do you feel inspired and happy? Or do you feel jealous, ugly, or "less than"?
If an account makes you feel like you aren't enough, **unfollow it**. Ruthlessly. You are inviting voices into your head that are lying to you about your worth. Curate a feed that reminds you of reality, not one that demands you chase a fantasy.

**2. Separate "Who" from "Do"**
Find one activity this week that you do simply because you love it, not because it’s "productive."
Draw something and don’t post it. Go for a run without your Apple Watch tracking the pace. Read a book that isn't for school. Play a video game just for fun, not for rank.
Remind your brain that you are allowed to enjoy things without monetizing them or measuring them. Practice being a human *being*, not a human *doing*.

**3. Change the Mirror Talk**
This sounds cheesy, but it works. When you mess up this week—and you will—watch how you talk to yourself.
If you fail a quiz, do you say, "I'm so stupid"?
Catch yourself. Correct it. Say, "I did poorly on this quiz. I’m disappointed, but I’m still me. My value hasn't changed."
Separate your performance from your personhood. Talk to yourself like you would talk to your best friend. You wouldn't destroy your best friend for making a mistake; don't do it to yourself.

**Conclusion: The Invitation**

I want to close with this image.

Imagine you are wearing a heavy suit of armor. You put it on to protect yourself, to look strong, to impress people. But it’s heavy. It’s hot. It’s hard to move. You’ve been wearing it for so long you’ve forgotten what your own skin feels like.

The invitation tonight is to take the armor off.

To realize that you don’t need the armor to be safe. You don’t need the perfect grades, the perfect body, or the perfect reputation to be worthy of love.

You are not a brand. You are not a profile. You are not a GPA.

You are a human being, fearfully and wonderfully made. You have a purpose that is unique to you—to bring light, creativity, and kindness into your corner of the world. But you can only do that if you stop wasting all your energy trying to prove you matter.

You already matter. That issue is settled. The check has cleared.

So take a deep breath. Let the pressure drop off your shoulders. You don't have to earn your life. You just have to live it.

Thanks, everyone.

YVh0hWjL7VK_TFNLPnfKM.text:
**Title:** The Character Creator vs. The Treasure Hunt: Finding Who You Actually Are
**Audience:** Youth Group (Ages 14-18)
**Tone:** Conversational, honest, encouraging.

***

**(The speaker walks out, maybe holding a phone, looking relaxed.)**

Hey everyone. It’s really good to be here with you guys tonight.

I want to start by talking about video games. Specifically, RPGs (Role Playing Games). You know the moment I’m talking about—right at the beginning. You haven’t killed a single monster, you haven’t explored a single map, and you haven’t completed a single quest. You are at the "Character Creation" screen.

You know how this goes. You spend forty-five minutes deciding on a hairstyle. You’re sliding the toggle bars back and forth—jawline width, eye color, height. You have to pick your class: Are you a Warrior? A Mage? A Stealth Archer (because let's be honest, we all end up playing Stealth Archers)? Then you have to allocate your stats. You have 10 points to spend. Do you put them into Strength? Intelligence? Charisma?

It’s stressful, right? Because you have this nagging feeling that if you pick the wrong build now, you’re going to get crushed at Level 20. You are trying to curate the perfect avatar before the game even begins.

I think the reason that screen is so stressful—and so addictive—is that it feels exactly like your actual life right now.

Somewhere around the age of 13 or 14, society basically handed you the controller and said, "Okay, time to build your avatar. Who are you going to be?"

And suddenly, you feel this massive pressure to curate the perfect version of yourself. You have to slide the toggle bars on your appearance until you fit the current trend. You have to allocate your "stat points" into grades, sports, or being the funny one in the group chat. You have to choose your class: The Smart Kid, The Athlete, The Artist, The Rebel.

And just like the game, you’re terrified that if you build your character wrong, you’re going to lose.

Tonight, I want to talk about that pressure. The pressure to *construct* an identity, and the exhaustion that comes with it. And then, I want to offer you a different way to view your life—one that doesn't require you to be your own PR manager 24/7.

### The Exhaustion of "Main Character Energy"

Let’s be honest about the air you breathe. You are the first generation in human history to grow up with a scoreboard in your pocket.

In the past, if you had an awkward hair day or said something dumb, maybe five people saw it, and they forgot about it by lunch. Now? Everything is documented. Everything is performative.

We talk a lot about "Main Character Energy," and it sounds fun on TikTok, but in reality, being the Main Character is exhausting. It means the camera is always on. It means the plot depends entirely on you.

I see three big lies that culture tells you about who you are.

**Lie #1: You are what you achieve.**
This is the pressure that says your value is tied to your output. It’s the voice that says, "If I don't get an A, I'm stupid." "If I don't make Varsity, I'm a failure." "If I don't get into *that* college, my future is over." It turns your life into a transaction: *I perform, therefore I am valuable.* The problem is, what happens when you have a bad day? If your identity is built on winning, then losing doesn't just feel like a setback; it feels like a death.

**Lie #2: You are what people think of you.**
This is the social media trap. We curate the "Highlight Reel." We post the photo with the perfect lighting, the fun hangout, the great outfit. But then we sit there refreshing the notifications. *Did they like it? Did she see it? Why didn't he comment?*
When you build your identity on the approval of others, you hand them the keys to your happiness. You become a shapeshifter, constantly changing your colors to fit whatever room you’re in, until you forget what you actually look like.

**Lie #3: You have to find your "Big Purpose" right now.**
This is a sneaky one. You’re 16 years old, and adults are constantly asking, "What are you going to do with your life?" We love superhero movies, so we think purpose has to be this massive, earth-shattering destiny. You feel like if you aren't starting a non-profit, becoming an influencer, or saving the planet by age 18, you’re falling behind. That is a crushing weight to carry.

If you feel tired, anxious, or like you’re just "acting" half the time... this is why. You are trying to build a self from scratch. It’s too heavy a burden for human shoulders.

### The Shift: Received, Not Achieved

So, what’s the alternative? If we don't build our identity, where does it come from?

I want you to imagine a different scenario. Imagine you are walking through a dusty attic, and you find an old, heavy chest. You open it up, and inside is a treasure. It’s gold, it’s diamonds, it’s priceless.

You didn't make the treasure. You didn't earn the treasure. You didn't assemble the treasure out of spare parts. You just *found* it. It was given to you.

The healthiest, most durable form of identity is **Received Identity**, not **Achieved Identity**.

This is the core message of faith and the core reality of being human: You are valuable not because of what you *do*, but because of who you *are*.

You are a created being. You were knit together intentionally. Before you ever took a test, scored a goal, or posted a photo, you were already infinitely valuable. Your worth is not a stock market price that fluctuates based on your performance today; it is a fixed fact.

Think about a newborn baby. What does a baby do? Nothing. They don't have jobs. They have zero Instagram followers. They are terrible at conversation. They just eat, sleep, and cry. And yet, their parents look at them with absolute, overwhelming love. They would die for that baby. Why? Because the baby *is* theirs.

That is who you are. You are loved simply because you exist.

When you really get this—when it moves from your head to your heart—it changes everything.

It means you can fail a test, and yes, it sucks, but it doesn't shatter you, because you aren't "The Smart Kid"—you are a loved human being who just happened to get a C.
It means you can get rejected by a crush, and it hurts, but it doesn't destroy you, because your value wasn't dependent on their opinion.
It means you can take off the mask. You can stop trying to be the "Avatar" you created, and just be the person you were created to be.

### Redefining Purpose: The Next Right Thing

"Okay," you might say. "That sounds nice. I’m valuable. Cool. But what am I supposed *to do*?"

This brings us to Purpose.

If your identity is secure—if you know you are loved and valuable regardless of your performance—then purpose changes. It stops being about *proving yourself* and starts being about *giving yourself*.

We need to lower the stakes on "Purpose." We tend to think Purpose means "What is my career for the next 50 years?" That’s too big. You can’t know that yet.

Instead, I want you to think about purpose as **"The Next Right Thing."**

There is an old saying: *"We can do no great things, only small things with great love."*

Your purpose right now, at 15 or 17 years old, isn't to be famous or to have your entire life mapped out. Your purpose is to look at the 10 square feet of space around you and bring light into it.

*   Your purpose is to be the friend who actually listens when someone is hurting, instead of just waiting for your turn to talk.
*   Your purpose is to treat your parents with respect, even when they’re annoying you.
*   Your purpose is to do your homework with integrity, not because grades are god, but because you’re faithful with what you’ve been given.
*   Your purpose is to notice the kid sitting alone in the cafeteria.

That doesn't feel as glamorous as being a Marvel superhero. But that is the stuff that actually changes the world. It’s the "ripple effect." You throw a small stone into a pond, and the ripples go out further than you can see.

When you stop trying to be "Impressive," you are free to be "Faithful." And trust me, faithfulness is rare these days. Being a steady, kind, honest person is a superpower in a world that is fake and flaky.

### Practical Takeaways

I want you to leave here with some tools. We talked about big concepts, but how do we live this out on a Tuesday morning when you’re tired and school is stressful? Here are three challenges for this week:

**1. The Social Media Audit**
I want you to take ten minutes tonight or tomorrow. Scroll through your "Following" list. Look at the accounts you follow. As you look at them, ask yourself: *Does looking at this person’s life inspire me, or does it make me feel inadequate? Does this account make me feel like I’m not enough?*
If the answer is "not enough," hit Unfollow. Or at least Mute. Curate your feed so it’s not constantly screaming at you that you need to be richer, hotter, or more popular to matter. Protect your head space.

**2. Change the "How Was Your Day?" Conversation**
We are programmed to talk about performance. "How was school?" usually means "What grades did you get?" "How was the game?" means "Did you win?"
This week, with your friends, try to ask questions about *them*, not their stats. Ask, "What made you laugh today?" or "How are you actually feeling about [X]?"
Practice seeing people for who they are, not what they achieved today. When you do that for others, it helps you accept it for yourself.

**3. Five Minutes of "Just Being"**
This is the hardest one. I challenge you to spend five minutes a day this week without your phone. No music, no podcasts, no scrolling. Just five minutes.
Sit in your room, or go for a walk. Remind yourself: *I exist even when I’m not online. I am real even when no one is watching. I am loved even when I’m not producing anything.*
It will feel awkward at first. You’ll reach for your pocket. But fight the urge. Reconnect with the reality that you are a human being, not a human doing.

### Closing

I want to end with this image.

Imagine you are an actor in a play. You’re wearing a heavy costume, a mask, and you’re under hot lights. You’ve been reciting lines for hours, trying to make the audience clap. You are exhausted, sweating, and terrified of forgetting a line.

Then, the curtain comes down. The show is over.
You walk backstage. You take off the heavy mask. You unzip the costume. You wipe off the makeup. You put on your sweatpants and your favorite hoodie. You walk out the back door, and there is your best friend, or your parent, or someone who loves you deeply, waiting in the car to take you home.

They don't care about the character you just played. They just want *you*.

That is what tonight is about. You can take the costume off. You can stop sliding the toggle bars on the character creator. You are already made. You are already known. You are already loved.

Your purpose isn't to create a fake version of yourself that the world will applaud. Your purpose is to be the real version of yourself that can love the world around you.

Thanks for listening, guys. Let’s break into our small groups.

**Title:** The Curator vs. The Creator: Finding Who You Are When the Screen Goes Dark
**Time:** Approx. 15-20 minutes
**Audience:** High School (14-18)

***

**(Open with a casual, relaxed stance. Maybe holding a phone, looking at it, then putting it away in a pocket.)**

Hey everyone.

I want to start by asking a question, but you don’t have to answer it out loud. In fact, it might be a little uncomfortable to answer out loud.

When you meet someone new—maybe you’re at a camp, or you’ve just joined a new team, or you’re sliding into a new discord server—and you have to introduce yourself, what is the first thing that goes through your mind?

Usually, it’s a quick mental scan of your "stats." We instantly think: *Okay, what am I good at? What’s my sport? What kind of music do I listen to? Who do I know that they might know?*

We immediately try to figure out our "Bio." You know what I mean? That little 150-character blurb on Instagram or TikTok that is supposed to summarize your entire existence. We agonize over those bios. We change the font. We add an emoji. We delete it. We write something cryptic so people think we’re mysterious. We write something funny so people think we’re chill.

We are all obsessed with curation. We act like museum curators, but the museum is our life. We carefully select which photos make the cut, which angles work, which grades we tell our parents about, and which parts of our personality we show to our friends versus our teachers.

It’s exhausting, isn’t it?

It’s like we are constantly auditioning for the role of "Myself."

Tonight, I want to talk about the heavy, often crushing weight of trying to invent your own identity, and I want to offer you a different way to live. A way that doesn’t require you to constantly perform. We’re going to talk about the difference between who the world says you are, and who you actually are.

**(The Pressure Cooker)**

Let’s be honest about the pressure. It’s not just in your head; it’s in the air you breathe. From the time you started middle school, you’ve been subtly (and sometimes loudly) told three lies about your identity.

**Lie #1: You are what you achieve.**
This is the "Report Card" lie. It says your value is a number. It’s your GPA, your SAT score, your batting average, or your rank in a video game. If you win, you matter. If you fail, you disappear. This makes life feel like a tightrope walk. If you slip up—if you bomb that math test or get cut from the varsity team—it feels like your actual worth as a human being drops. You feel like *you* are a failure, not just that you *experienced* a failure.

**Lie #2: You are what you look like.**
This is the "Mirror" lie, but today it’s mostly the "Filter" lie. It tells you that if you aren’t aesthetic, if you don’t have the right fit, the right body type, or the right hair, you aren’t worth paying attention to. We doom-scroll through feeds of people who have been photoshopped to perfection, and we compare our messy, behind-the-scenes reality with their curated highlight reel. And we always lose that comparison.

**Lie #3: You are what people say about you.**
This is the "Comment Section" lie. It says your identity is a democracy—that if enough people "like" you, then you must be valuable. But if people ignore you, or worse, if they roast you in a group chat, your value evaporates. It turns you into a chameleon, constantly changing your colors to fit in with whoever you’re standing next to, just to stay safe.

When you mix these three lies together, you get a generation—your generation, and honestly, mine too—that is riddled with anxiety. Why? Because if your identity is built on achievements, looks, or popularity, *it is unstable.*

Those things can be taken away in a second. You can get injured and lose the sport. You can have a bad hair day. You can say the wrong thing and get "cancelled" or ignored.

If your identity is something you have to build and sustain yourself, you will always be tired. You will always be wondering, "Have I done enough? Am I enough?"

**(The Pivot: A Better Vision)**

I want to suggest that there is a massive difference between your *image* and your *identity*.

Your image is what you project. It’s the Avatar. It changes. It’s fragile.
Your identity is who you are when the phone creates a black mirror—when the screen is off, the lights are out, and it’s just you and your thoughts.

The antidote to the pressure of performance is realizing that true identity isn’t achieved; it is *received*.

Think about a $100 bill. If I take a crisp, fresh $100 bill from the bank, it’s worth $100. If I crumple it up into a ball, stomp on it, throw it in the dirt, and tear a tiny corner off... how much is it worth?

It’s still worth $100.

Why? Because its value doesn’t come from how clean it is. It doesn’t come from how crisp it looks. Its value comes from the authority that issued it. The Treasury says, "This has value," so it has value.

You are the same. Your value is not determined by your performance, your aesthetic, or your follower count. Your value is intrinsic. It is built-in.

**(The Spiritual Anchor)**

*Note: If this is a secular group, focus on human dignity. If this is a faith-based group, this is where you bring in the theology.*

In the Christian worldview, we say that you are made in the *Imago Dei*—the image of God. That means before you ever took a test, before you ever scored a goal, before you ever posted a photo, you were already infinitely valuable.

There is a profound freedom in realizing: **"I do not have to earn my right to exist."**

When you understand that you are loved simply because you exist, it breaks the chains of performance. You stop working *for* approval, and you start working *from* approval.

Imagine how different your week would be if you walked into school tomorrow knowing, "I’m already accepted. I’m already loved. The most important thing about me is settled."

If you bomb the test? It sucks, but it doesn’t destroy you.
If someone makes a mean comment? It hurts, but it doesn’t define you.
Because your foundation is deeper than your circumstances.

**(Connecting Identity to Purpose)**

So, if you don’t have to spend all your energy building your identity and proving your worth, what do you do with your life?

That brings us to **Purpose**.

A lot of people ask, "What is my purpose?" as if it’s a hidden treasure map they have to find. They think purpose is a job title, like "My purpose is to be a doctor" or "My purpose is to be a YouTuber."

But purpose isn't a job. Purpose is a posture.

If your identity is "I am loved and valuable," then your purpose is simply **to give that value away.**

When you are insecure, you use people. You use them to make yourself feel better, to look cool, to not feel lonely. You suck energy out of the room because you need validation.

But when you are secure in your identity, you become a source of life. You walk into a room and you aren’t thinking, "What do these people think of me?" You’re thinking, "How can I love these people?"

That is a massive shift.

Your purpose right now, at 15 or 16 or 17, isn't to figure out your entire career path. Your purpose is to look at the unique way you were designed—your personality, your talents, the things that make you angry, the things that make you cry, the things that make you laugh—and ask, "How can I use this to make the world around me a little bit brighter?"

Maybe you’re really good at listening. Your purpose this week is to find the friend who is hurting and just listen.
Maybe you’re hilarious. Your purpose is to bring joy to a stressful classroom.
Maybe you’re athletic. Your purpose is to be the teammate who encourages everyone else, rather than the one who hogs the ball.

Purpose is what happens when your unique design meets the world’s needs.

**(Practical Takeaways)**

I don’t want to just leave you with nice philosophical thoughts. I want to give you three things you can actually do this week to shift from "Performance" to "Purpose."

**1. The "Unfollow" Audit.**
This is a challenge. Tonight, before you go to bed, look at your social media. Scroll through the first 20 people or accounts. As you look at each one, ask yourself: *Does this account make me feel inspired and capable, or does it make me feel insecure and competitive?*
If an account constantly makes you feel like you aren’t enough—even if it’s a friend, even if it’s a celebrity—mute them or unfollow them. Protect your headspace. You cannot build a healthy identity if you are constantly feeding your brain garbage data that says you aren't enough.

**2. The Mirror Talk.**
We all talk to ourselves. Most of the time, we are our own worst bullies. We look in the mirror and say, "Ugh, my skin." "I’m so awkward." "I’m stupid."
I want you to try to catch yourself doing that this week. When you hear that negative voice, I want you to literally stop and flip the script. Remind yourself of the $100 bill. Say, "I am valuable. I am made on purpose." It feels cheesy at first. Do it anyway. You have to rewire your brain to accept your own worth.

**3. Do One Secret Thing.**
We live in a world where if you didn’t post it, it didn’t happen. This week, I want you to do one act of kindness or service that nobody else knows about. Clean the kitchen for your parents without being asked (and don’t mention it). Leave an encouraging note in someone’s locker unsigned. Donate some of your own money to a cause.
Why? Because doing good things without getting "credit" for them proves to your own soul that you are doing them for the right reasons. It builds character, not just reputation. It reminds you that your purpose is to give, not to get likes.

**(Conclusion)**

Look, I know this isn’t easy. We are swimming upstream. The whole world is screaming at you to buy more, achieve more, and post more to be happy.

But the most radical, rebellious thing you can do as a teenager today is to refuse to play that game.

To decide that you are not a product to be sold. You are not a resume to be polished. You are a human being, full of complexity, messy parts, and brilliant light.

You are loved. You have a purpose that is bigger than your popularity.

So, take a deep breath. Drop the shoulders. Let go of the need to be perfect. And go out there and just be the person you were actually created to be.

Thanks, guys.

**Title:** The Avatar and the Anchor: Finding Who You Are in a World of Noise
**Audience:** High School Youth Group (Ages 14–18)
**Time:** Approx. 15-20 Minutes

***

**[The Opening]**

I want to start by asking you a question that is simultaneously very simple and completely terrifying.

Imagine you are setting up a profile on a new app. Or maybe you’re at a college interview. Or maybe you’re just on a first date. And someone looks at you and says:

*"So, tell me about yourself."*

Does anyone else’s brain just immediately flatline when that happens? It’s panic, right? Because you know what they’re asking. They aren’t asking for your biological stats. They’re asking: *Who are you?*

And suddenly, you feel this pressure to curate a version of yourself that sounds impressive but casual, successful but humble, interesting but not weird.

We live in a world that is obsessed with the "Bio." We are constantly being asked to summarize our existence in 150 characters, or a grid of nine photos, or a resume of extracurriculars. We treat our identity like it’s an avatar in a video game that we have to build from scratch. We have to pick the outfit, pick the skills, pick the aesthetic, and then hope that the other players in the game like what we’ve built.

And honestly? It is exhausting.

I look around this room, and I see a lot of talent, a lot of humor, and a lot of potential. But if I’m being honest, I think I also see a lot of exhaustion. Because trying to invent yourself, day after day, is the hardest job in the world.

Tonight, I want to talk about why that pressure feels so heavy, and I want to offer you a different way to look at who you are—a way that doesn’t require you to hustle for your worth.

**[The Three Lies of Identity]**

If we look at the culture we’re swimming in, there are three main lies we are told about how to build an identity. You probably hear these whispered in your ear—or shouted from your phone screen—every single day.

**Lie #1: I am what I achieve.**
This is the pressure of the report card and the scoreboard. It’s the voice that says you are only as valuable as your last success. If you get the A, if you make the varsity team, if you get into the "right" college, then you matter.

The problem with tying your identity to your achievements is that you are only ever one bad day away from losing your identity. If you are the "smart kid," who are you when you fail a test? If you are the "athlete," who are you when you tear your ACL? If your identity is built on winning, you will live in constant fear of losing.

**Lie #2: I am how I appear.**
We all know this one. It’s the tyranny of the image. It’s the belief that if you can just get your skin clear, your style right, and your gym routine perfect, you will finally feel good about yourself.

Social media has weaponized this. We don’t just live our lives anymore; we perform them. We curate the highlights. But we all know the truth, don’t we? We know that the person in the post is a filtered, edited version of the person holding the phone. When we anchor our identity in our appearance, we become obsessed with the mirror, constantly checking to see if we still measure up.

**Lie #3: I am what people say about me.**
This is the popularity trap. It’s the idea that your worth is a democracy—that if enough people "like" you, follow you, or invite you to the party, then you must be valuable.

But the crowd is fickle. The same people who hype you up on Tuesday can ghost you on Friday. If you give people the power to define your worth, you also give them the power to destroy it.

**[The Performance Trap]**

When you combine these three things—achievement, appearance, and approval—you get what I call the **Performance Trap**.

The Performance Trap tells you that identity is something you *achieve*, not something you *receive*. It tells you that you are a project to be managed.

I want you to imagine a house of cards. It can look impressive. It can be tall and intricate. But because it’s held up by nothing but balance and tension, you have to be terrified of the wind. You can’t breathe too hard. You can’t relax. You have to constantly maintain it.

That is how so many of us are living. We are walking around terrified that if we slip up, if we aren’t funny enough, or smart enough, or good-looking enough, the whole house of cards will collapse, and we’ll be exposed as frauds.

And deep down, we are all asking the same question: *If I stripped away the filters, the grades, and the accolades... is the person underneath actually enough?*

**[A Different Vision: The Anchor]**

I want to suggest that the world has it backward.

Real, lasting identity isn’t built from the outside in; it’s found from the inside out. It’s not something you achieve; it’s something you receive.

Think about an anchor. An anchor doesn’t work because it’s pretty. It doesn’t work because it tries really hard. An anchor works because it connects to something solid, something immovable outside of the boat.

If you want an identity that can handle the storms of high school—the breakups, the failures, the stress—you need to hook into something deeper than your performance.

So, what is that solid ground?

*(Note: Depending on the specific context of the group—secular, Christian, or general spiritual—you can adapt the following section. Below is written for a broad spiritual/Christian context, which is typical for youth groups).*

The solid ground is this: **You are known, and you are loved.**

I believe that before you ever took a test, before you ever posted a photo, and before you ever impressed anyone, you already had value. Your value is inherent. It is built-in.

There is a concept in philosophy and theology called "imago Dei"—the image of God. It means that you are not an accident. You aren’t just a random collection of cells fighting for survival. You are a masterpiece, designed with intention.

When your identity is grounded in the fact that you are loved by your Creator (and by the people who truly see you), the pressure lifts.

Suddenly, you don’t *have* to get the A to be valuable; you try to get the A because you want to steward your mind.
You don’t *have* to look perfect to be worthy of love; you take care of yourself because you respect the body you were given.
You don’t *have* to impress people to earn your spot; you are free to love people because you already have a spot.

See the difference?
The world says: *Do this, and you will be someone.*
Grace says: *You are someone, so now you are free to do.*

When you know who you are, you don’t have to shout. You don’t have to flex. You don’t have to prove anything. You can just *be*.

**[Purpose: The Result of Identity]**

And here is the cool part. When you stop obsessing over your *identity*, you finally find your *purpose*.

When you are trapped in the Performance Trap, your purpose is just "Self-Preservation." Your whole life is about protecting your ego and making yourself look good. It’s a very small, cramped way to live.

But when you are secure—when you know you are loved and that your worth is not on the line—you can finally look outward. You can stop looking in the mirror and start looking out the window.

You can ask different questions. Instead of asking, "How do I make people like me?", you can ask, "How can I love people?"
Instead of asking, "How can I be the most successful person in the room?", you can ask, "How can I help the people in this room succeed?"

Real purpose isn’t about becoming famous. It’s about becoming useful. It’s about taking your unique mix of talents, weirdness, and passions, and using them to make the world a little less broken and a little more beautiful.

**[Practical Takeaways]**

Okay, that’s the philosophy. But how do we actually live this out on a Tuesday morning when you’re tired and stressed?

I want to give you three challenges for this week. Three ways to shift from Performance to Presence.

**1. The "Social Media Audit"**
I want you to take ten minutes tonight and look at your feed. Pay attention to your body and your brain as you scroll. When you see certain accounts, do you feel inspired and happy? Or do you feel jealous, anxious, and "less than"?
If an account makes you feel like you aren’t enough, **mute them or unfollow them.** You are not obligated to consume content that poisons your sense of self. Protect your headspace. Curate a feed that reminds you of reality, not one that demands you perform.

**2. Change Your "Scoreboard"**
Most of us go to bed asking, "What did I achieve today?" or "Did I mess up?"
I want you to change the metric. Before you go to sleep, ask yourself: *"Who did I encourage today?"* or *"Where was I brave today?"*
Start valuing your character more than your resume. If you were kind to the kid sitting alone at lunch, that matters more to your actual identity than getting a 95 on your chem quiz. Remind yourself of that.

**3. The "Phone-Free 15"**
We are terrified of silence because in the silence, the questions of identity come up. So we drown them out with podcasts and music.
Every day this week, spend 15 minutes without headphones and without a screen. Walk the dog, sit in your room, wash the dishes. Just be with yourself.
Learn to be comfortable in your own skin without needing to be entertained. It’s in the quiet that you remember who you actually are.

**[Conclusion]**

I’ll close with this.

There is a Japanese art form called *Kintsugi*. When a precious bowl or vase breaks, they don’t throw it away. Instead, they put it back together using gold lacquer to fill the cracks.

The result is that the object becomes even more beautiful and valuable *because* of its broken history. The cracks aren’t hidden; they are highlighted.

The world tells you to hide your cracks. It tells you to use a filter, to pretend you’re perfect, to present a flawless avatar.

But true identity—the kind that gives you deep, unshakable purpose—is like *Kintsugi*. It embraces your whole story. It embraces your struggles, your quirks, and your imperfections, and it holds them together with love.

You do not need to be perfect to be powerful. You do not need to be famous to be significant.

You just need to be you—the real you, the one behind the screen. That person is enough. That person is loved. And that person has a purpose that the world is waiting for.

Thanks for listening, guys.

Have you ever been sitting in a circle on the first day of school, or maybe even here at youth group, and the leader says those dreaded words: *“Let’s go around the room. Say your name, your grade, and a fun fact about yourself.”* 

I don’t know about you, but the moment I hear “fun fact,” my brain completely short-circuits. Suddenly, I forget every hobby I’ve ever had. I forget where I’ve traveled. I forget what music I listen to. I sit there sweating, thinking, *Am I fun? Have I ever done a fact? Who am I?* 

It’s a funny kind of panic, but it points to something much deeper. We live in a world that is obsessed with asking you to define yourself. 

Think about the bio section on your Instagram or TikTok. You get about 150 characters to sum up your entire existence. What do you put? A witty quote? Your graduation year? Your sport? Your relationship status? A string of carefully curated emojis that make you look mysterious but approachable? 

It is exhausting. And it’s exhausting because you are currently living in a pressure cooker. 

You guys are the most measured, tested, and observed generation in human history. From the moment you wake up to the moment you go to sleep, you are being handed different scorecards, and the world is demanding that you prove your worth. 

There are really three main scorecards the world hands you right now. 

The first is **Achievement**. This is the pressure of the grade portal. It’s the pressure of making the varsity team, getting the lead in the play, or building the perfect college resume by the time you’re sixteen. Society tells you: *You are what you achieve. If you are successful, you matter. If you fail, you are a failure.*

The second scorecard is **Appearance**. This isn't just about physical looks, though that pressure is massive. It’s about the "aesthetic." Do you have the right clothes? The right vibe? Do you look like you’re trying too hard, or do you look effortlessly flawless? Society tells you: *You are how you are perceived. If you look good, you are good.*

The third scorecard is **Social Standing**. This is the group chat. It’s your follower count. It’s who you sit with at lunch. It’s the anxiety of seeing your friends hang out on Snapchat maps without you. Honestly, managing your social life today is like running a 24/7 public relations firm for yourself, and you don’t even get paid for it. Society tells you: *You are who likes you. If you are popular, you are important.*

Here is the brutal truth about building your identity on achievement, appearance, or social standing: The goalpost always moves. 

If your identity is your grades, what happens when you take a class that is just too hard? If your identity is your sport, who are you if you blow out your knee? If your identity is how many likes you get, what happens when the algorithm changes or people move on? 

Building your identity on these things is like trying to build a house on the ocean. You will spend your entire life desperately trying to keep your head above water, terrified of the next wave. It leads to burnout, anxiety, and a deep, quiet loneliness. You start to wonder, *If I stop performing, will anyone still love me?*

I want to offer you a completely different way to look at who you are. 

What if your identity isn’t something you have to **achieve**? What if it’s something you **receive**?

Think about a masterpiece in a museum. Imagine the *Mona Lisa* hanging in the Louvre. That painting doesn't *do* anything. It doesn't get good grades. It doesn't post on TikTok. It just hangs there behind bulletproof glass. 

So why is it priceless? Two reasons: Because of the Artist who painted it, and because of the price someone is willing to pay to protect it. 

The same is true for you. In the deepest, truest, spiritual sense, your identity is a masterpiece. You were made on purpose, with deliberate intention, by a Creator who looks at you and says, “That one is mine. And they are incredibly valuable.” 

Your identity is not "straight-A student." It is not "point guard." It is not "the funny one in the friend group." 

Your core identity is simply this: **You are known, and you are beloved.** 

You don’t have to earn it. You can’t lose it. You can’t ruin it with a bad mistake, and you can’t improve it by being perfect. Before you ever do a single productive thing today, you have infinite worth. 

When you actually start to believe that—when you let that sink into your bones—it changes everything. Especially how you view your **purpose**.

We get identity and purpose backward all the time. We think, *I need to find a great purpose—like becoming a doctor, or an influencer, or an activist—so that I can finally be somebody.* We use our purpose to try and build our identity. 

But when you already know who you are—when you know you are infinitely loved and valuable—your purpose completely changes. You no longer do things to *become* someone. You do things because of *who you already are*. 

Purpose isn’t a job title you’re going to get when you’re 25. Purpose is how you live out your true identity right now, today, in the specific corner of the world you’ve been placed in. 

Your purpose tomorrow morning is to walk into the cafeteria and look for the person who feels invisible. Your purpose is to use your talents—whether that’s music, math, empathy, or humor—to bring a little bit of light into a world that can be really dark. Your purpose is to be a good friend, a kind sibling, and a person of integrity. 

You don't have to change the whole world to have a profound purpose; you just have to change the temperature of the rooms you walk into.

So, how do we actually live this out? It’s easy to sit in a youth group room, listen to a talk, and nod along. It’s much harder on a Tuesday morning when your alarm goes off at 6:00 AM, you have a history test you didn't study enough for, and someone left you on read. 

I want to give you three practical things—three challenges—to try this week to help anchor yourself in this deeper identity.

**Number One: Audit your mirrors.** 
We all use mirrors to tell us who we are. For a lot of us, our primary mirror is a six-inch glowing screen. This week, I want you to pay attention to how you feel after you scroll. If you spend an hour looking at a mirror that tells you you aren't attractive enough, smart enough, or cool enough, you are going to believe it. Try an "input fast." Pick one day this week, or even just one evening, where you put the phone in another room. Break the cycle of constantly comparing your behind-the-scenes to everyone else’s highlight reel. Look into better mirrors: the people who actually know you and love you, and the quiet moments where you can just breathe and be yourself.

**Number Two: The "Rest Test."**
So much of your life is about performance and getting better at things. This week, I want you to do one thing that you are completely, spectacularly bad at—and I want you to do it just for fun. If you are terrible at art, get some cheap watercolors and paint a terrible picture. If you have two left feet, put on music in your room and dance badly. Why? Because you need to remind your brain and your soul that your worth is not tied to your excellence. You are allowed to just exist. You are allowed to enjoy things without having to monetize them or put them on a college application. 

**Number Three: The "Mirror Flip."**
The best way to remember your own true identity is to help someone else see theirs. Sometime this week, I want you to call out the gold in someone else. And I don’t mean just complimenting their outfit. Tell a friend, "Hey, I noticed how you included that new kid the other day. You are a really kind person." Tell your sibling, "You always know how to make me laugh when I'm stressed." When we affirm the deeper identity in others—when we see them for who they truly are—it builds a culture where we don't have to fake it anymore. It gives everyone permission to drop the masks.

Guys, high school is a messy, beautiful, chaotic, stressful time. You are figuring out who you are, and that is a process. It’s okay if you don’t have it all figured out. 

But I want you to hear this loud and clear: You do not need to shrink your soul down to fit into a 150-character bio. You are infinitely complex, beautifully flawed, and deeply loved. 

You don't have to perform anymore. You don't have to hustle for your worth. You can step off the treadmill. 

Take a deep breath. Remember who you are. Remember *whose* you are. And then go out into your schools, your teams, and your families, and live with the quiet, unshakeable confidence of someone who knows they are a masterpiece. 

Thank you.

Do you look like you’re trying too hard, or have you mastered that perfectly curated, “I just woke up like this” look? Society tells you: *You are how you are perceived. If you look good, you are good.*

It is exhausting. And it’s exhausting because you are currently living in a pressure cooker. 

You guys are the most measured, tested, and observed generation in human history. From the moment you wake up to the moment you go to sleep, you are being handed different scorecards, and the world is demanding that you prove your worth. It’s the feeling when an adult asks, “What are you going to do after graduation?” and your stomach drops. You know they’re not just asking about your college or career plans; it feels like they’re really asking, *“What is your value going to be?”*

There are really three main scorecards the world hands you right now. 

The first is **Achievement**. This is the pressure of the grade portal that updates constantly. It’s the pressure of making the varsity team, getting the lead in the play, or building the perfect, flawless college resume by the time you’re sixteen. Society tells you: *You are what you achieve. If you are successful, you matter. If you fail, you are a failure.*

The second scorecard is **Appearance**. This isn't just about physical looks, though that pressure is massive and relentless. It’s about the "aesthetic." Do you have the right clothes? The right vibe? Do you look like you’re trying too hard, or do you look effortlessly flawless? Society tells you: *You are how you are perceived. If you look good, you are good.*

The third scorecard is **Social Standing**. This is the group chat. It’s your follower count. It’s who you sit with at lunch. It’s the anxiety of opening your phone and seeing your friends hanging out on Snapchat maps without you. Honestly, managing your social life today is like running a 24/7 public relations firm for yourself, and you don’t even get paid for it. Society tells you: *You are who likes you. If you are popular, you are important.*

Here is the brutal truth about building your identity on achievement, appearance, or social standing: The goalpost always moves. 

If your identity is your grades, what happens when you take a class that is just too hard? If your identity is your sport, who are you if you blow out your knee? If your identity is how many likes you get, what happens when the algorithm changes or people move on? 

Building your identity on these things is like trying to build a house on the ocean. You will spend your entire life desperately trying to keep your head above water, terrified of the next wave. It leads to burnout, anxiety, and a deep, quiet loneliness. You start to wonder, *If I stop performing, will anyone still love me?*

I want to offer you a completely different way to look at who you are. 

What if your identity isn’t something you have to **achieve**? What if it’s something you **receive**?

Think about a masterpiece in a museum. Imagine the *Mona Lisa* hanging in the Louvre. That painting doesn't *do* anything. It doesn't get good grades. It doesn't post on TikTok. It doesn't hustle to make sure the other paintings like it. It just hangs there behind bulletproof glass. 

So why is it priceless? Two reasons: Because of the Artist who painted it, and because of the incredible price someone is willing to pay to protect it. 

Now, I know that might sound like a nice, poetic theory. In a world obsessed with scorecards, the idea of having unconditional worth can feel incredibly abstract. It might even sound a little naive. How do you actually *feel* priceless when you’re staring at a C- on a chemistry test, or when someone leaves a mean comment on your post, or when you’re sitting alone at lunch? It is really hard to believe you are a masterpiece when you feel like a sketch someone erased.

I get that. But the truth of your value doesn't change based on your ability to feel it on your worst days. 

In the deepest, truest, spiritual sense, your identity is a masterpiece. You were made on purpose, with deliberate intention, by a Creator who looks at you and says, “That one is mine. And they are incredibly valuable.” 

Your identity is not "straight-A student." It is not "point guard." It is not "the funny one in the friend group." 

Your core identity is simply this: **You are known, and you are beloved.** 

You don’t have to earn it. You can’t lose it. You can’t ruin it with a bad mistake, and you can’t improve it by being perfect. Before you ever do a single productive thing today, you have infinite worth. 

When you actually start to believe that—when you let that sink into your bones—it changes everything. Especially how you view your **purpose**.

We get identity and purpose backward all the time. We think purpose is this giant, distant thing—*“I need to be a famous marine biologist or a massive influencer to matter.”* We use our purpose to try and build our identity. 

But if your core identity is already "beloved," then your purpose today isn't about *becoming* valuable. It's about *reflecting* that value. When you finally believe you're a masterpiece, your job isn't to frantically repaint yourself to match the current trends; your job is just to let people see the art. 

You no longer do things to *become* someone. You do things because of *who you already are*. 

Purpose isn’t a job title you’re going to get when you’re 25. Purpose is how you live out your true identity right now, today, in the specific corner of the world you’ve been placed in. Your purpose tomorrow morning is to walk into the cafeteria and look for the person who feels invisible. Your purpose is to use your talents—whether that’s music, math, empathy, or humor—to bring a little bit of light into a world that can be really dark. Your purpose is to be a good friend, a kind sibling, and a person of integrity. 

You don't have to change the whole world to have a profound purpose; you just have to change the temperature of the rooms you walk into.

So, how do we actually live this out? It’s easy to sit in a youth group room, listen to a talk, and nod along. It’s much harder on a Tuesday morning when your alarm goes off at 6:00 AM, you have a history test you didn't study enough for, and someone left you on read. 

I want to give you three practical things—three challenges—to try this week to help anchor yourself in this deeper identity.

**Number One: Audit your mirrors.** 
We all use mirrors to tell us who we are. For a lot of us, our primary mirror is a six-inch glowing screen. This week, I want you to pay attention to how you feel after you scroll. If you spend an hour looking at a mirror that tells you you aren't attractive enough, smart enough, or cool enough, you are going to believe it. Try an "input fast." Pick one day this week, or even just one evening, where you put the phone in another room and do something else instead. Read a book you actually like, go for a walk without your AirPods, play an instrument badly, or cook something. Break the cycle of constantly comparing your behind-the-scenes to everyone else’s highlight reel. Look into better mirrors: the people who actually know you and love you, and the quiet moments where you can just breathe and be yourself.

**Number Two: The "Rest Test."**
So much of your life is about performance and getting better at things. This week, I want you to do one thing that you are completely, spectacularly bad at—and I want you to do it just for fun. If you are terrible at art, get some cheap watercolors and paint a terrible picture. If you have two left feet, put on music in your room and dance badly. Why? Because you need to remind your brain and your soul that your worth is not tied to your excellence. You are allowed to just exist. You are allowed to enjoy things without having to monetize them, perfect them, or put them on a college application. 

**Number Three: The "Mirror Flip."**
The best way to remember your own true identity is to help someone else see theirs. Sometime this week, I want you to call out the gold in someone else. And I don’t mean just complimenting their outfit. Try using the phrase, "I see you." Tell a friend, "I see how hard you worked on that project, and I’m proud of you." Tell your sibling, "I see your kindness when you included that new kid." Or, "I see how you always know how to make me laugh when I'm stressed." When we affirm the deeper identity in others—when we see them for who they truly are—it builds a culture where we don't have to fake it anymore. It gives everyone permission to drop the masks.

Guys, high school is a messy, beautiful, chaotic, stressful time. You are figuring out who you are, and that is a process. It’s okay if you don’t have it all figured out. 

But I want you to hear this loud and clear: You do not need to shrink your soul down to fit into a 150-character bio. You are infinitely complex, beautifully flawed, and deeply loved. 

You don't have to perform anymore. You don't have to hustle for your worth. You can step off the treadmill. 

Take a deep breath. Remember who you are—a masterpiece, not a scorecard. Remember the Artist who made you, and whose love for you is the frame that holds your life together. And then go out into your schools, your teams, and your families, and live with the quiet, unshakeable confidence of someone who knows exactly what they are worth. 

Thank you.

Have you ever noticed how terrifying the simplest questions can be? 

If I walked up to you right now and asked, “What is the square root of 81?” or “What’s the capital of Australia?”, you might know the answer, or you might not. But if you didn't know it, you wouldn't have a minor existential crisis. You’d just pull out your phone and Google it. 

But what if we are sitting in a circle, and someone says those dreaded words: *“Let’s go around the room. Tell us your name, what you do, and a fun fact about yourself.”*

Suddenly, your heart rate spikes. Your palms start sweating. You forget every interesting thing that has ever happened to you. You sit there thinking, *“A fun fact? I don’t have fun facts. I eat cereal and watch YouTube. Am I funny? Am I smart? Who am I? What is my life?”*

Why does that happen? Why does introducing ourselves feel like defusing a bomb? 

I think it’s because that simple icebreaker pokes at the single heaviest, most overwhelming question you are carrying around right now: *Who are you?* 

And closely followed by its equally stressful cousin: *What are you going to do with your life?*

If you are between the ages of fourteen and eighteen right now, you are living in the crosshairs of those two questions. Every day, from the moment you wake up to the moment you finally put your phone on the charger at night, you are being asked to define your identity and figure out your purpose. 

And I just want to start by being completely honest with you: It is exhausting. I know it is. I see it. 

You are growing up in a world that has handed you a very specific, very toxic formula for figuring out who you are. The world tells you: **Identity = Performance + Audience.**

Let’s break that down. 

First, performance. We are told that we are what we *do*. We are what we achieve. So, you build your identity on your grades. You are the "smart kid." Or you build it on the field or the court. You are the "athlete." Or maybe it's your appearance. You are the "attractive one," the one who knows how to put together the perfect fit, the one whose aesthetic is always flawless. 

Second, the audience. Performance doesn't matter if nobody is clapping. So, we take those achievements, and we put them on a stage. And today, that stage is in your pocket. Social media has turned all of us into our own PR managers. You aren't just living your life; you are *curating* it. You post the photo, you tweak the caption, you check the views, you count the likes. It’s like an identity slot machine. You pull the lever and hold your breath, hoping the metrics will tell you that you matter today.

But here is the brutal truth about the "Performance + Audience" formula: It is a treadmill that never, ever stops. 

If your identity is built on being the smartest person in the room, what happens when you get to a room where you aren’t? If your identity is built on being the star athlete, what happens when you tear your ACL? If your identity is built on how you look or how many people view your TikTok, what happens when the algorithm shifts, or somebody younger and cooler comes along? 

When you build your identity on things you have to achieve, your identity is incredibly fragile. You are only ever as good as your last success. It creates a quiet, lingering anxiety—a voice whispering in the back of your head: *“If they really knew me, if I stopped performing, if I dropped the ball... would I still matter?”*

I want to offer you a different way to live. I want to offer you a vision of your identity that doesn't shatter when you have a bad day. 

What if your identity isn't something you have to *achieve*? What if it is something you simply *receive*?

Think about a $100 bill. If I hold up a crisp, brand new $100 bill, how much is it worth? A hundred dollars. Now, what if I crumple it up into a tiny ball? What if I throw it on the ground and step on it? What if I drag it through the mud? How much is it worth now? 

It’s still worth $100. Its value didn't drop because it got dirty. Its value didn't change because it got crushed. Why? Because the value of that bill isn't determined by what it has been through, or how crisp and perfect it looks. Its value is determined by the stamp of the Treasury that created it. Its worth is intrinsic. It is baked in.

You need to know tonight that your worth is exactly the same. 

You are not a human *doing*. You are a human *being*. Before you ever get a good grade, before you ever make a varsity team, before you ever get a single like, comment, or acceptance letter—you have immeasurable, profound, unshakable worth. 

For those of us coming from a faith perspective, we believe this is because you carry the fingerprint of the Divine. You were made intentionally. You are a masterpiece crafted by a Creator who looked at you and said, "This one is very good." But regardless of where you are at with faith tonight, the truth remains: Your value is not up for debate. It is not on a sliding scale. You do not have to hustle for your right to take up space in this world. 

When you finally grasp that—when you move from an *achieved* identity to a *received* identity—it changes absolutely everything. It is the deepest exhale your soul can take. You can finally step off the treadmill. You can still play sports, you can still study hard, you can still create cool things—but you do them for the joy of it, not because your soul depends on the outcome. You are no longer performing to *get* an identity; you are living *from* an identity. 

And this brings us to the second big question: *Purpose.* 

If identity is *who* you are, purpose is *what* you are supposed to do. 

A lot of you are stressing out because you think "purpose" means picking your college major right now, or knowing exactly what career you want for the next fifty years. Let me let you in on a secret: Adults don’t have it all figured out either. Most of us are just making it up as we go. 

Purpose is not a job title. Purpose is a posture. 

Your purpose is simply to take the unique, inherently valuable person that you are, and spend your life giving that away to the world around you. Your purpose is to leave people, places, and spaces a little better, a little brighter, and a little more loved than how you found them. 

You don't have to wait until you are twenty-five to find your purpose. Your purpose is sitting next to you in the cafeteria tomorrow. Your purpose is in how you treat your sibling when they are annoying you. Your purpose is in how you respond to the kid at school who always sits alone. 

So, how do we actually live this out? How do we stop defining ourselves by the pressure, and start living from this deeper place? I want to give you three practical things you can do this week.

**Number one: Audit your inputs.** 
We are shaped by the voices we listen to. If you are following accounts on Instagram or TikTok that constantly make you feel like you aren't pretty enough, rich enough, or successful enough—unfollow them. Mute them. Seriously, do it tonight. Take control of your feed. If a voice in your life is feeding the "performance" treadmill, turn the volume down. Replace it with voices, friends, and mentors who remind you of your inherent worth.

**Number two: Take the "Who am I when I fail?" test.** 
Sometime this week, you are going to mess up. You’ll bomb a quiz, you’ll miss a shot, you’ll say something awkward. When it happens, I want you to pause and pay attention to how you talk to yourself. Do you say, "I am a failure"? If so, correct it. Say out loud, "I *experienced* a failure, but I *am* deeply valuable." Separate your worth from your outcome. Practice giving yourself the same grace you would give your best friend.

**Number three: Shift from "Prove" to "Provide."** 
When you walk into a room—a classroom, a party, a youth group—the natural human instinct is to ask, *“How do I look? What do they think of me? How can I prove I belong here?”* This week, I want you to try flipping the script. When you walk into a room, ask, *“Who here needs encouragement? What can I provide?”* When you stop worrying about proving your own worth, you are finally free to notice the people around you. And there is nothing more purposeful than making someone else feel seen.

Life is going to keep asking you to introduce yourself. It’s going to keep demanding that you boil yourself down to a resume, a bio, or a highlight reel. 

When that happens, I want you to smile, take a deep breath, and remember that you are so much more than your stats. You are not your grades. You are not your followers. You are not your worst mistake, and you are not your greatest achievement. 

You are a deeply loved, intentionally crafted human being. Your worth is secure. Your purpose is right in front of you. Now go out there, step off the treadmill, and just be who you were made to be. 

Thank you.
