Let me start with a question you don’t have to answer out loud:

If I took your phone right now—opened your camera roll, your messages, your search history, your notes app, and your most-used apps… what version of you would I think you are?

Not the “you” you are in your head. Not the “you” you are when you’re alone. The “you” that shows up in what you save, what you scroll, what you laugh at, what you obsess over, what you compare yourself to, what you keep going back to when you’re bored or stressed.

Because honestly, a lot of us feel like we’re living in public even when we’re by ourselves.

And that gets right to tonight’s topic: identity and purpose—who you are, and what you’re here for.

---

## 1) The pressure to be “someone”

Being a teenager right now is like being handed a blank profile and being told, “Fill it in—correctly.” And not just once. Every day.

You’re not only trying to figure out what you like; you’re trying to figure out what will *work*.

- What will get noticed.
- What will get approval.
- What will get you into the team, the program, the friend group.
- What will make you look like you have a life.
- What will keep you from being judged.
- What will keep you safe.

And you feel it from a bunch of directions at once.

**Achievement pressure:** “Be impressive. Be productive. Be exceptional.” Grades, sports, leadership, awards, college, future, future, future. Sometimes it feels like your value is a moving target—like you’re only as good as your last test score or your last game.

**Appearance pressure:** “Be attractive. Be stylish. Be put together.” And not even in a normal way—more like, “Be camera-ready, at all times.” Which is exhausting. And the standard keeps changing.

**Social pressure:** “Be likable. Be included. Be interesting.” And social media doesn’t just show you other people’s lives—it shows you what they chose to post. Which is basically their highlight reel, with good lighting and a soundtrack.

Here’s the tricky part: none of these are evil things. Achievements can be great. Taking care of yourself matters. Friends matter. The problem isn’t having these things. The problem is when they start having *you*.

When achievement becomes your identity, a bad grade doesn’t just disappoint you—it threatens you.  
When appearance becomes your identity, a breakout or an unflattering photo feels like a crisis.  
When social approval becomes your identity, being left on read can mess with your whole day.

And then you start asking questions that sound like purpose questions, but they’re actually identity questions:

- “What should I do with my life?” sometimes really means “What will make me matter?”
- “What am I good at?” sometimes really means “What makes me worth keeping around?”
- “What do I want to be?” sometimes really means “What will make people respect me?”

If you’ve ever felt that kind of pressure, you’re not dramatic. You’re human.

---

## 2) The problem with building your identity on fragile things

Here’s a hard truth: most of the things we’re tempted to build our identity on are fragile.

Achievement is fragile because there’s always someone better, and there’s always another level. Even if you win, it doesn’t last long. The moment you succeed, the next expectation shows up.

Appearance is fragile because your body changes, trends change, and people’s opinions definitely change. And no one—no matter how “perfect” they look online—can hold that standard forever.

Popularity is fragile because relationships shift, drama happens, friend groups change, people move, people ghost, people misunderstand you. And social media attention is honestly one of the most unstable currencies on earth.

If your identity is built on fragile things, your confidence will always feel fragile too. You’ll feel like you’re constantly defending who you are.

And you can end up living like this:

- performing instead of being,
- scrolling instead of resting,
- comparing instead of enjoying,
- proving instead of growing.

Some of you are tired, and you don’t even know what you’re tired from. It’s not just school. It’s not just your schedule. It’s the constant feeling that you have to *earn* your place.

---

## 3) A deeper foundation: identity you don’t have to audition for

So what’s the alternative?

A compelling vision of identity is one that doesn’t require you to audition.

Identity that is grounded in something deeper says:

- You are not your GPA.
- You are not your body.
- You are not your worst moment.
- You are not your best moment either.
- You are not the version of you that gets the most likes.
- You are not the version of you that people misunderstand.

You are a person with inherent worth.

Now, depending on what you believe, you might ground that in different places. But I want to offer a foundation that is strong enough to hold the weight we put on identity.

Here it is: **your worth is given, not earned.**  
You have value before you achieve anything, before you look a certain way, before you get picked, before you get it together.

If you’re coming at this from a faith perspective, you might say: you’re created on purpose, and loved on purpose. Your identity isn’t something you hustle into existence; it’s something you receive. That doesn’t make you passive—it makes you secure.

And security changes everything.

Because when you believe your identity is secure, you can:

- try hard without being crushed by failure,
- care about your appearance without obsessing,
- want friends without needing everyone’s approval,
- grow without hating yourself in the process.

A deeper identity doesn’t erase your personality or your goals. It puts them in the right place.

---

## 4) Purpose comes out of identity—not the other way around

A lot of people think it goes like this:

**Find your purpose → then you’ll know who you are.**

But most of the time it actually goes like this:

**Know who you are → then you’ll live with purpose.**

Because purpose isn’t just a job title or a major or a “big dream.” Purpose is the direction of your life. It’s what you’re becoming. It’s what you’re giving yourself to.

If your identity is “I am only valuable when I succeed,” then your purpose becomes “Don’t fail.” That’s not purpose; that’s survival.

But if your identity is “I am valuable because I’m human—because I’m loved, known, and made on purpose,” then your purpose becomes something like:

- “I want to become someone who loves well.”
- “I want to use what I’m good at to serve real people.”
- “I want to bring honesty into a world full of performance.”
- “I want to build, not just consume.”
- “I want to be faithful with what’s in front of me, not obsessed with proving myself.”

That’s a kind of purpose that works whether you’re 16 or 60. It’s not dependent on being famous or perfect. It’s something you can live this week.

---

## 5) Three questions to re-center your identity

When you feel the pressure creeping in, here are three questions that help you step back from the performance treadmill.

**1) Who am I trying to impress right now?**  
Name it. A friend group? A parent? A coach? An ex? People online? A version of yourself?  
Sometimes just naming it breaks the spell.

**2) What am I afraid will happen if I’m not impressive?**  
This one’s deeper. Are you afraid you’ll be overlooked? Rejected? Seen as “not enough”?  
That fear is usually where your identity is trying to attach itself to something fragile.

**3) What’s true about me even if none of this works out?**  
If the post flops. If you don’t make the team. If you don’t get the grade. If you get rejected.  
What’s still true?

Write it down. Say it out loud if you can. Build a list of truths that don’t change when your circumstances do.

---

## 6) Practical takeaways for this week

I don’t want this to stay abstract, so here are some concrete things you can actually try in the next seven days. Not because they’ll fix your entire life, but because small practices shape your inner world.

### Takeaway #1: Do one thing “offline” that reminds you you’re a real person
Choose something that’s not for content. Not for proof. Not for a streak.

- Take a walk without headphones for ten minutes.
- Cook something simple.
- Shoot hoops alone.
- Draw, write, build, play an instrument.
- Clean your room while listening to music that calms you down.

The point is to practice existing without performing.

### Takeaway #2: Replace one comparison habit with one gratitude habit
Comparison is basically telling yourself, “My life is behind.” It steals your joy.

This week, when you catch yourself comparing, do this instead:

- Name one thing you genuinely appreciate about your life right now.
- Name one thing you respect about the other person without turning it into self-hate.
- Then come back to your lane.

You can admire someone without turning them into a judge.

### Takeaway #3: Audit what’s shaping you
Pick one app—just one—and ask: “Is this making me more grounded or more anxious?”

Then make one small change:

- Unfollow one account that always makes you feel worse.
- Turn off notifications for a day.
- Move the app off your home screen.
- Set a time limit.

This isn’t about “social media bad.” It’s about you being in charge of what shapes you.

### Takeaway #4: Talk to someone who knows the real you
Identity gets distorted in isolation.

This week, choose one person you trust and have an honest conversation. If you’re not sure who counts, think simple: **a parent or caregiver, a trusted teacher, a coach, a youth leader, an older sibling or cousin, or a really close friend**—someone who wants your good, not just your image.

You don’t have to be dramatic. You can literally say:

“I’ve been feeling pressure to have it all together, and I don’t think I do.”  
or  
“I don’t really know who I am right now, and I’m trying to figure it out.”

The right people won’t use your honesty against you.

### Takeaway #5: Write a one-sentence identity statement
Not a flex. Not a bio. Something true and steady.

Examples:

- “I’m a person in progress, and I’m allowed to grow.”
- “My worth isn’t up for voting.”
- “I am loved, even when I’m not impressive.”
- “I don’t have to prove I deserve to exist.”

Put it somewhere you’ll see it—lock screen, notes app, mirror. Repetition matters.

---

## 7) Closing: you don’t have to earn the right to be you

Here’s what I hope you hear tonight:

You don’t have to spend your teenage years trying to justify your existence.

You are allowed to be a work in progress. You are allowed to have ordinary days. You are allowed to not know exactly what you want to do with your life yet. You are allowed to be more than one thing. You are allowed to be misunderstood sometimes. You are allowed to change.

And you are allowed to build your identity on something deeper than the opinions of people who can’t even remember what they posted last week.

If you can walk out of here with one shift, let it be this:

Instead of asking, “How do I become someone?”  
start asking, “What if I already have worth—and I’m learning how to live from it?”

That’s where purpose becomes possible. Not the kind of purpose that’s a pressure cooker, but the kind that’s a compass.

This week, pick one practice. Just one. Try it honestly. And pay attention to what changes—not just in your schedule, but in your breathing, your peace, your relationships, and the way you speak to yourself.

Because the goal isn’t to create a perfect life. The goal is to become a whole person.

Like: *What does that say about me? Do people like me? Am I embarrassing? Am I behind? Am I doing this wrong?*

That’s identity pressure. It sneaks in through normal moments and turns them into a scoreboard.

### 1) The pressure to be “someone”

Being a teenager right now is like being handed a blank profile and being told, “Fill it in—correctly.” And not just once. Every day.

You’re not only trying to figure out what you like; you’re trying to figure out what will *work*.

What will get noticed.  
What will get approval.  
What will get you into the team, the program, the friend group.  
What will make you look like you have a life.  
What will keep you from being judged.  
What will keep you safe.

And you feel it from a bunch of places.

**Achievement pressure:** Be impressive. Be productive. Be exceptional. Grades, sports, leadership, awards, college, future, future, future. Sometimes it feels like your value is a moving target—like you’re only as good as your last test score or your last game.

**Appearance pressure:** Be attractive. Be stylish. Be put together. And not even in a normal way—more like “be camera-ready at all times.” Which is exhausting, because the standard keeps changing.

**Social pressure:** Be likable. Be included. Be interesting. And social media doesn’t just show you other people’s lives—it shows you what they chose to post. It’s the highlight reel. Good lighting. Best angles. The version they felt safe sharing.

Here’s the tricky part: none of these are bad things. Achievements can be great. Taking care of yourself matters. Friends matter.

The problem isn’t having these things. The problem is when they start having *you*.

When achievement becomes your identity, a bad grade doesn’t just disappoint you—it threatens you.  
When appearance becomes your identity, one unflattering photo can ruin your whole mood.  
When social approval becomes your identity, being left on read can mess with your entire day.

And then you start asking questions that sound like purpose questions, but they’re actually identity questions:

- “What should I do with my life?” sometimes really means “What will make me matter?”
- “What am I good at?” sometimes really means “What makes me worth keeping around?”
- “What do I want to be?” sometimes really means “What will make people respect me?”

If you’ve ever felt that kind of pressure, you’re not dramatic. You’re human.

### 2) The problem with building your identity on fragile things

Here’s a hard truth: most of the things we’re tempted to build our identity on are fragile.

Achievement is fragile because there’s always another level. Even if you win, it doesn’t last long. The moment you succeed, the next expectation shows up.

Appearance is fragile because your body changes, trends change, and people’s opinions definitely change.

Popularity is fragile because relationships shift. Drama happens. Friend groups change. People move. People ghost. People misunderstand you. And social media attention? It’s probably the least reliable thing you can build yourself on.

And when your identity is built on fragile things, your confidence starts to feel fragile too. You end up defending who you are all the time—proving, performing, explaining, editing.

Some of you are tired, and you don’t even know what you’re tired from.

It’s not just homework. It’s not just practice. It’s the constant feeling that you have to earn your place. Like you’re on a never-ending tryout for your own life.

### 3) A deeper foundation: identity you don’t have to audition for

So what’s the alternative?

Identity that’s grounded in something deeper is identity you don’t have to audition for.

It sounds like this:

You are not your GPA.  
You are not your body.  
You are not your worst moment.  
You are not your best moment either.  
You are not the version of you that gets the most likes.  
You are not the version of you that people misunderstand.

You are a person who matters—not because of what you’ve done, but because of what you are.

And since we’re in youth group, I want to say this clearly, not vaguely: the Christian claim is that your worth is not something you hustle to earn. It’s something you receive.

That you were made on purpose, by God, and loved on purpose.

Before you “figure it out.” Before you fix what you hate about yourself. Before you become impressive. Before you get picked. Before you stop messing up.

Your worth is given, not earned.

And that doesn’t make you lazy. It makes you secure.

And security changes everything.

When you believe your identity is secure, you can try hard without being crushed by failure. You can care about how you look without obsessing. You can want friends without needing everyone’s approval. You can grow without hating yourself the whole way there.

A deeper identity doesn’t erase your personality or your goals. It just puts them in the right place.

### 4) Purpose comes out of identity—not the other way around

Here’s where it gets interesting: once your identity is secure, purpose stops being a pressure and starts being a direction.

A lot of people assume life works like this:

**Find your purpose → then you’ll know who you are.**

But most of the time it actually works the other way:

**Know who you are → then you’ll live with purpose.**

Because purpose isn’t just a job title or a college major or one “big dream.” Purpose is the direction of your life. It’s what you’re becoming. It’s what you’re giving yourself to.

If your identity is “I’m only valuable when I succeed,” your “purpose” turns into something like: *don’t mess up, don’t fall behind, don’t disappoint anyone.* That’s not a life-giving purpose. That’s just trying to survive while looking fine.

But if your identity is “I matter because God made me and loves me,” then your purpose opens up into something steadier:

- I want to become someone who loves well.
- I want to use what I’m good at to serve real people, not just impress them.
- I want to bring honesty into a world full of performance.
- I want to build, not just consume.
- I want to be faithful with what’s in front of me, not obsessed with proving myself.

That kind of purpose works whether you’re 16 or 60. You can live it this week, even if you have no idea what your future job is.

### 5) Three questions to re-center when you feel the pressure

When you feel the performance pressure creeping back in—and it will—these three questions can help you step off the treadmill for a minute.

**1) Who am I trying to impress right now?**  
Name it. A friend group? A parent? A coach? Someone online? An ex? A version of yourself you’re trying to become?  
Sometimes naming it breaks the spell.

**2) What am I afraid will happen if I’m not impressive?**  
This one goes deeper. Are you afraid you’ll be overlooked? Rejected? Laughed at? Seen as “not enough”?  
That fear is usually where your identity is trying to attach itself to something fragile.

**3) What’s true about me even if none of this works out?**  
If the post flops. If you don’t make the team. If you don’t get the grade. If you get rejected.  
What’s still true?

If faith is part of your life, this is a good place to say something like:  
“God is still God. I’m still loved. I’m still not alone. I’m still growing.”

Write it down. Put words to it. Your brain needs something solid to stand on when your feelings are loud.

### 6) Practical options for this week (pick one—seriously, one)

I’m going to give you a menu. Not a checklist. You do not need to do all of these.

Pick one. Just one. Try it honestly this week.

#### Option 1: Talk to someone who knows the real you
Identity gets distorted in isolation.

This week, choose one person you trust and have one honest conversation. You don’t have to make it dramatic. You can say:

- “I’ve been feeling pressure to have it all together, and I don’t.”
- “I don’t really know who I am right now, and it’s stressing me out.”
- “I feel like I’m performing all the time.”

And let me say this in a way that’s real: being honest can be risky. Some people are not safe with your story. So start small, pick wisely, and look for someone who’s shown they can handle truth without turning it into gossip or judgment.

It takes courage to be that open—and it’s worth finding the people who are safe enough to hear it.

#### Option 2: Do one thing “offline” that reminds you you’re a real person
Choose something that’s not for content. Not for proof. Not for a streak.

- Take a 10-minute walk without headphones.
- Cook something simple.
- Shoot hoops alone.
- Draw, write, build, play an instrument.
- Clean your room while listening to music that calms you down.

The point isn’t productivity. The point is remembering what it feels like to exist without performing.

#### Option 3: Replace one comparison spiral with one tiny gratitude step
Comparison usually hits fast. It’s a spike: *I’m behind. I’m less than. I’m not enough.*

So make the replacement step small enough that you can actually do it on a bad day:

When you catch yourself comparing, do this:

1) Name one thing you genuinely appreciate about your life right now.  
2) If your brain goes blank, go even smaller: name one thing that happened today that wasn’t terrible.  
3) Then name one thing you respect about the other person *without* turning it into self-hate.  
4) Come back to your lane.

You can admire someone without making them your judge.

#### Option 4: Audit what’s shaping you (one app, one change)
Pick one app—just one—and ask: “Does this make me more grounded or more anxious?”

Then make one small change:

- Unfollow one account that consistently makes you feel worse.
- Turn off notifications for 24 hours.
- Move the app off your home screen.
- Set a time limit.

This isn’t “social media is evil.” It’s you deciding what gets access to your mind.

#### Option 5: Write a one-sentence identity statement
Not a flex. Not a bio. Just something steady and true.

Examples:

- “I’m a person in progress, and I’m allowed to grow.”
- “My worth isn’t up for voting.”
- “I am loved, even when I’m not impressive.”
- “I don’t have to prove I deserve to exist.”

Put it somewhere you’ll see it—lock screen, notes app, mirror. Repetition matters.

### A simple challenge for tonight (before you sleep)

Before you go to bed tonight, write one sentence about who you are that has nothing to do with achievement, appearance, or what people think of you.

One sentence.

If faith is part of your life, it can be as simple as: “I’m God’s kid, and I’m not alone.”  
If you’re not sure what you believe yet, it can still be true and grounding: “I’m a person who matters, and I’m allowed to grow.”

Don’t overthink it. Just write it. Give your mind something kinder to come back to.

### 7) Closing: you don’t have to earn the right to be you

Here’s what I hope you hear tonight:

You don’t have to spend your teenage years trying to justify your existence.

You are allowed to be a work in progress. You are allowed to have ordinary days. You are allowed to not know exactly what you want to do with your life yet. You are allowed to be more than one thing. You are allowed to be misunderstood sometimes. You are allowed to change.

And you are allowed to build your identity on something deeper than the opinions of people who can’t even remember what they posted last week.

If you walk out of here with one shift, let it be this:

Instead of asking, “How do I become someone?”  
start asking, “What if I already matter—and I’m learning how to live from that?”

That’s where purpose becomes possible. Not the kind that feels like a pressure cooker, but the kind that feels like a compass.

Pick one option. Try it this week. And pay attention to what changes—not just in your schedule, but in your breathing, your peace, your relationships, and the way you speak to yourself.

Because the goal isn’t to create a perfect life. The goal is to become a whole person.

And that gets right to tonight’s topic: identity and purpose—who you are, and what you’re here for.

Before we go further, quick cultural check: you know that whole “main character” vibe? Like, “This is my era. This is my glow-up. This is my story arc.” Some of that is fun. But it also comes with pressure: if you’re the main character, you’re supposed to have a clear aesthetic, a clear brand, a clear plan, a clear personality… like you’re already fully written.

Most of us don’t feel fully written. We feel like a draft.

### 1) The pressure to be “someone”

You’re not only trying to figure out what you like; you’re trying to figure out what will *work*.

- What will get noticed.
- What will get approval.

Here’s the tricky part: none of these are evil things. Achievements can be great. Taking care of yourself matters. Friends matter.

The problem isn’t having these things. The problem is when they start having *you*.

When achievement becomes your identity, a bad grade doesn’t just disappoint you—it threatens you.  
When appearance becomes your identity, an unflattering photo feels like evidence.  
When approval becomes your identity, being left on read can mess with your whole day.

And then you start asking questions that sound like purpose questions, but they’re actually identity questions:

- “What should I do with my life?” sometimes really means “What will make me matter?”
- “What am I good at?” sometimes really means “What makes me worth keeping around?”
- “What do I want to be?” sometimes really means “What will make people respect me?”

If you’ve ever felt that kind of pressure, you’re not dramatic. You’re human.

### 2) A quick personal confession

I want to say something that’s not polished, because I don’t want this to sound like a TED Talk.

There was a season—this is embarrassing, but it’s true—where I checked one specific person’s profile basically every day. Not because I even liked their content that much. I was measuring myself against them. Their friends. Their photos. Their confidence. Their life.

And I knew it was making me feel worse. I knew it. And I still did it.

That’s what comparison does. It doesn’t just show you someone else’s life. It gives you a scoreboard you didn’t ask for, and then it tells you you’re losing.

So if part of you is like, “Yeah, I know this is unhealthy, but I can’t stop,” you’re not broken. You’re just living in a world that is really good at turning people into products—including you.

### 3) The problem with building on fragile stuff

Here’s a hard truth: most of the things we’re tempted to build our identity on are fragile.

Achievement is fragile because there’s always someone better, and there’s always another level. Even when you win, the feeling fades fast, and the next expectation shows up.

Appearance is fragile because your body changes, trends change, and people’s opinions definitely change. No one can hold a perfect standard forever.

Popularity is fragile because relationships shift. People move. Drama happens. Friend groups change. And social media attention is one of the most unstable currencies on earth.

If your identity is built on fragile things, your confidence will feel fragile too. You’ll end up living like you’re constantly defending who you are.

You start performing instead of being.  
Scrolling instead of resting.  
Comparing instead of enjoying.  
Proving instead of growing.

And some of you are tired, and you don’t even know what you’re tired from.

It’s not only school. It’s not only your schedule.

It’s the constant feeling that you have to *earn your place*.

### 4) A deeper foundation: worth you don’t have to audition for

So what’s the alternative?

Here’s the claim I want to make—and I want to slow down here because this is the load-bearing wall:

**Your worth is given, not earned.**

Not “your worth is given if you’re talented.” Not “your worth is given if people like you.” Just: your worth is given.

Now—why should you believe that? Who decided that?

If we’re in a youth group setting, I’m going to be honest about where I’m coming from: I believe the Christian story is true, and it says something really specific about you.

It says you are not an accident. You were created on purpose. You are made in the image of God. Which means your value is not something you achieve; it’s something you *carry* because of who made you.

And even if you’re not sure what you believe about God yet, you still get this intuitively in real life.

Think about a newborn. A baby has no achievements. No résumé. No aesthetic. No followers. And if anyone tried to tell you, “That baby only matters if they become impressive,” you’d be like, “What is wrong with you?”

Or think about someone who can’t “produce” the way other people can—because of disability, illness, mental health, whatever. Most of us have this deep sense that their life is not worth less. Why? Because we know people aren’t machines. People aren’t products. People aren’t “valuable” only when they’re useful.

So when I say, “Your worth is given,” I’m not just saying a nice sentence. I’m saying: the way we instinctively know a person should be treated—with dignity, with care, with respect—points to something real about what a human being *is*.

You are a person before you are a performer.

And that kind of identity doesn’t erase your goals. It puts them in the right place.

Because when your identity is secure, you can try hard without being crushed.

Here’s what that can look like in a real teen moment:

You study for the test. You do your best. You get the grade back—and it’s not what you wanted.

If achievement is your identity, that moment becomes: “I *am* a failure.” Or, “I’m falling behind.” Or, “I’m not enough.” You spiral. You hide it. You get angry or numb. You feel like you have to fix your worth.

But if your worth is given, that moment becomes: “This hurts. I’m disappointed. I need help. I need a different plan.” You still care. You still grow. But the grade is feedback, not a verdict on your existence.

That’s the difference. Not apathy—freedom.

### 5) Purpose comes out of identity—not the other way around

A lot of people think it goes like this:

**Find your purpose → then you’ll know who you are.**

But most of the time it goes like this:

**Know who you are → then you’ll live with purpose.**

Because purpose isn’t just a job title or a major or a “big dream.” Purpose is the direction of your life. It’s what you’re becoming. It’s what you’re giving yourself to.

If your identity is “I am only valuable when I succeed,” then your purpose becomes “Don’t fail.” That’s not purpose; that’s survival.

But if your identity is “I have worth because I’m made and loved on purpose,” then your purpose starts sounding different:

- “I want to become someone who loves well.”
- “I want to use what I’m good at to serve real people.”
- “I want to tell the truth in a world full of performance.”
- “I want to build a life I don’t have to fake.”

That kind of purpose works whether you’re 16 or 60. It isn’t dependent on being famous or perfect. It’s something you can live this week.

### 6) Three question-and-action “experiments” for this week

I’m not giving you homework. You already have enough. Think of these as experiments—small things you can try for three days and just notice what happens in your mind and your body.

**Experiment 1: When you feel the pressure, ask: “Who am I trying to impress right now?”**  
Be specific. A friend group? A parent? A coach? Someone online? A version of yourself?

Then do one tiny action that breaks the performance loop:
- Move the app you use most to the last page of your phone, or off your home screen.
- Turn off notifications for one evening.
- Unfollow one account that consistently makes you feel worse.

Not because “social media bad.” Because you’re practicing being in charge of what shapes you.

**Experiment 2: Ask: “What am I afraid will happen if I’m not impressive?”**  
This one gets real fast. Are you afraid you’ll be forgotten? Rejected? Laughed at? Not chosen?

Then do one offline thing that reminds you you’re a real person—not a profile.
And I want you to pick something you used to enjoy before you worried if it was cool or postable.

- Walk for ten minutes without headphones.
- Shoot hoops, lift, run, stretch—no filming, no stats, just movement.
- Draw, write, bake something simple, play an instrument, build something, clean your room with music on.

The goal is not self-improvement. The goal is to practice existing without performing.

**Experiment 3: Ask: “What’s true about me even if none of this works out?”**  
If the post flops. If you don’t make the team. If you get rejected. If you don’t get the grade. What’s still true?

Then write a one-sentence identity statement—something steady, not a flex.

Examples:
- “I’m a person in progress, and I’m allowed to grow.”
- “My worth isn’t up for voting.”
- “I am loved, even when I’m not impressive.”
- “I don’t have to earn the right to exist.”

Put it somewhere you’ll see it: lock screen, notes app, mirror. You’re not brainwashing yourself; you’re training your mind to return to what’s solid when everything else is loud.

And one more thing—just as a sentence, not a whole fourth experiment: don’t do this alone. Tell one trustworthy person, “I’ve been feeling pressure to be someone, and I’m tired.” Identity gets distorted in isolation.

### 7) Closing: purpose as a compass, not a pressure cooker

Here’s what I hope you hear tonight:

You don’t have to spend your teenage years trying to justify your existence.

You are allowed to be a work in progress.  
You are allowed to have ordinary days.  
You are allowed to not know your whole future yet.  
You are allowed to try, and to fail, and to learn without hating yourself in the process.

And if you’re willing to sit with this possibility—even for a minute—consider this: what if your worth is not something you have to hustle for? What if it’s something you already have, because you’re a person made on purpose?

Instead of asking, “How do I become someone?” try asking, “What if I already matter—and I’m learning how to live from that?”

That’s where purpose becomes possible.

Not purpose as a pressure cooker. Purpose as a compass.

So pick one experiment. Three days. No perfection. Just honesty. Pay attention to what changes—not just in your schedule, but in your breathing, your peace, your relationships, and the way you talk to yourself.

And if you forget everything else, remember this: you don’t have to audition for a life that’s worth living.

If your identity is “I am only valuable when I succeed,” then your purpose becomes “Don’t fail.” That’s not purpose; that’s survival.

But if your identity is “I have worth before I win anything,” then purpose can sound like:

- “I want to become someone who loves well.”
- “I want to use what I’m good at to help real people.”
- “I want to bring honesty into a world full of performance.”
- “I want to build, not just consume.”
- “I want to be faithful with what’s in front of me, not obsessed with proving myself.”

That’s purpose you can live right now. At 15. On a Tuesday. Without being famous. Without being perfect.

### 5) When the pressure hits: an emergency kit

Okay—so what do you do when you’re actually in it?

Like, when you’re sitting there, and your brain is spiraling because you saw someone’s post and suddenly you feel behind. Or you got a grade back and it didn’t hit the number you needed. Or you feel like you’re not “enough” in some group chat you’re in.

When that pressure cooker starts to boil, you need an emergency exit—a quick way to pull yourself off the performance treadmill.

Here are three questions. Think of them like an identity fire drill.

**1) Who am I trying to impress right now?**  
Name it. A parent. A coach. A friend group. An ex. People online. Even a version of yourself you think you’re supposed to become.

Naming it takes away some of its power.

**2) What am I afraid will happen if I’m not impressive?**  
This one gets real fast. Are you afraid you’ll be overlooked? Rejected? Not chosen? Not taken seriously? Not loved?

That fear is usually the place where your identity is trying to attach itself to something fragile.

**3) What’s true about me even if this doesn’t work out?**  
If the post flops. If you don’t make the team. If you don’t get invited. If you mess up. If you get rejected.

What is still true?

Write down a few truths that don’t change when your circumstances do. Because your feelings will be loud, but truth is what keeps you steady.

### 6) Practical takeaways for this week (pick one)

Now I want to get super practical.

These aren’t just productivity hacks. These are small ways to practice living from security instead of scarcity—living like your worth is real, not like it’s constantly up for voting.

And hear me on this: **don’t try to do all of them.** If you do, it’ll turn into another performance thing. Just pick one. Do it honestly this week.

#### Takeaway #1: Do one thing offline that reminds you you’re a real person
Choose something that’s not for content. Not for proof. Not for a streak.

- Take a ten-minute walk without headphones.
- Cook something simple.
- Lift, run, shoot hoops—alone.
- Draw, write, build, play an instrument.
- Clean your room with music that calms you down.

The point is to practice existing without performing.

#### Takeaway #2: Replace one comparison spiral with one gratitude move
Comparison is basically telling yourself, “My life is behind.” It steals your joy and makes you mean to yourself.

This week, when you catch yourself comparing, do this instead:

- Name one thing you genuinely appreciate about your life right now.
- Name one thing you respect about the other person *without turning it into self-hate*.
- Come back to your lane.

You can admire someone without making them your judge.

#### Takeaway #3: Audit what’s shaping you (one app)
Pick one app—just one—and ask: “After I use this, do I feel more grounded or more anxious?”

Then make one small change:

- Unfollow one account that always makes you feel worse.
- Turn off notifications for a day.
- Move the app off your home screen.
- Set a time limit.

This isn’t “social media is evil.” It’s you deciding what gets access to your mind.

#### Takeaway #4: Talk to someone who knows the real you
Identity gets distorted in isolation.

This week, pick one safe person and say something honest. You don’t have to make it dramatic. You can literally say:

“I’ve been feeling pressure to have it all together, and I don’t think I do.”  
or  
“I don’t really know who I am right now, and I’m trying to figure it out.”

The right people won’t use your honesty against you.

#### Takeaway #5: Write a one-sentence identity statement
Not a bio. Not a flex. Something steady.

Examples:

- “I’m a person in progress, and I’m allowed to grow.”
- “My worth isn’t up for voting.”
- “I am loved, even when I’m not impressive.”
- “I don’t have to prove I deserve to exist.”

Put it somewhere you’ll see it—lock screen, notes app, mirror. Repetition matters because pressure is repetitive.

### 7) Closing: you don’t have to earn the right to be you

Here’s what I hope you hear tonight:

You don’t have to spend your teenage years trying to justify your existence.

You are allowed to be a work in progress. You are allowed to have ordinary days. You are allowed to not know your whole future yet. You are allowed to be more than one thing. You are allowed to change your mind. You are allowed to be misunderstood sometimes and still be okay.

And you are allowed to build your identity on something deeper than the opinions of people who can’t even remember what they posted last week.

So if you walk out of here with one shift, let it be this:

Instead of asking, **“How do I become someone?”**  
start asking, **“What if I already have worth—and I’m learning how to live from it?”**

That’s where purpose becomes possible. Not the kind of purpose that feels like a pressure cooker, but the kind that acts like a compass.

This week, pick one practice. Just one. Try it honestly. And pay attention to what changes—not just your schedule, but your breathing, your peace, your relationships, and the way you talk to yourself.

Because the goal isn’t to create a perfect life.

The goal is to become a whole person.

Hey, quick show of hands—who here has ever googled “How to be interesting”?  
No judgment, I did it at 2 a.m. last Tuesday because I’m writing this talk and still sometimes think a better version of me lives on the other side of a search bar.

That photo you just saw is from my grade-9 track meet. I came 7th out of 8 runners, yet I’m grinning like I just outran Usain Bolt. My mum found it while clearing the attic and, honestly, I stared at it for five minutes thinking: “That kid looks happy—what happened?” Because somewhere between 7th place and today, I learned to edit. First it was the caption (“Medal? Nah, let’s crop that”), then it was the whole story (“I basically almost won”), then it was the whole person.  

We all do it. We crop. We filter. We curate. And little by little, the question stops being “Who am I?” and becomes “What will make them double-tap?”  

Tonight I want to press undo on some of that cropping. I don’t want to give you three hacks for a better bio; I want to hand back the wide-angle lens. Deal?

––––––––––

1. The three fake IDs

Let’s name the loudest voices that try to write our ID cards:

a) The Achievement ID  
It whispers: You are your grades, your stats, your uni offers. I listened to it the night I cried over a B+ in chemistry—until my mate Sam, who got an A, cried harder because his Instagram only got 97 likes. Achievement is a treadmill that speeds up the minute you hop on.

b) The Mirror ID  
It says: You are how you look today—skin, shape, outfit, symmetry. One bad-hair morning and the whole you collapses like a Jenga tower. Research from the UK found teens now take 1.6 selfies for every one they post. That means we literally delete half of our own faces. If identity rests on appearance, we’re building a home on quicksand.

c) The Follower ID  
It shouts: You are the sum of your notifications. Ever posted something, turned your phone over to “focus,” then flipped it face-up four minutes later? Same. Scientists call this “variable-ratio reinforcement”—the slot-machine principle. Pull the lever, maybe jackpot, maybe crickets. We keep pulling because the little red bubble feels like oxygen. But it’s a rigged game; the house always wins and the house is not you.

Notice what these IDs have in common: they’re all external, they all fluctuate, and they all sell you back to yourself like a product. No wonder we wake up tired.

––––––––––

2. A different starting line

I want to tell you about another 14-year-old. She was undocumented, living in a garage in L.A., and her first “classroom” was the tailgate of a pickup truck where her dad tutored her in English by lamplight. Kids at school mocked her accent, so she stayed quiet. One teacher, Ms. Rivera, refused to let her hide. She kept saying, “Your voice is needed, not liked—needed.”  

That girl is now America’s first Afro-Latina poet laureate, Amanda Gorman. At 22 she stood on the Capitol steps and spoke a poem that out-viewed the Super Bowl. Same voice they once laughed at.

What changed? Not the pitch of her voice—just the direction of the question. Instead of “What will they think?” she learned to ask “What am I carrying that the world is waiting for?”

That’s the pivot. From performance to purpose. From mirror to mission. From proving to serving.

––––––––––

3. The Anchored Self

I’m a church kid, so I’ll put it in my language, but feel free to translate:

The Hebrew Bible has this wild image: God says, “I have called you by name; you are mine.” Not “I have called you by follower count,” not “I have called you by grade average.” By name. A name isn’t something you earn; it’s something you receive. Before you post, before you score, before you mess up, you’re already spoken for.

If faith isn’t your thing, hear it as philosophy: What if identity is not a trophy to win but a gift to unwrap? And what if the Giver is someone who delights in the unfiltered version?

Either way, the implication is massive: Your worth is non-negotiable. Which means you can try, fail, trend, flop, gain, lose, grow, shrink—and none of it moves the needle on your value. That’s the anchored self. Everything else is weather.

––––––––––

4. Why this isn’t just a nice idea

I can hear the sceptic in the third row: “Cool speech, bro, but my UCAS form still wants grades and my crush still wants six-pack abs.” I get it. Anchors are great, but we still have to sail the ship. So here’s the bridge.

When your worth is safe, your risk tolerance goes up. You can audition for the play even if you might flop, because your identity isn’t riding on the cast list. You can post the art that isn’t “on brand” because your creativity isn’t a brand—it’s blood. You can stick up for the kid being roasted in group chat because you don’t need the mob to validate you.

Security breeds courage. That’s not theology, it neuroscience. When your brain isn’t in threat mode, your prefrontal cortex—the bit that solves problems and dreams dreams—comes online. Translation: feeling safe makes you smarter and braver. Who doesn’t want that?

––––––––––

5. Practical take-aways (a.k.a. try this before Thursday)

I promised no abstract fluff, so here are five micro-experiments. Pick one, punk it, report back.

1. The 24-hour mute.  
Log out of every social app for one full day. Not to punish yourself, but to hear your own voice again. When the itch hits, open the Notes app and answer: “What am I actually feeling right now?” You’ll be shocked how many emotions have been smooshed into “I guess I’ll scroll.”

2. The reverse selfie.  
Take a photo where your face is NOT the focus—your hands painting, your legs running, your messy desk creating. Caption it with one thing you’re proud of that can’t be seen in a mirror. Post it if you want, or keep it just for you. Either way, widen the definition of “worth looking at.”

3. The three-name gratitude.  
Text three people who knew you before you were “aesthetic.” Thank them for something they saw in you back then. Watch how quickly you remember a version of yourself that predates filters.

4. The failure brag.  
Share a recent flop in conversation or on your story. Nothing traumatic, just “I tried X and ate dirt.” Do it without self-deprecation. Normalise the fact that growth has bloopers. You’ll give the rest of us permission to breathe.

5. The purpose plug-in.  
Each morning ask: “Who could I serve today?” Not “What can I prove?” Help a classmate before they ask, surprise your mum by hoovering without being bribed, send the voice-note that says “I believe in you.” Small acts tether you to purpose faster than any TED Talk.

––––––––––

6. One-sentence send-off

You are not the sum of your notifications, your reflection, or your achievements; you are the sum of a love that got to you first—so walk into the week like someone who’s already approved, and watch how much braver you become.

Thanks for listening. Now go crop the crops, unfilter the filters, and I’ll see you on the other side of brave.

**The Real You (When No One's Scrolling)**

Let me ask you something. How many of you have, sitting in your camera roll right now, at least three photos that look like *you*—but that you’d never actually post? Maybe the lighting is weird, or your smile’s too real, or it’s just not the version of yourself you want the world to see. And how many of you have felt that strange disconnect between who you are when you’re alone, scrolling, and who you are when you’re performing for an audience of any size—even an audience of four friends at lunch?

I ask because I remember being 16 and having this unsettling feeling that I was made of layers. There was the school me, who cared way too much about AP scores. The home me, who was exhausted from being school me. The Instagram me, who seemed way more put-together than either of those people. And the late-at-night me, lying in bed wondering which one—if any—was the real me.

That question—“Who am I, really?”—is the question underneath everything right now. It’s the engine driving what you post, what you study, who you hang with, and what you panic about at 2 AM. And here’s the thing: we’re living in a moment that is *obsessed* with identity, but absolutely terrible at helping you find one that lasts.

**The Achievement Trap**

Let’s start with the obvious pressure: achievement. You’re told that your GPA is your worth. That your college acceptance is your validation. That if you can just stack enough accomplishments—club president, varsity starter, volunteer hours, side hustle—you’ll finally be enough. But have you noticed how the goalposts keep moving? You hit one target, and suddenly there’s a new one. The acceptance letter arrives, and now it’s about the internship. The internship happens, and now it’s about the fellowship. It’s a treadmill that never stops. And the dirty secret? No achievement has ever answered the question “Am I valuable?”—it just postpones it.

**The Appearance Trap**

Then there’s appearance. We live in a world where you can filter your face, edit your body, and curate your life until it’s unrecognizable. And the math is brutal: if your worth is tied to how you look, you’re competing with a billion edited images, and you’re aging in real time. That’s a losing game. But more than that, it’s exhausting to perform “effortless beauty” or “aesthetic life” when the reality is you’re just trying to get through math class without dissociating. The version of you that gets likes isn’t a person—it’s a product. And products have to be constantly updated, rebranded, and remarketed, or they become irrelevant.

**The Algorithm Trap**

Which brings us to the third pressure: social media itself. Not just the appearance side, but the performance side. The algorithm rewards consistency, certainty, and hot takes. It wants you to have a “brand.” Are you the funny one? The activist? The fashion kid? The deep thinker? And because the feedback is instant—likes, comments, shares—you start to believe that your identity is whatever gets the most engagement. But here’s what no one tells you: the algorithm doesn’t care about your soul. It’s designed to keep you scrolling, not to help you become whole.

**A Different Anchor**

So what’s the alternative? If you’re not your achievements, your appearance, or your algorithm, then who are you?

I want to offer you a different metaphor. Think of yourself like a smartphone. Bear with me. Your apps—those are your roles. Student, athlete, friend, content creator. They’re important. They do things. But they’re not the operating system. And if you’ve ever had a phone glitch out, you know: when the OS is corrupted, no amount of app updates will fix it. The whole thing crashes.

Your identity is the operating system. It’s the thing underneath that says, “This is what I’m for. This is what’s true about me when everything else is stripped away.”

And the only way to build an operating system that doesn’t crash is to anchor it in something that doesn’t change.

**The Real You (When No One's Scrolling)**

Let me ask you something. How many of you have, sitting in your camera roll right now, at least three photos that look like *you*—but that you’d never actually post? Maybe the lighting is weird, or your smile’s too real, or it’s just not the version of yourself you want the world to see. And how many of you have felt that strange disconnect between who you are when you’re alone, scrolling, and who you are when you’re performing for an audience of any size—even an audience of four friends at lunch?

I ask because I know that feeling. That feeling like you’re wearing a mask that’s slowly getting heavy. That unsettling sense that you’re made of layers. There’s the school you, who cares way too much about AP scores. The home you, who is exhausted from being school you. The Instagram you, who seems way more put-together than either of those people. And the late-at-night you, lying in bed wondering which one—if any—is the real you.

That question—“Who am I, really?”—is the engine underneath everything right now. It’s what drives what you post, what you study, who you hang with, and what you panic about at 2 AM. And here’s the thing: we’re living in a moment that is *obsessed* with identity, but absolutely terrible at helping you find one that lasts.

**The Achievement Trap**

Let’s start with the obvious pressure: achievement. You know the feeling. You get the A, but it’s not an A in the *hard* class. You make the team, but you’re not a starter. You get the followers, but not as many as her. You’re told that your GPA is your worth. That your college acceptance is your validation. That if you can just stack enough accomplishments—club president, varsity starter, volunteer hours, side hustle—you’ll finally be enough.

But have you noticed how the goalposts keep moving? You hit one target, and suddenly there’s a new one. The acceptance letter arrives, and now it’s about the internship. The internship happens, and now it’s about the fellowship. It’s a treadmill that never stops. And the dirty secret? No achievement has ever answered the question “Am I valuable?”—it just postpones it. It’s like drinking salt water to quench your thirst. The more you consume, the emptier you feel.

**The Appearance Trap**

Then there’s appearance. We live in a world where you can filter your face, edit your body, and curate your life until it’s unrecognizable. And the math is brutal: if your worth is tied to how you look, you’re competing with a billion edited images, and you’re aging in real time. That’s a losing game.

But more than that, it’s exhausting to perform “effortless beauty” or “aesthetic life” when the reality is you’re just trying to get through math class without dissociating. The version of you that gets likes isn’t a person—it’s a product. And products have to be constantly updated, rebranded, and remarketed, or they become irrelevant.

**The Algorithm Trap**

Which brings us to the third pressure: social media itself. Not just the appearance side, but the performance side. The algorithm rewards consistency, certainty, and hot takes. It wants you to have a “brand.” Are you the funny one? The activist? The fashion kid? The deep thinker? And because the feedback is instant—likes, comments, shares—you start to believe that your identity is whatever gets the most engagement.

But here’s what no one tells you: the algorithm doesn’t care about your soul. It’s designed to keep you scrolling, not to help you become whole.

**A Different Anchor**

So what’s the alternative? If you’re not your achievements, your appearance, or your algorithm, then who are you?

Let me ask you something weird. Think about a newborn baby. They can’t do anything. They have no GPA, no abs, no followers. They can’t even hold their own head up. But are they valuable? Yes. Why? Just because they’re *here*. Worth isn’t something you earn; it’s something you start with. The rest of your life is just remembering what you started with.

There’s a difference between **net worth** and **self worth**. Net worth is what you accumulate—grades, trophies, followers. It’s external. It can be gained and lost. Self worth is what you *are*. It’s internal. It’s the baseline. And if you’re trying to build an identity on net worth, you’ll always be one failure away from collapse.

Your identity has to be anchored in something that doesn’t change. For me, that anchor is this: I am a person of inherent worth, not because of what I do, but because I exist. I am loved before I perform. I am valuable before I produce. And my purpose is not to become someone impressive, but to become someone *real*—someone who can love, create, heal, and show up for others.

Now, I get that some of you are hearing that and thinking, “That sounds nice, but also like a motivational poster.” So let me make it concrete.

**The Real You Is Not a Brand**

The real you is not a brand. Brands are consistent, marketable, and two-dimensional. You are contradictory, evolving, and three-dimensional. You contain multitudes. You can be the person who loves TikTok dances *and* reads philosophy. You can be the athlete who cries during movies. You can be the straight-A student who has no idea what you want to do with your life.

That’s not inconsistency—that’s humanity.

And your purpose? It’s not a job title. It’s a direction. Purpose is less about *what* you do and more about *how* you do it and *why*. It’s the through-line that connects your moments. Maybe your purpose is to be someone who brings peace into chaotic rooms. Maybe it’s to be a truth-teller in a world of spin. Maybe it’s to create beauty, or defend the vulnerable, or make people laugh when everything feels heavy.

That purpose can show up in a thousand different careers. It’s not a destination—it’s a way of being.

**Three Things You Can Do This Week**

So here’s the practical part. If any of this resonates, I want to give you three things you can actually *do* this week to start building an identity that doesn’t depend on the external noise.

**1. Mute the Metrics**

For one hour today, turn off the numbers. Hide your like counts. Scroll one feed without mentally ranking yourself against every post. When you catch yourself comparing, pause and say, “That’s their story, not mine.” Then ask: “What do *I* need right now?” Not “What would look good?” but “What would feel true?” It’s a small reset, but small resets matter.

**2. The “Three Things” Journal**

Tonight, get a notebook or open a notes app and answer this: *What are three things that are true about me when I’m not trying to impress anyone?* Not “I’m good at soccer.” More like: “I notice when people are left out.” “I feel most alive when I’m making something.” “I’m the friend who remembers the small details.” These are clues to your operating system. These are the things that don’t require an audience.

**3. The Purpose Experiment**

Do one thing this week that serves someone else, but do it *invisibly*. Not for credit. Not for a photo. Not so you can tell someone later and seem selfless. Send an encouraging text to someone who’s struggling. Pick up trash in the hallway. Let someone cut you in line. Notice how it feels to do something good that no one will celebrate.

That feeling? That’s what purpose feels like when it’s not a performance. That’s your operating system running the way it was designed to.

**You Are Not a Project**

I want to end with this. You are not a project to be completed. You are not a problem to be solved. You are messy and complicated, and that is actually better than being a brand.

The world will try to sell you a thousand identities: the hustler, the influencer, the genius, the icon. But none of those will fit because they’re all costumes.

The real you is the person who emerges when the pressure to perform drops away. The real you is the person who can hold both joy and pain, ambition and uncertainty, strength and tenderness. The real you is not your GPA, your follower count, or your reflection in the mirror. The real you is the person who can look at another human being and see their worth, even on the days you struggle to see your own.

And that person? They’re already in there. They’re not something you have to build from scratch. They’re something you have to uncover, protect, and practice being.

So the next time you’re scrolling and you feel that old pang of “I’m not enough,” or the next time you’re staring at a grade that feels like a verdict, remember this: you have an operating system that is older, deeper, and more resilient than any app the world can download. Connect to it. Trust it. Let it run.

The real you doesn’t need a filter. The real you doesn’t need a brand. The real you just needs permission to be seen—first by you, then by the people who matter.

And when you start living from that place? You stop performing and you start *living*. You stop asking “Who am I supposed to be?” and you start asking “What does love require of me right now?”

That’s the question that will carry you. That’s the identity that will last.

Thanks for listening. Now go be the you that no one’s scrolling for. That’s the one we actually need.

The real you is not a brand. Brands are consistent, marketable, and two-dimensional. You are contradictory, evolving, and three-dimensional. You contain multitudes. You can be the person who loves TikTok dances *and* reads philosophy. You can be the athlete who cries during movies. You can be the straight-A student who has no idea what you want to do with your life. That’s not inconsistency—that’s humanity.

And your purpose? It’s not a job title. It’s a direction. Purpose is less about *what* you do and more about *how* you do it and *why*. It’s the through-line that connects your moments. Maybe your purpose is to be someone who brings peace into chaotic rooms. Maybe it’s to be a truth-teller in a world of spin. Maybe it’s to create beauty, or defend the vulnerable, or make people laugh when everything feels heavy. That purpose can show up in a thousand different careers. It’s not a destination—it’s a way of being.

**Three Things You Can Do This Week**

So here’s the practical part. If any of this resonates, I want to give you three things you can actually *do* this week to start building an identity that doesn’t depend on the external noise.

**1. The 24-Hour Comparison Fast**

For one full day—24 hours—commit to not comparing yourself to anyone. Not their grades, not their followers, not their outfit, not their highlight reel. When you catch yourself doing it (and you will, probably by hour 3), pause and say, “That’s their story, not mine.” Then ask: “What do *I* need right now?” Not “What would look good?” but “What would feel true?” It’s harder than it sounds, but it’s like a reset button for your brain. And when you fail—and you will—just notice it and start again. That’s not failure; that’s data about how deep the programming goes.

**2. The “Three Things” Journal**

Tonight, get a notebook or open a notes app and answer this: *What are three things that are true about me when I’m not trying to impress anyone?* Not “I’m good at soccer.” More like: “I notice when people are left out.” “I feel most alive when I’m making something.” “I’m the friend who remembers the small details.” These are clues to your operating system. These are the things that don’t require an audience.

Then, because you’ll forget by Monday morning, put one of those truths in your phone’s lock screen. When you catch yourself performing—perfecting your lunch table persona, rehearsing a TikTok in your head—look at it. That’s your home button. That’s you, no app required.

**3. The Purpose Experiment**

Do one thing this week that serves someone else, but do it *invisibly*. Not for credit. Not for a photo. Not so you can tell someone later and seem selfless. Send an encouraging text to someone who’s struggling—then delete the message thread so you can’t screenshot it later. Pick up trash in the hallway when no one’s around. Let someone cut you in the lunch line and don’t tell your friends about your “sacrifice.” Notice how it feels to do something good that no one will celebrate. That feeling? That’s what purpose feels like when it’s not a performance. That’s your operating system running the way it was designed to.

**You Are Not a Project**

I want to end with this. You are not a project to be completed. You are not a problem to be solved. You are a person becoming. And the world will try to sell you a thousand identities: the hustler, the influencer, the genius, the icon. But none of those will fit because they’re all costumes.

The real you is the person who emerges when the pressure to perform drops away. The real you is the person who can hold both joy and pain, ambition and uncertainty, strength and tenderness. The real you is not your GPA, your follower count, or your reflection in the mirror. The real you is the person who can look at another human being and see their worth, even on the days you struggle to see your own.

The real you is also the person who sometimes eats cereal for dinner, has that embarrassing nickname from middle school stuck in your head, and still isn’t sure what you want to major in. That person is enough.

And that person? They’re already in there. They’re not something you have to build from scratch. They’re something you have to uncover, protect, and practice being.

So the next time you’re scrolling and you feel that old pang of “I’m not enough,” or the next time you’re staring at a grade that feels like a verdict, remember this: you have an operating system that is older, deeper, and more resilient than any app the world can download. Connect to it. Trust it. Let it run.

The real you doesn’t need a filter. The real you doesn’t need a brand. The real you just needs permission to be seen—first by you, then by the people who matter.

And when you start living from that place? You stop performing and you start *living*. You stop asking “Who am I supposed to be?” and you start asking “What does love require of me right now?”

That’s the question that will carry you. That’s the identity that will last.

Thanks for listening. Now go be the you that no one’s scrolling for. That’s the one we actually need.

**Who Are You Without Your Bio?**

Let me ask you something real quick. If I asked you to describe yourself right now—like, right this second—what would you say? And I don’t mean the rehearsed answer you give adults when they ask what you want to do with your life. I mean the honest one. The one that might sound like: “I’m the person who posts thirst traps on Instagram but still feels invisible.” Or “I’m the smart kid who’s one bad grade away from losing my mind.” Or maybe just “I’m not really sure anymore.”

Here’s why I’m asking. Last week, I was helping my little cousin set up her TikTok account, and she got stuck on the bio line. You know the one—those 80 characters that are supposed to capture your entire existence. She typed and deleted “Lover of sunsets ☀️” seven times. Then “Just vibing ✨” five times. Finally she looked up at me and said, “What if I pick the wrong one and everyone gets the wrong idea about who I am?”

And I thought: *Wow. She just summed up the entire anxiety of being a teenager in 2024.*

---

**The Performance of Being Yourself**

Let’s be honest. You’re living in a world where your identity isn’t just something you *have*—it’s something you *perform*. Every day. On Snapchat, Instagram, BeReal, whatever’s next. You’re not just living your life; you’re curating it, editing it, filtering it, and then waiting for the verdict. How many likes? Who watched? Did I nail the aesthetic?

And it’s not just social media. It’s the grades you stress over, the sports you play, the clubs you join, the way your body looks in that mirror. Every part of you feels like it’s being measured and evaluated. Your parents want the college resume. Your coaches want the stats. Your friends want the vibe. And somewhere in the middle of all that, you’re supposed to figure out who *you* are.

But here’s the trap: when you build your identity on performance, you become a house of cards. One bad post, one missed goal, one awkward interaction, and the whole thing feels like it’s collapsing. You start believing that your worth is tied to your last achievement, your last photo, your last whatever. And that’s exhausting.

I remember being 16 and thinking I had it figured out. I was the “funny friend,” the guy who could make anyone laugh. That was my thing. Until one day I was going through some stuff at home, and I didn’t have the energy to be funny. And suddenly I felt like I’d disappeared. Like without that performance, I was nobody. It took me way too long to realize I’d mistaken my act for my identity.

---

**The Source Code vs. The User Interface**

So let me offer a different way to think about this. You know how your phone has a user interface—what you see on the screen, the apps, the layout, the colors? But underneath that is the actual code, the programming that makes everything run. If the code is solid, the interface works. If the code is broken, the prettiest design in the world doesn’t matter.

Most of us are trying to fix our lives by messing with the interface. We’re tweaking our bios, changing our hair, chasing the next accomplishment, hoping that if we can just get the outside looking right, the inside will follow. But identity doesn’t work that way. Your *real* identity is the source code. It’s the deeper programming that says: This is who I am regardless of what’s happening on my screen.

And here’s the wild part: that source code isn’t something you write. It’s something you *discover*. It’s already there. You are already someone. Not because of what you do, but because of something deeper. Call it your soul, your essence, the core of who you are—whatever language works for you. But it’s the part of you that exists before the performance, before the likes, before the achievements.

The question isn’t “Who do I need to become?” It’s “Who am I underneath all the noise?”

---

**Purpose Isn’t a Job Title**

Which brings us to purpose. We love to ask teenagers, “What do you want to be when you grow up?” as if purpose is a career path you pick from a menu. But purpose isn’t a destination. It’s not a job. It’s not even a passion you need to discover by age 18 or you’re screwed.

Purpose is simpler and harder than that. Purpose is about alignment. It’s when the person you are on the inside lines up with what you do on the outside. It’s when you stop asking “What will make me look good?” and start asking “What feels true?”

Think about the people you actually admire. Not the influencers—the real ones. The teacher who stays after class to help you get it. The friend who actually listens when you’re falling apart. The coach who cares more about who you’re becoming than whether you win. Their purpose isn’t in their job description. It’s in how they show up. It’s in the small, consistent ways they make the world around them a little more human.

Your purpose is the same. It’s not waiting for you in some future college major or dream job. It’s waiting for you in the next conversation where you choose to be real instead of impressive. The next time you stand up for someone who’s getting picked on. The next time you create something because you *have* to, not because it’ll look good on your feed.

---

**Four Things You Can Actually Do This Week**

Alright, enough theory. Let’s get practical. Here are four things you can actually do in the next seven days to start living from your source code instead of your interface.

**1. Do a Social Media Audit (But Not the Boring Kind)**

Tonight, scroll through your own profile for 10 minutes. Not to judge yourself, but to ask one question: “Does this look like me, or does this look like who I think I’m supposed to be?” Not every post has to be deep, but if your entire digital self is a performance, that’s a clue. Try posting one thing this week that’s true but not impressive. A photo of your messy desk. A thought about something that actually matters to you. Something that feels like *you* on a Tuesday, not you at your highlight reel.

**2. Start a “Gratitude Inventory” (Hear Me Out)**

I know “gratitude” sounds like something your mom’s yoga instructor would say. But here’s the teenage version: Every night, text yourself three things that made you feel like *yourself* that day. Not three things that were awesome. Three moments where you felt real. Maybe it was that weird deep conversation at lunch. Maybe it was when you were alone listening to music and actually felt something. Maybe it was when you helped someone and didn’t post about it. Over time, you’ll start seeing patterns. Those patterns are clues to your source code.

**3. Conduct a “Purpose Experiment”**

Pick one small thing this week that’s just for you—not for your resume, not for your followers, not for anyone’s approval. Write a poem and don’t show anyone. Learn three chords on a guitar. Go for a run without tracking it. Cook something weird. The goal isn’t to be good at it. The goal is to do something where the *doing* is the point. That’s what purpose feels like. It’s not about being the best; it’s about being *present*.

**4. Have One “No-Filter” Conversation**

Find one person—friend, sibling, whatever—and ask them a real question. Not “How are you?” but “What’s actually been hard lately?” Or “What do you think about when you can’t sleep?” And then listen. Don’t fix. Don’t perform. Just listen. Because here’s the secret: you find your identity not by searching for yourself, but by showing up for other people. We become ourselves in connection, not isolation.

---

**The Bottom Line**

You are not your GPA. You are not your follower count. You are not your sport, your body, your brand, your latest achievement, or your biggest failure.

You are the person who exists underneath all of that. And that person is enough. Not perfect, not finished, but enough. Worthy. Valuable. Already.

The world will try to sell you a million versions of who you should be. It’ll tell you that you’re a product to be marketed, a résumé to be built, a brand to be managed. But you don’t have to buy it. You can choose to build your life from the inside out instead of the outside in.

It’s scarier that way. It’s harder. You can’t measure it with metrics. But it’s the only way to build something that doesn’t collapse when the performance stops.

So who are you without your bio? You’re not a mystery to be solved. You’re a person to be discovered. And you’ve already started.

The rest is just living into it.

---

Let me ask you something real quick. If I asked you to describe yourself right now—like, right this second—what would you say? And I don’t mean the rehearsed answer you give adults when they ask what you want to do with your life. I mean the honest one. The one that might sound like: “I’m the person who posts the photos but still feels invisible.” Or “I’m the smart kid who’s one bad grade away from losing my mind.” Or maybe just “I’m not really sure anymore.”

Here’s why I’m asking. Last week, I was helping my little cousin set up her TikTok account, and she got stuck on the bio line. You know the one—those 80 characters that are supposed to capture your entire existence. She typed and deleted “Lover of sunsets ☀️” seven times. Then “Just vibing ✨” five times. Finally she looked up at me and said, “What if I pick the wrong one and everyone gets the wrong idea about who I am?”

And I thought: *Wow. She just summed up the entire anxiety of being a teenager in 2024.*

---

**The Performance of Being Yourself**

Let’s be honest. You’re living in a world where your identity isn’t just something you *have*—it’s something you *perform*. Every day. On Snapchat, Instagram, TikTok, or whatever new app just dropped yesterday. You’re not just living your life; you’re curating it, editing it, filtering it, and then waiting for the verdict. How many likes? Who watched? Did I nail the aesthetic?

And it’s not just social media. It’s the grades you stress over, the sports you play, the clubs you join, the way your body looks in that mirror. Every part of you feels like it’s being measured and evaluated. Your parents want the college resume. Your coaches want the stats. Your friends want the vibe. And somewhere in the middle of all that, you’re supposed to figure out who *you* are.

But here’s the trap: when you build your identity on performance, you become a house of cards. One bad post, one missed goal, one awkward interaction, and the whole thing feels like it’s collapsing. You start believing that your worth is tied to your last achievement, your last photo, your last whatever. And that’s exhausting.

I remember being 16 and thinking I had it figured out. I was the “funny friend,” the guy who could make anyone laugh. That was my thing. Until one day I was going through some stuff at home, and I didn’t have the energy to be funny. And suddenly I felt like I’d disappeared. Like without that performance, I was nobody. It took me way too long to realize I’d mistaken my act for my identity.

---

**The Source Code vs. The User Interface**

So let me offer a different way to think about this. You know how your phone has a user interface—what you see on the screen, the apps, the layout, the colors? But underneath that is the actual code, the programming that makes everything run. If the code is solid, the interface works. If the code is broken, the prettiest design in the world doesn’t matter.

Most of us are trying to fix our lives by messing with the interface. We’re tweaking our bios, changing our hair, chasing the next accomplishment, hoping that if we can just get the outside looking right, the inside will follow. But identity doesn’t work that way. Your *real* identity is the source code. It’s the deeper programming that says: This is who I am regardless of what’s happening on my screen.

And here’s the wild part: that source code isn’t something you write. It’s something you *discover*. It’s already there. You are already someone. Not because of what you do, but because of something deeper. Call it your soul, your essence, the core of who you are—whatever language works for you. But it’s the part of you that exists before the performance, before the likes, before the achievements.

You access that code not by looking in the mirror, but by looking at what you love, what makes you angry, and what makes you feel alive. The question isn’t “Who do I need to become?” It’s “Who am I underneath all the noise?”

---

Once you stop trying to fix the interface and start trusting the source code, you stop trying to *become* someone and start *being* someone. And that’s where purpose lives.

Don’t fix. Don’t perform. Just listen. Because here’s the secret: you find your identity not by searching for yourself, but by showing up for other people. We become ourselves in connection, not isolation.

---

Here is the truth I’m betting my life on: You are not your GPA. You are not your follower count. You are not your sport, your body, your brand, your latest achievement, or your biggest failure.

You are the person who exists underneath all of that. And that person is enough. Not perfect, not finished, but enough. Worthy. Valuable. You don’t have to earn the space you take up.

The world will try to sell you a million versions of who you should be. It’ll tell you that you’re a product to be marketed, a résumé to be built, a brand to be managed. But you don’t have to buy it. You can choose to build your life from the inside out instead of the outside in.

It’s scarier that way. It’s harder. You can’t measure it with metrics. But it’s the only way to build something that doesn’t collapse when the performance stops.

So who are you without your bio? You’re not a mystery to be solved. You’re a person to be discovered. And you’ve already started.

The rest is just living into it.
