Here’s why I’m asking. Last week, I was helping my little cousin set up her TikTok account, and she got stuck on the bio line. You know the one—those 80 characters that are supposed to capture your entire existence. She typed and deleted “Lover of sunsets ☀️” seven times. Then “Just vibing ✨” five times. Finally she looked up at me and said, “What if I pick the wrong one and everyone gets the wrong idea about who I am?”

And I thought: *Wow. She just summed up the entire anxiety of being a teenager in 2024.*

---

**The Performance of Being Yourself**

Let’s be honest. You’re living in a world where your identity isn’t just something you *have*—it’s something you *perform*. Every day. On Snapchat, Instagram, BeReal, whatever’s next. You’re not just living your life; you’re curating it, editing it, filtering it, and then waiting for the verdict. How many likes? Who watched? Did I nail the aesthetic?

And it’s not just social media. It’s the grades you stress over, the sports you play, the clubs you join, the way your body looks in that mirror. Every part of you feels like it’s being measured and evaluated. Your parents want the college resume. Your coaches want the stats. Your friends want the vibe. And somewhere in the middle of all that, you’re supposed to figure out who *you* are.

But here’s the trap: when you build your identity on performance, you become a house of cards. One bad post, one missed goal, one awkward interaction, and the whole thing feels like it’s collapsing. You start believing that your worth is tied to your last achievement, your last photo, your last whatever. And that’s exhausting.

I remember being 16 and thinking I had it figured out. I was the guy who always had the perfect comeback in the group chat, the one who turned every awkward moment into a meme-worthy Instagram story. My streaks depended on me being "on." That was my thing. Until one day I was going through some stuff at home, and I didn’t have the energy to be funny. I left people on read. I skipped posting. And suddenly I felt like I’d disappeared. Like without that performance, I was nobody. It took me way too long to realize I’d mistaken my act for my identity.

We can’t live like that forever. We need something solid to stand on, something that doesn’t rely on the next performance, the next laugh, the next streak. So let me offer a different way to think about this...

---

**The Source Code vs. The User Interface**

So let me offer a different way to think about this. You know how your phone has a user interface—what you see on the screen, the apps, the layout, the colors? But underneath that is the actual code, the programming that makes everything run. If the code is solid, the interface works. If the code is broken, the prettiest design in the world doesn’t matter.

Most of us are trying to fix our lives by messing with the interface. We’re tweaking our bios, changing our hair, chasing the next accomplishment, hoping that if we can just get the outside looking right, the inside will follow. But identity doesn’t work that way. Your *real* identity is the source code. It’s the deeper programming that says: This is who I am regardless of what’s happening on my screen.

And here’s the wild part: that source code isn’t something you write. It’s something you *discover*. It’s already there. You are already someone. Not because of what you do, but because of something deeper. Call it your soul, your essence, the core of who you are—whatever language works for you. But it’s the part of you that exists before the performance, before the likes, before the achievements.

What does that actually feel like? It’s that quiet feeling you get when you’re alone and actually content, not lonely. It’s the sense of rightness when you stand up for something you believe in, even if no one claps for it. It’s the way you feel more like yourself when you’re listening to that one song that nobody else gets, or when you’re having a conversation where you forget to perform and just *are*. It’s not loud. It doesn’t need validation. It just *is*.

The question isn’t “Who do I need to become?” It’s “Who am I underneath all the noise?”

---

**Purpose Isn’t a Job Title**

Which brings us to purpose. We love to ask teenagers, “What do you want to be when you grow up?” as if purpose is a career path you pick from a menu. But purpose isn’t a destination. It’s not a job. It’s not even a passion you need to discover by age 18 or you’re screwed.

Purpose is simpler and harder than that. Purpose is about alignment. It’s when the person you are on the inside lines up with what you do on the outside. It’s when you stop asking “What will make me look good?” and start asking “What feels true?”

Think about the people you actually admire. Not the influencers—the real ones. The teacher who stays after class to help you get it. The friend who actually listens when you’re falling apart. The coach who cares more about who you’re becoming than whether you win. Their purpose isn’t in their job description. It’s in how they show up. It’s in the small, consistent ways they make the world around them a little more human.

Your purpose is the same. It’s not waiting for you in some future college major or dream job. It’s waiting for you in the next conversation where you choose to be real instead of impressive. The next time you stand up for someone who’s getting picked on. The next time you create something because you *have* to, not because it’ll look good on your feed.

---

**Four Things You Can Actually Do This Week**

Alright, enough theory. Let’s get practical. Here are four things you can actually do in the next seven days to start living from your source code instead of your interface.

**1. Do a Social Media Audit (But Not the Boring Kind)**

Tonight, scroll through your own profile for 10 minutes. Not to judge yourself, but to ask one question: “Does this look like me, or does this look like who I think I’m supposed to be?” Not every post has to be deep, but if your entire digital self is a performance, that’s a clue. Try posting one thing this week that’s true but not impressive. A photo of your messy desk. A thought about something that actually matters to you. Something that feels like *you* on a Tuesday, not you at your highlight reel.

**2. Start a “Gratitude Inventory” (Hear Me Out)**

I know “gratitude” sounds like something your mom’s yoga instructor would say. But here’s the teenage version: Every night, text yourself three things that made you feel like *yourself* that day. Not three things that were awesome. Three moments where you felt real. Maybe it was that weird deep conversation at lunch. Maybe it was when you were alone listening to music and actually felt something. Maybe it was when you helped someone and didn’t post about it. Over time, you’ll start seeing patterns. Those patterns are clues to your source code.

**3. Conduct a “Purpose Experiment”**

Pick one small thing this week that’s just for you—not for your resume, not for your followers, not for anyone’s approval. Write a poem and don’t show anyone. Learn three chords on a guitar. Go for a run without tracking it. Cook something weird. The goal isn’t to be good at it. The goal is to do something where the *doing* is the point. That’s what purpose feels like. It’s not about being the best; it’s about being *present*.

**4. Have One “No-Filter” Conversation**

Find one person—friend, sibling, whatever—and ask them a real question. Not “How are you?” but “What’s actually been hard lately?” Or “What do you think about when you can’t sleep?” And then listen. Don’t fix. Don’t perform. Just listen. Because here’s the secret: you find your identity not by searching for yourself, but by showing up for other people. We become ourselves in connection, not isolation.

---

**The Bottom Line**

You are not your GPA. You are not your follower count. You are not your sport, your body, your brand, your latest achievement, or your biggest failure.

You are the person who exists underneath all of that. And that person is enough. Not perfect, not finished, but enough. Worthy. Valuable. Already.

The world will try to sell you a million versions of who you should be. It’ll tell you that you’re a product to be marketed, a résumé to be built, a brand to be managed. But you don’t have to buy it. You can choose to build your life from the inside out instead of the outside in.

It’s scarier that way. It’s harder. You can’t measure it with metrics. But it’s the only way to build something that doesn’t collapse when the performance stops.

So who are you without your bio? You’re not a mystery to be solved. You’re a person to be discovered. And you’ve already started.

The rest is just living into it.

---

**Who Are You When No One's Watching?**

Let me ask you something. If I pulled out my phone right now and opened Instagram, and you had to write your bio in 150 characters—no emojis, no filters, no carefully curated highlight reels—what would you write?

Maybe you'd start with the obvious: your name, your school, your sport, your GPA. Maybe you'd list your achievements: "Honor roll, varsity captain, 4.0 GPA, 10K followers." Or maybe you'd describe yourself by what you love: "Music, skateboarding, gaming, hanging with friends."

Now let me ask a harder question: If you stripped all of that away—the grades, the followers, the trophies, the cute outfits, the witty captions—who's left?

I've been thinking about this because a friend recently asked me, "When did you stop feeling like a person and start feeling like a brand?" And that question hit me like a truck. Because somewhere between posting our first selfie and obsessing over our follower-to-following ratio, many of us have started treating ourselves like products that constantly need better marketing.

**The Performance Trap**

Let's be honest about the pressure you're living under. It's not just pressure to be good—it's pressure to be *seen* being good.

There's the achievement pressure: Every test feels like it defines your future. Every college app feels like it's measuring your worth. You're told you need to be excellent at something, preferably multiple somethings, and you need to document that excellence. Your value gets reduced to a transcript and a resume.

Then there's the appearance pressure: Not just how you look, but how you *present*. The right clothes, the right body, the right aesthetic. The subtle art of looking effortlessly perfect while trying harder than ever. You know the drill—take 47 photos, find the one where the lighting hits just right, spend 20 minutes editing, post, then obsessively check likes.

And social media? That's the pressure multiplier. It's not enough to *be* anymore. You have to *perform being*. You become your own PR manager, curating a highlight reel that makes your actual life feel like the blooper reel. You compare your behind-the-scenes to everyone else's director's cut.

Here's what no one tells you: This is exhausting. It's like running on a treadmill that keeps speeding up, and the moment you stumble, you feel like you're falling behind forever. You're building an identity on a foundation of sand, and the tide of other people's opinions keeps washing it away.

**The Question Beneath the Question**

But what if we've been asking the wrong question? What if "Who do I want to be?" is less important than "Who am I already?"

I want to offer a different way to think about this. Imagine you're walking through an art museum. You see a painting that stops you in your tracks. Maybe it's beautiful, maybe it's strange, maybe it's raw. But you don't stand there thinking, "This painting needs to earn its worth by being more popular." You don't think, "If more people photographed this, it would matter more." You experience it for what it is—a creation that exists, that has inherent value because an artist made it with intention.

Now stay with me here: What if you are that painting?

What if your identity isn't something you have to construct, curate, or hustle for? What if it's something you already *have*, something that was given to you before you ever posted your first photo, before you ever got your first grade, before you ever made your first team?

This is where we get to the deeper truth. In the Christian tradition, there's this idea that you are "fearfully and wonderfully made." Not "fearfully and wonderfully performing." Made. Created. Already complete before you ever achieved a thing. Your identity isn't a project to complete; it's a gift to receive.

Your purpose? It's not something you have to go find like it's hidden treasure. It's woven into your DNA. It's in the things that make you come alive, the ways you naturally show compassion, the creativity that bubbles up when no one's grading you. Purpose isn't about becoming someone impressive. It's about becoming more fully yourself.

**The Freedom of Being Known**

Here's what changes when you start from this place: You get to rest.

Not quit-everything rest, but deep-down rest. The rest that comes from knowing you're not a brand to manage, you're a person to be. You get to stop performing and start *being*. You get to have a terrible day and not worry that it's ruining your image. You get to try something and fail because your worth isn't on the line.

You also get to have real relationships. Because when you're not performing, you can actually let people in. You can drop the "I'm fine" mask and say "I'm struggling." You can celebrate other people's wins without feeling like they're stealing your spotlight. You can be the friend who doesn't need the photo op to prove the friendship happened.

Most importantly, you get to live from a center that holds. When your identity is grounded in something deeper than performance, you become unshakable. Not because you're strong, but because you're held by something stronger than your GPA, your follower count, or your reflection in the mirror.

**Your Homework (Yeah, I'm Giving You Homework)**

This isn't just a feel-good talk. I want you to actually try this. This week, do three things:

**1. Practice the 24-hour social media Sabbath.** Pick one full day where you don't post, don't check stories, don't curate. Just live. Eat the amazing meal without photographing it. Hang with friends without proving you have friends. Notice how it feels to exist without documenting your existence.

**2. Find your "true mirror."** Identify one person in your life who sees you without the performance. Someone you can be unfiltered with. Then, actually be unfiltered with them. Share something real this week—something you're scared of, something you're struggling with, something you're dreaming about that has nothing to do with your resume.

**3. Do something pointless and beautiful.** Create something no one will see. Write a poem and delete it. Draw something and burn it. Make music you don't record. Build something just for the joy of building. Prove to yourself that your creativity doesn't need an audience to matter.

**4. Ask a better question.** When you catch yourself thinking "Am I good enough?" or "Am I impressive enough?"—pause. Ask instead: "Am I being true to who I was made to be?" That's it. That's the question that actually matters.

**The Real You**

So back to that Instagram bio. If I asked you again to describe yourself, maybe this time you'd say something different. Not what you do, but who you are. "Curious." "Compassionate." "Learning." "Beloved."

Because here's the truth: You are not your achievements. You are not your appearance. You are not your follower count.

You are a person of profound worth, created with intention, known fully and loved anyway. And your purpose isn't to build an impressive identity—it's to live into the one you've already been given.

The world doesn't need another perfectly curated brand. It needs you—unfiltered, unperformed, fully alive. The you that exists when no one's watching. That you is more than enough.

So who are you when no one's watching? That's not a question to fear. It's an invitation to come home.

**The You That Exists When No One's Watching**

Okay, real talk: how many of you have laid in bed at 1 AM, scrolling through TikTok or Instagram, and felt this weird hollow feeling? Like everyone else is living their best life—perfect skin, perfect friends, perfect plans for their perfect future—while you're just… here. In your messy room, in your messy thoughts, wondering if you're falling behind some invisible race you never signed up for.

I know I did when I was your age. Except back then, we had flip phones and MySpace, so at least I could only feel inadequate at dial-up speed. But that feeling? It's the same. And if we're honest, it doesn't really go away when you get older—it just changes outfits.

Here's what I want to talk about tonight: that pressure you feel to *perform* yourself into existence. To become someone through achievements, appearance, and the carefully curated highlight reel we all pretend is casual.

**The Three-Headed Monster**

Let's name the beast. First head: **Achievement**. The GPA that determines your worth. The extracurriculars that prove you're "well-rounded." The college acceptance that validates your entire existence. You're told your future self is a CEO or surgeon or influencer, and every choice now is a step toward that—or a failure. You're not a person; you're a resume in training.

Second head: **Appearance**. Not just how you look, but how you *seem*. Are you chill enough? Dramatic enough? Do you have the right aesthetic? The right friends? The right vibe? You're constantly adjusting, like a thermostat in a room full of people who all want a different temperature.

Third head: **Social Media**. This is where the other two heads have babies. It's the performance arena where achievement and appearance merge into a single, addictive metric: likes, follows, views. We post our wins, filter our faces, and then measure our worth in engagement. And here's the kicker: even when we *know* it's a highlight reel, even when we *know* it's fake, our brains still absorb it as truth. You see someone's post about their Ivy League acceptance or their flawless morning routine, and your stomach drops. Not because you're a bad person, but because you're human. Comparison is the default setting of the human brain, and social media is comparison on steroids.

And it's exhausting. You're running a marathon where the finish line keeps moving, the crowd is judging your form, and you're not even sure you want the trophy.

**The House of Cards Problem**

Here's why this matters: when your identity is built on performance, it's built on shifting sand. Or maybe more accurately, it's a house of cards. One bad test score, one awkward photo, one ignored DM, and the whole thing feels like it could collapse.

I have a friend—let's call her Maya. Maya was the definition of "has it together." Straight A's, student council, captain of the volleyball team, 10,000 Instagram followers. She was building her brand before she could legally drive. Then, junior year, she got a B+ in AP Chem. Not a big deal, right? Except for Maya, it was catastrophic. She told me later that she sat in her car and cried for an hour, not because of the grade, but because that B+ felt like proof she was a fraud. If she wasn't the "smart one," who was she? If she wasn't achieving, did she even exist?

Maya had built her identity on being impressive. And when the impression cracked, so did she.

This is what happens when we let the external define the internal. We become human doing’s instead of human beings. We’re not rooted; we’re just reacting.

**Finding the Real Thing**

So what's the alternative? Some adults will tell you "just be yourself!" which is the most useless advice ever, because *who is that*? If I knew, I wouldn't be in this crisis.

I want to offer a different image. Instead of a house of cards, think of a tree. A tree doesn't spend energy trying to look like the tree next to it. It doesn't check how many rings the oak has before deciding how many rings to grow. It just… reaches. Down into the soil for nutrients, up toward the sun for energy. It grows slowly, often invisibly. Its roots matter more than its leaves, even though no one sees them.

Your identity works the same way. The real you—the one that exists when no one's watching, when the phone is off, when the grade hasn't posted yet—that's the root system. And purpose? Purpose isn't some grand, far-off destination. It's the sun and water. It's what you're reaching for.

So how do we find that? It starts with a simple but radical shift: **from mirror to window**.

Social media, achievement culture, appearance pressure—they're all mirrors. They force you to look *at* yourself, to evaluate, to perform. But purpose comes from looking *through* a window. It comes from asking different questions: What do I care about beyond myself? What hurts my heart when I see it in the world? What makes me feel alive when I'm not performing?

The poet Mary Oliver wrote: "Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?" Notice she didn't say "What will you achieve?" or "How will you impress?" She said "plan to *do*." Not accomplish. *Do*. The doing is the purpose. The being is the identity.

**This Week's Homework (That Actually Matters)**

Alright, let's get practical. I'm giving you three challenges. Not to add to your pressure, but to help you breathe.

**Challenge 1: The Unfollow Audit**
Tonight, go through your social media. For every account you follow, ask: *Does this make me feel more like myself, or more like I should be someone else?* Unfollow three accounts that make you feel "less than." Not out of spite—out of self-respect. You curate your feed; it shapes your brain. Choose wisely.

**Challenge 2: The 5-Minute Root Check**
Before you go to bed each night this week, grab a notebook. Answer these two questions—honestly, no one will read it:
- When did I feel most like *me* today? (Not most impressive. Most *real*.)
- What did I do that served someone or something beyond my own image?

This isn't a gratitude journal. It's an archaeology dig. You're looking for evidence of the real you.

**Challenge 3: The Purpose Micro-Act**
Do one thing this week that serves your actual values, not your performative ones. Like animals? Volunteer at the shelter for an hour—not for your college app, but because you want to. Hate how lonely people seem? Sit with the kid who eats lunch alone. Don't post about it. Don't tell anyone. Let it be a secret between you and your actual self. Purpose isn't found in the spotlight; it's found in the small, unglamorous acts of faithfulness.

**The You That Exists**

Look, I know this sounds like a lot. And I know that tomorrow, you'll still feel the pressure. The college emails will still come. The group chat will still be stressful. The mirror will still be there.

But maybe—just maybe—you can remember this: **You are not a project to be completed. You are a person to be uncovered.**

The achievements, the followers, the aesthetic? They're accessories. They're not the main character. The main character is the you that exists when no one's watching. The you that laughs at dumb memes, that gets angry at injustice, that feels that hollow 1 AM feeling and still chooses to reach for something real.

That you is enough. Not "enough for now" or "enough until you get your act together." Just… enough. The roots are already there. They just need more sun than a screen can provide.

So this week, close the mirror. Open a window. And see what—*who*—you find there.

I think you'll be surprised.

**The Character Creation Screen**

You know that moment in a video game when you first boot it up, and you’re staring at the character creation screen? You’ve got the sliders. Jawline definition. Eye shape. Whether you want to be the rogue with the mysterious backstory or the warrior with the tragic destiny. You spend forty-five minutes tweaking the cheekbones, choosing the aesthetic, optimizing your stats. You’re building *you*—or at least, the version of you that’s going to face the world.

Then you hit “start,” and within ten minutes of actual gameplay, you realize something slightly horrifying: none of those choices mattered as much as you thought. The character you actually become? That’s determined by the split-second decisions you make when the dragon shows up, or when you decide whether to help the NPC who can’t pay you, or when you choose to explore the cave that’s not on the map. The real character development happens in the un-curated moments, not the setup screen.

We’re living in a world that wants us to believe life *is* the character creation screen. Forever.

You feel it, right? The pressure to keep adjusting the sliders. Optimize your GPA. Curate your Instagram grid. Pick the aesthetic—cottagecore, dark academia, clean girl, whatever’s next week. Build the brand. Define the vibe. You’re told, implicitly and explicitly, that you are a project to be completed, a product to be marketed, a resume with a heartbeat. And if you can just get the settings right—thin enough, smart enough, connected enough, accomplished enough—then you’ll unlock the next level. Then you’ll be valid. Then you’ll know who you are.

But here’s the thing about living on the character creation screen: it’s exhausting. Because you’re not actually playing the game. You’re just managing your own branding, and the metrics are brutal. The likes, the views, the college acceptance letters, the comparison when you see someone else’s highlight reel. It’s like trying to build a house while standing outside it, constantly checking if the neighbors approve of the paint color, never actually going inside to see if there’s furniture, or warmth, or room to breathe.

And the worst part? It’s never finished. There’s always another slider to adjust. Another achievement to unlock. Another way to be slightly more marketable, slightly more optimized, slightly less… you.

So what if there’s a different way? Not a return to some fake “just be yourself” platitude that ignores how hard that actually is, but something deeper. Something that doesn’t ask you to *construct* an identity, but to *receive* one.

What if you’re not a billboard?

Think about that. A billboard is designed to be looked at, assessed, rated. It advertises. It performs. It changes based on what’s trending. Most of us are living like we’re billboards—constantly managing the surface, terrified of the wrong impression, optimizing for engagement. But what if you’re actually a home? A place with foundations, with hidden rooms, with a backyard that nobody sees but where real life happens. Homes aren’t judged by their curb appeal in the same way. They’re judged by whether they’re safe, whether they’re true, whether there’s space for people to come in and be real.

Being a home means your identity isn’t something you earn. It’s something you dwell in.

This isn’t about lowering the bar or saying achievement doesn’t matter. It’s about changing the foundation. When you know, deep in your bones, that you’re already enough—not because you’re perfect, but because you’re *here*, because you’re beloved, because your value isn’t a stock price that fluctuates with your productivity—then the achievements stop being identity-defining emergencies and start becoming expressions of who you already are. You study not to become smart, but because you’re curious and you have the freedom to learn without your worth hanging in the balance. You create not to become an artist, but because you’re already someone with something to say. You rest not because you’ve earned it, but because you’re a human being, not a human doing.

The ancient writers called this “being before doing.” They believed that you weren’t a problem to be solved or a product to be launched, but a mystery to be unfolded. That you were loved into existence, and that love doesn’t depend on your performance reviews. It means you can fail a test and not be a failure. You can be rejected by someone and not be rejectable. You can post a photo that gets no likes and still be fully real.

But let’s be honest: this sounds nice in theory and is brutal in practice. Because the world is loud, and the character creation screen is addictive. So I want to give you three things you can actually try this week. Not “find your purpose in five easy steps,” but small experiments in being a home instead of a billboard.

**First: The Offline Hour.**

Pick one hour this week—just one—where you go completely off the grid. No phone, no camera, no documentation. Do something real—take a walk, have a conversation, make something with your hands—and let it be *unseen*. Notice how terrifying that feels, and then notice what happens after the terror. Usually, there’s relief. You’re practicing being real without an audience. That’s where your actual self lives.

**Second: The No-Achievement Conversation.**

Find someone you trust—a friend, a parent, a youth leader—and ask them to hang out with zero performance pressure. Tell them explicitly: “I don’t want to talk about grades, or college, or what we’re accomplishing. I just want to exist with you.” See what comes up when you’re not trying to prove your value. It might be awkward. It might be holy.

**Third: The Invisible Inventory.**

Get a piece of paper and write down three things that are true about you that cannot be photographed, graded, or posted. Things like: “I’m the kind of person who notices when someone’s left out.” “I feel things deeply.” “I’m good at asking questions.” “I’m loyal.” These are the structural beams of your house. They don’t change when the trends do.

Here’s the closing thought. In most video games, there’s a moment where you realize that all the armor you’ve been chasing, all the cosmetic upgrades, were just distractions from the actual quest. The real game was about connection, courage, and becoming someone who could face the darkness without losing their light.

You’re already in the game. The dragon is here. And you don’t need to spend one more minute adjusting your cheekbones on the setup screen. You have permission to log out of the optimization trap and step into the story. Not because you’ve earned the right to be the main character, but because you already are—and the world doesn’t need your perfect performance. It needs your honest presence.

So close the menu. Look up. The adventure is waiting, and it’s asking for the real you—not the curated version, not the optimized brand, but the home-built, deeply loved, un-finishable, unfolding *you*. 

Let’s go play.

**The Character Select Screen**

You know that moment in a video game when you hit "New Game" and you’re dropped into the character creation screen? You spend forty-five minutes adjusting the jawline slider, picking the perfect hair color, debating whether your rogue should have a tragic backstory or a mysterious one. You’re building an identity from scratch, piece by piece, before you’ve even played a single minute of the actual game.

Sometimes I think that’s what being a teenager in 2024 feels like—except there’s no “Reset to Default” button, and the game is running in real-time while you’re still trying to build the character.

We’re living in an era of total customization. Your Spotify Wrapped becomes a personality type. Your aesthetic—cottagecore, dark academia, clean girl, whatever—becomes a full-time curation project. Your Instagram is a highlight reel that requires a production team of one (you) working overtime. And somewhere in the middle of managing all these versions of yourself, you’re supposed to figure out who you actually *are*.

But here’s the thing nobody’s saying out loud: it’s exhausting. And it’s not working.

**The Three Traps**

Let’s name the pressure, because unspoken pressure becomes shame. First, there’s **the achievement trap**. You’re told that you are your GPA, your college acceptance letters, your varsity letters, your internship at sixteen. You become a human resume, stacking credentials like armor against the question: “So, what are you going to do with your life?” As if your worth is a forecast, and you’re only valuable if your future looks profitable.

Then there’s **the appearance trap**. And I don’t just mean clear skin and fitting into certain sizes—though that’s brutal enough. I mean the way we’ve learned to aestheticize our entire existence. Your bedroom has to look like a Pinterest board. Your mental health struggles need to be “valid” but also “vibe” with your brand. Even your sadness gets filtered through Lightroom. You’re not just living; you’re art-directing a life, and the camera is always on.

Finally, **the metrics trap**. The quantified self. The follower count, the likes, the streaks, the ratio. We’ve built an economy where attention equals value, and suddenly your identity is a stock price that fluctuates hourly. Did the post flop? Did they leave you on read? Did you get invited? Every interaction becomes a referendum on whether you matter.

Here’s what happens when you live inside these traps for too long: you start to believe that you are a project to be completed. A product to be marketed. A problem to be optimized. You wake up every morning not as a person, but as a start-up founder pitching to venture capitalists, except the investors are your peers, your parents, the algorithm, and that voice in your head that sounds suspiciously like a TikTok comment section.

**The Alternative: Given, Not Constructed**

But what if there’s another way? What if identity isn’t something you build from the ground up, like that video game character, but something you uncover? Something you *receive*?

I want to offer you a different image. Instead of thinking of yourself as a billboard—constantly needing new content, fresh paint, better lighting to attract attention—what if you’re more like a tree? A tree doesn’t wake up and decide its value based on how many people took photos of it today. It doesn’t compare its rings to the oak next door. It simply grows from roots it didn’t plant, toward light it didn’t create, becoming more itself with every season.

Your identity is not a performance. It’s a foundation. It’s not something you earn; it’s something you inhabit.

This means you are allowed to be a mystery to yourself. You don’t need to have your “personal brand” figured out at seventeen. You don’t need to monetize your hobbies or turn your pain into content or know exactly what you’ll be doing in ten years. You are allowed to be unfinished. In fact, you’re supposed to be.

The ancient wisdom traditions—and honestly, modern psychology backs this up—suggest that you are not primarily a “doer” who needs to prove yourself through action. You are a “being” who is already inherently worthwhile. Your value isn’t in your output. It’s in your existence. You are not a human *doing*; you are a human *being*.

This sounds abstract, so let me get practical.

**Three Experiments for This Week**

You don’t need to overhaul your life overnight. But try these three things before next Sunday:

**First, the Input Audit.** Pull up your “Following” list on whatever app eats most of your attention. Scroll through it and ask one brutal question: *Does this account make me feel like a project, or a person?* If every post whispers that you need to be more productive, more beautiful, more optimized—unfollow. Not because you’re weak, but because you’re protecting your sanity. Curate your inputs like you’re curating a garden. Some things are weeds.

**Second, the Embodied Hour.** Pick one hour this week where you do something with your hands that produces no content. Cook something ugly but delicious. Go for a walk without headphones or GPS. Paint badly. Build something from LEGO. Do anything where the goal is not to capture it, post it, or improve yourself—just to feel the physical world resisting and responding to you. Your body is not a sculpture for display; it’s an instrument for experiencing the world. Use it for something besides being looked at.

**Third, the “I Am” Statement.** Before you check your phone tomorrow morning, write down three sentences: *I am [your name]. I am here. I am enough.* That’s it. Do this before you’ve checked your grades, your notifications, or your schedule. This is an act of defiance against the achievement machine. It’s a reminder that you existed before you produced anything today, and you will still exist—still be you—regardless of what you accomplish before sundown.

**The Real Main Character Energy**

There’s this phrase going around—“main character energy.” Usually, it means aesthetic lighting, dramatic playlists, and treating your life like a movie where you’re the star. But real main character energy isn’t about being the most dramatic person in the room. It’s about knowing that your story matters because it’s *yours*, not because it’s trending.

You are not a character select screen. You are not a work in progress. You are not a brand to be managed. You are a complex, contradictory, unrepeatable mystery, and you are allowed to take up space without proving why.

The world will keep selling you the lie that you need to be more, do more, prove more, before you’re allowed to rest. Don’t buy it. Your identity is not a trophy to be won. It’s a gift to be unwrapped, slowly, over a lifetime.

So step off the hamster wheel of self-construction for a minute. Breathe. You don’t have to build yourself from scratch. You just have to come home to who you already are.

And who you are? That’s enough. That’s always been enough.

**The Character Select Screen**

You know that moment in a video game when you hit "New Game" and you’re dropped into the character creation screen? You spend forty-five minutes adjusting the jawline slider, picking the perfect hair color, debating whether your rogue should have a tragic backstory or a mysterious one. You’re building an identity from scratch, piece by piece, before you’ve even played a single minute of the actual game.

Sometimes I think that’s what being a teenager right now feels like—except there’s no “Reset to Default” button, and the game is running in real-time while you’re still trying to build the character.

We’re living in an era of total customization. Your Spotify Wrapped becomes a personality type. Your aesthetic—cottagecore, dark academia, clean girl, whatever—turns into a second job. Your Instagram is a highlight reel that requires a production team of one (you) working overtime. And somewhere in the middle of managing all these versions of yourself, you’re supposed to figure out who you actually *are*.

But here’s the thing nobody’s saying out loud: it’s exhausting. And it’s not working.

**The Three Traps**

Let’s name the pressure, because unspoken pressure becomes shame. 

First, there’s **the achievement trap**. You’re told that you are your GPA, your college acceptance letters, your varsity letters, your internship at sixteen. You become a human resume, stacking credentials like armor against the question: “So, what are you going to do with your life?” As if your worth is a forecast, and you’re only valuable if your future looks profitable.

Then there’s **the appearance trap**. And I don’t just mean clear skin and fitting into certain sizes—though that’s brutal enough. I mean the way we’ve learned to aestheticize our entire existence. Your bedroom has to look like a Pinterest board. Your mental health struggles need to be “valid” but also “vibe” with your brand. Even your sadness gets filtered through Lightroom. You’re not just living; you’re art-directing a life, and the camera is always on.

Finally, **the metrics trap**. The quantified self. The follower count, the likes, the streaks, the ratio. We’ve built an economy where attention equals value, and suddenly your identity is a stock price that fluctuates hourly. Did the post flop? Did they leave you on read? Did you get invited? Every interaction becomes a referendum on whether you matter.

Here’s what happens when you live inside these traps for too long: you start to believe that you are a project to be completed. A product to be marketed. A problem to be optimized. It simply grows from roots it didn’t plant, toward light it didn’t install, becoming more itself with every season.

**The Character Select Screen**

You know that moment in a video game when you hit "New Game" and you’re dropped into the character creation screen? You spend forty-five minutes adjusting the jawline slider, picking the perfect hair color, debating whether your rogue should have a tragic backstory or a mysterious one. You’re building an identity from scratch, piece by piece, before you’ve even played a single minute of the actual game.

Sometimes I think that’s what being a teenager right now feels like—except there’s no “Reset to Default” button, and the game is running in real-time while you’re still trying to build the character.

We’re living in an era of total customization. Your Spotify Wrapped becomes a personality type. Your aesthetic—cottagecore, dark academia, clean girl, whatever—becomes a full-time curation project. Your Instagram is a highlight reel that requires a production team of one (you) working overtime. And somewhere in the middle of managing all these versions of yourself, you’re supposed to figure out who you actually *are*.

But here’s the thing nobody’s saying out loud: it’s exhausting. And it’s not working.

**The Three Traps**

Let’s name the pressure, because unspoken pressure becomes shame. First, there’s **the achievement trap**. You’re told that you are your GPA, your college acceptance letters, your varsity letters, your internship at sixteen. You become a human resume, stacking credentials like armor against the question: “So, what are you going to do with your life?” As if your worth is a forecast, and you’re only valuable if your future looks profitable.

Then there’s **the appearance trap**. And I don’t just mean clear skin and fitting into certain sizes—though that’s brutal enough. I mean the way we’ve learned to aestheticize our entire existence. Your bedroom has to look like a Pinterest board. Your mental health struggles need to be “valid” but also “vibe” with your brand. Even your sadness gets filtered through Lightroom. You’re not just living; you’re art-directing a life, and the camera is always on.

Finally, **the metrics trap**. The quantified self. The follower count, the likes, the streaks, the ratio. We’ve built an economy where attention equals value, and suddenly your identity is a stock price that fluctuates hourly. Did the post flop? Did they leave you on read? Did you get invited? Every interaction becomes a verdict on whether you matter.

Here’s what happens when you live inside these traps for too long: you start to believe that you are a project to be completed. A product to be marketed. A problem to be optimized. You wake up every morning not as a person, but as a brand manager pitching to a board of directors, except the client (you) is never satisfied and the board (everyone else) is always voting.

**The Alternative: Given, Not Constructed**

I know what you’re thinking: *Cool, but I can’t just opt out. The game is still running. The college applications still exist. The algorithm still refreshes. You’re right. You can’t opt out of the systems. But you can opt out of letting them define you.*

What if there’s another way? What if identity isn’t something you build from the ground up, like that video game character, but something you uncover? Something you *receive*?

I want to offer you a different image. Instead of thinking of yourself as a billboard—constantly needing new content, fresh paint, better lighting to attract attention—what if you’re more like a tree? A redwood doesn’t wake up anxious because the pine next door is growing needles faster. It doesn’t check how many tourists took photos of it today. It simply grows toward the light it’s given, using the roots it already has, becoming more itself with every season.

Your identity is not a performance. It’s a foundation. It’s not something you earn; it’s something you inhabit.

This means you are allowed to be a mystery to yourself. You don’t need to have your “personal brand” figured out at seventeen. You don’t need to monetize your hobbies or turn your pain into content or know exactly what you’ll be doing in ten years. You are allowed to be unfinished. In fact, you’re supposed to be.

You don’t have to earn your spot on the planet every single day. Your value isn’t a subscription service you renew through productivity. Psychologists, poets, and ancient wisdom traditions all agree: you are not primarily a “doer” who needs to prove yourself through action. You are a “being” who is already inherently worthwhile. Your value isn’t in your output. It’s in your existence. You are, in the truest sense, beloved—not because of what you produce, but simply because you are here.

This sounds abstract, so let me get practical.

**Three Experiments for This Week**

You don’t need to overhaul your life overnight. But try these three things before next Sunday:

**First, the Input Audit.** Pull up your “Following” list on whatever app eats most of your attention. Scroll through it and ask one brutal question: *Does this account make me feel like a project, or a person?* If every post whispers that you need to be more productive, more beautiful, more optimized—curate your inputs like you’re curating a garden. Some things are weeds. 

Now, I know the social stakes. If unfollowing that person from third period feels like a declaration of war, use the mute button instead. Muting is just pruning the view while keeping the peace. The algorithm doesn’t deserve a vote on your worth.

**Second, the Embodied Hour.** Pick one hour this week where you do something with your hands that produces no *content*—meaning, nothing that needs to be photographed, posted, or performed. Make something that doesn’t need documentation: cook food that tastes amazing but looks like a crime scene. Go for a walk without headphones or GPS. Build a LEGO set that would never trend on TikTok. Paint badly. 

Do anything where the goal is not to capture it or improve yourself—just to feel the physical world resisting and responding to you. Your body is not a sculpture for display; it’s an instrument for experiencing the world. Use it for something besides being looked at.

# The Edit You Can't See

**[Opening]**

Let me tell you about the worst ten minutes of my week. I posted a photo on Saturday—nothing special, just coffee and a book in decent lighting—and I spent the next ten minutes watching the likes come in. Refresh. Three more. Refresh. Nothing. Refresh. Someone I know from school posted something similar and got triple the engagement in half the time. I actually considered deleting mine.

I'm twenty-six. I've got a degree, a job, friends who would show up at 2 AM if I called. And I'm still performing for an algorithm that doesn't know my name.

So if you're fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, and you feel like your entire worth is tied to a number on a screen? I get it. The machinery is just better at selling you the lie now.

---

**[The Pressure]**

Here's what I wish someone had said to me at your age: almost every message you receive about who you are is trying to sell you something.

*Define yourself by achievement.* The college prep industrial complex starts early now. You're not just taking classes—you're building a "portfolio." Every hobby becomes a "spike" for your application. I knew a kid who genuinely loved marine biology, spent three summers at research programs, and by senior year couldn't remember why he'd started. The achievement had eaten the joy.

*Define yourself by appearance.* This one's relentless. The beauty industry has figured out that if they can make you feel broken at fifteen, they have a customer for life. But it's not just products anymore. It's the constant documentation—the awareness that any moment might be captured, filtered, posted. You're not just living; you're curating a brand called You, Inc.

*Define yourself by social media metrics.* Followers. Likes. The dreaded "ratio." These numbers feel like evidence, like proof of your place in the social hierarchy. But here's the thing about metrics: they're designed to keep you producing, not to tell you the truth about your value. A post that "flops" isn't data about your worth. It's data about an algorithm's priorities. We just forget the difference.

And underneath all three? The same whisper: *You are not enough yet. Keep performing. Keep producing. Keep proving.*

---

**[The Problem]**

The philosopher Charles Taylor talks about what he calls the "buffered self"—this idea that modern people experience themselves as isolated units, creating our identities from scratch like we're decorating a dorm room. Pick your aesthetic. Curate your vibe. Build your personal brand.

But there's a cost to this DIY approach to identity. When you are solely responsible for creating yourself, you are also solely responsible for maintaining yourself. Every failure becomes existential. Every rejection feels like evidence that you've built the wrong self.

I see this in the anxiety statistics. In the way brilliant, kind young people I know describe themselves as "frauds" or "failures" because they didn't make some cutoff. In the exhaustion of performing a self that needs constant updating.

The theologian Miroslav Volf puts it starkly: "When identity is made, not received, it becomes a burden too heavy to bear."

---

**[A Different Story]**

So what if there's another way? Not a return to some imaginary past where everything was simple—let's be honest, those pasts had their own brutal constraints—but a different foundation entirely.

The ancient Hebrew writers had this phrase: *tselem Elohim*. Image of God. It shows up in the very first chapter of their scriptures, describing every human being. Not the talented ones. Not the attractive ones. Not the ones with good engagement rates. Everyone.

This isn't about religion as performance. It's about ontology—what fundamentally *is*. The claim is radical: before you do anything, achieve anything, post anything, you already bear something sacred. Not because you've earned it. Because you've been given it.

The Christian tradition takes this further. In the New Testament, there's this idea that your identity isn't primarily something you construct but something you're *grafted into*—connected to something larger, older, more durable than your individual performance. The apostle Paul writes about being "in Christ" the way you might talk about being "in a family"—not as an achievement but as a belonging.

This changes the math. If your fundamental worth is given, not earned, then:

- Failure becomes information, not verdict
- Rest becomes possible, not lazy
- Comparison becomes mostly irrelevant
- Your value doesn't fluctuate with your metrics

I'm not saying this solves everything. I still refresh my notifications. But I have something to appeal to when the anxiety rises—a deeper story about who I am that doesn't depend on my performance.

---

**[The Practice]**

Theory is cheap. Here's what this might actually look like this week:

**One: Audit your inputs.** For three days, notice what makes you feel like you need to *become* versus what reminds you that you already *belong*. Certain accounts? Certain conversations? Certain internal narratives? You can't always control what shapes you, but you can start seeing the machinery.

**Two: Practice "unproductive" presence.** Do one thing this week with no documentation, no optimization, no future utility. Make something ugly. Have a conversation that goes nowhere. Walk without a destination. You're not wasting time—you're reminding yourself that your value isn't tied to output.

**Three: Name your givenness.** This sounds woo-woo, but try it. Before sleep, name three things you received today that you didn't earn. A conversation. A sunset. The fact of your breathing. Gratitude isn't just positive thinking; it's an identity practice. It trains you to see yourself as recipient, not just producer.

**Four: Find your "we."** Isolation makes the performance economy worse. Who knows you outside your achievements? Who would show up if you failed publicly? If you don't have that, start building it—one risky honest conversation at a time. Vulnerability is how we escape the curated self.

---

**[Closing]**

There's a scene in the film *The Social Network* where Jesse Eisenberg's Zuckerberg keeps refreshing his friend request to his ex-girlfriend. It's devastating because we recognize it—the way we outsource our worth to external validation, then find that validation hollow.

But the film gets something wrong. It suggests this is just what humans do now, that we've traded depth for connectivity and there's no going back.

I don't believe that. I've seen too many young people—maybe you—hungry for something real, something that doesn't dissolve when the wifi drops. The performance economy is powerful, but it's not inevitable. You can choose to root yourself in something older, deeper, more durable.

Not because you're supposed to. Because you're already beloved. The rest is just learning to believe it.

---

*[Optional discussion questions: When do you feel most like yourself? When do you feel most like you're performing? What's one thing you do only because it would look good, not because you actually want to?]*

# Who Are You, Really?

So here's a scenario. It's 11 PM. You're in bed. You should be sleeping, but instead you're scrolling. And you land on someone's post—maybe someone from school, maybe someone you follow who seems to have everything figured out. Perfect photo. Amazing life. And suddenly you feel something tighten in your chest. Like you're behind. Like you're not enough. Like everyone else got a manual for this whole "being a person" thing and you somehow missed yours.

Does that land? Good. Because I want to talk about that feeling tonight.

Because here's what's weird: we live in an era where we're more "connected" than ever, but also more confused about who we actually are. We have Instagram profiles and TikTok accounts and SnapChat scores—all these little digital mirrors showing us who we're supposed to be. And the pressure to perform, to curate, to be impressive—it is *intense*. I know some of you feel it even if you don't always name it.

So let's name it.

There's this massive pressure right now—especially at your age—to define yourself by what you've achieved. Your grades. Your GPA. Your SAT scores. Your sports stats. Your follower count. It's like your worth is a scoreboard that's constantly updating, and if you're not winning at something, you're losing. And it sucks the joy right out of things you used to love, because now everything is a competition. Everything is a metric.

And alongside that, there's the appearance pressure. You know what I'm talking about. The pressure to look a certain way, to have the right style, to post the right photos. The endless comparing. The "am I hot enough, skinny enough, cool enough" loop that never actually lets you rest. Social media has turned beauty into a moving target that's always one filter away from being "good enough."

And then there's the identity pressure. The question everyone asks: "What do you want to be when you grow up?" Like you're supposed to have it figured out by now. Like you need to pick a lane and commit. And if you don't know? You feel lost. Broken. Behind.

Here's the truth: *all of this is lying to you.*

It's lying when it says your worth is your GPA. It's lying when it says your value is your follower count. It's lying when it says you need to have your whole life mapped out by seventeen. These systems—school, social media, culture—they're not bad exactly. But they keep asking the wrong question. They keep asking: "What can you produce? What can you prove? What can you perform?"

And the question they never ask is: "Who are you, really? Not what you do. *Who you are.*"

So what if I told you that your identity doesn't start with what you achieve? What if it starts with something given to you, not something you have to earn?

Here's what I mean. What if your worth isn't something you build—it's something you're already *given*? Not by a grade. Not by a like. Not by a college acceptance letter. What if there's something deeper going on beneath all that noise?

I think there is.

I think you are known. I think you are seen—not by the algorithm, but by something or someone that actually knows you. The real you. The messy you. The you that doesn't have it figured out. And I think that knowledge of being known changes everything. It means you're not performing for a scoreboard. You're *responding* to a love that's already there.

Now, I'm not going to stand here and pretend that's easy to feel or believe. It's not. Some days it feels abstract. Some days it feels like a nice idea but not a real thing you can hold onto. But what I can tell you is this: the people I know who are most secure in who they are—who don't crumble when they fail, who don't need the approval of everyone around them—they've found something outside themselves to anchor to. Something that says "you matter not because of what you do, but because of what you've been given."

That's the shift. From "I am what I produce" to "I am held by something bigger than my performance."

So what does this actually look like, practically? Let me give you a few things you can try this week. Not because following this list will solve everything, but because small shifts in habit can open up space for something bigger.

**One: Do a social media audit.** Look at who you follow. Not the numbers—the *vibe*. Does your feed leave you feeling inspired and seen, or does it leave you feeling like you're not enough? Unfollow a few accounts that make you feel worse, not better. Protect your mental space. Your brain is being shaped by what you consume. Feed it something healthier this week.

**Two: Have a real conversation.** Not about grades or plans or what you're "doing." Ask someone: "What do you think is true about me? What do you see in me?" And actually listen. Let someone speak identity into you, not the scoreboard. This could be a friend, a parent, a youth leader—anyone who knows you and sees you. You don't have to figure this out alone.

**Three: Notice when you're performing.** This one is subtle. Here's how it works: pay attention to moments when you're making choices based on how they'll be *perceived* rather than what you actually want or value. When you catch yourself performing, pause. Ask: "Who am I trying to be right now? And is that actually me?" That awareness is the beginning of something important.

Here's the thing. You are not a brand. You're not a product to be optimized. You're a person—complex, messy, still forming, already known. And the pressure to define yourself by achievement and appearance and follower counts? It's real, but it's not *true*. You get to live from something deeper than that.

That doesn't mean you won't still care about grades or looks or what people think. You'll probably care about those things for a while. But you can care about them differently. You can care about them *less*. Because your worth isn't on the line anymore. It's already secure.

So this week, try one of these. See what opens up. And remember: you don't have to have it figured out. You just have to start somewhere.

And then it happens—someone posts a BeReal and suddenly you're seeing their real life, their real face, in this weirdly vulnerable two-minute window. And it hits you: everyone else seems to be actually *living* something interesting, and you're just here. Watching. And that feeling tightens in your chest. Like you're behind. Like everyone else got a manual for this whole "being a person" thing and you somehow missed yours.

Does that land? Good. Because I want to talk about that feeling tonight.

Here's what's weird: we live in an era where we're more "connected" than ever, but also more confused about who we actually are. We have Instagram profiles and TikTok accounts and BeReal notifications—all these little digital mirrors showing us who we're supposed to be. And the pressure to perform, to curate, to be impressive—it is *intense*. I know some of you feel it even if you don't always name it.

So let's name it.

There's this massive pressure right now—especially at your age—to define yourself by what you've achieved. Your grades. Your GPA. Your SAT scores. Your sports stats. Your follower count. It's like your worth is a scoreboard that's constantly updating, and if you're not winning at something, you're losing. And it sucks the joy right out of things you used to love, because now everything is a competition. Everything is a metric.

And alongside that, there's the appearance pressure. You know what I'm talking about. The pressure to look a certain way, to have the right style, to post the right photos. The endless comparing. The "am I hot enough, skinny enough, cool enough" loop that never actually lets you rest. Social media has turned beauty into a moving target that's always one filter away from being "good enough." And now there's even the pressure to seem *casual* about it—the photo dump trend where your laid-back life becomes another thing you have to perform.

And then there's the identity pressure. The question everyone asks: "What do you want to be when you grow up?" As if you're a project plan that needs milestones. As if "I don't know yet" isn't a valid answer. As if your value is your future utility to the economy. And if you don't know? You feel lost. Broken. Behind. Adults ask this because they don't know what else to say, but it accidentally trains you to believe you *are* your productivity.

Here's the truth: *all of this is selling you a lie.*

Here's why that's exhausting: every scoreboard has a bottom half. If your worth is your GPA, what happens when you bomb a test? If it's your follower count, what happens when the algorithm changes? You're building a house on sand that shifts every day. These systems aren't bad exactly—school has value, social media can be fun. But they keep asking the wrong question. They keep asking: "What can you produce? What can you prove? What can you perform?"

And the question they never ask is: "Who are you, really? Not what you do. *Who you are.*"

So what if I told you that your identity doesn't start with what you achieve? What if it starts with something given to you, not something you have to earn?

Here's what I mean. Think about being someone's kid. You didn't earn that. You didn't perform your way into being your parents' child. You just *are* theirs. No GPA required. No audition. They didn't look at you and say, "We'll take this one if they get good grades." They said, "This one. Ours." That's what it's like—not the religion part, not the rules part, but the *relationship* part. You are held by something that doesn't need you to be impressive. You are known by someone who sees the messy, confused, still-forming you and says, "Mine."

Now, I'm not going to stand here and pretend that's easy to feel or believe. It's not. Some days it feels abstract. Some days it feels like a nice idea but not a real thing you can hold onto. But what I can tell you is this: the people I know who are most secure in who they are—who don't crumble when they fail, who don't need the approval of everyone around them—they've found something outside themselves to anchor to. Something that says "you matter not because of what you do, but because of what you've been given."

That's the shift. From "I am what I produce" to "I am held by something bigger than my performance."

And here's what changes when you actually believe that: you're free to *give* something. You can be present instead of productive. You can listen instead of waiting for your turn to impress. Your purpose stops being "become impressive" and starts being "become present." That's actually way harder, but it's real. It's the difference between running on a treadmill that's always speeding up and actually going somewhere.

So what does this actually look like, practically? Let me give you a few things you can try this week. Not because following this list will solve everything, but because small shifts in habit can open up space for something bigger.

**One: Do a social media audit.** Here's a simple test: scroll through your feed and notice the *after-feeling*. Do you feel open and inspired, or contracted and like you're not enough? Your brain is being shaped by what you consume. Unfollow a few accounts that leave you feeling worse. Protect your mental space.

**Two: Have a real conversation.** Not about grades or plans or what you're "doing." Ask someone: "What do you think is true about me? What do you see in me?" And actually listen. Let someone speak identity into you, not the scoreboard. This could be a friend, a parent, a youth leader—anyone who knows you and sees you. You don't have to figure this out alone.

**Three: Notice when you're performing.** This one is subtle. Pay attention to moments when you're making choices based on how they'll be *perceived* rather than what you actually want or value. When you catch yourself performing, pause. Ask: "Who am I trying to be right now? And is that actually me?" That awareness is the beginning of something important.

**Four: Do one thing anonymously.** Do something kind or creative this week that no one will know about. Not for the story, not for the credit. Just because you can. It trains your brain to separate your value from visibility.

Here's the thing. You are not a brand. You're not a product to be optimized. You're a person—complex, messy, still forming, already known. And the pressure to define yourself by achievement and appearance and follower counts? It's real, but it's not *true*. You get to live from something deeper than that.

That doesn't mean you won't still care about grades or looks or what people think. You'll probably care about those things for a while. But you can care about them differently. You can care about them *less*. Because your worth isn't on the line anymore. It's already secure.

So this week, when you're lying in bed at 11 PM and that tight feeling hits your chest, try this: exhale. Literally. Let your shoulders drop. Remind yourself that the scoreboard is off. You're not a brand to be optimized. You're a person to be present. And that is enough.

You don't have to have it figured out. You just have to start somewhere.

# Who Are You, Really?

So here's a scenario. You open Instagram, tap on your profile, and there's that little "Edit Profile" button. And for a second, you just stare at it. Because you have to sum up who you are—in a bio, in a grid, in a username. Like your entire existence can be captured in 150 characters or less.

What do you even write? Your grades? Your team? That thing you did that one time that was kind of cool? The aesthetic you spent three hours curating?

And then you scroll. And everyone else seems to have it figured out. That kid from your math class just got accepted into some program. Your feed is full of people who look like they know exactly who they are and exactly where they're going. And you're just... here. Trying to figure it out.

Does that feel familiar? Because I've talked to a lot of people your age, and here's what I've heard over and over: *I don't know who I am. I don't know what I'm supposed to be. And everyone else seems to have it together.*

So let's talk about it. Not in a "you're perfect just the way you are" kind of way—because honestly, that can feel hollow. But in an honest, let's-get-real way. About who you actually are. And why that matters.

---

Here's what I think is happening. Somewhere along the way, we started believing that identity is something you *build*. Like it's a project. You collect achievements, you curate an image, you perform a version of yourself that you hope people will like. And if you get enough of the right stuff—good grades, the right friends, the right look—then you'll finally feel like you know who you are.

But here's the thing about building your identity on achievements: there's always a bigger mountain. You get the grade, but there's another test. You make the team, but there's always a higher level. You get the followers, but there's always someone with more. It's exhausting. And it never actually ends.

Or maybe it's appearance. You spend hours on how you look, what you wear, how you present yourself. And for a while, it works—you feel confident, you feel seen. But then you see someone else, someone who seems to have what you want, and suddenly your own appearance doesn't feel like enough. The goalposts keep moving.

Or maybe it's social media itself. You post, you curate, you perform. And for a moment, you feel like yourself—the edited, filtered, carefully selected version of yourself. But then the likes don't come in as fast, or someone says something, or you just feel hollow after scrolling for an hour. Because the version of you that lives on a screen isn't really *you*. It's a performance. And performing forever is exhausting.

Here's the hard truth: none of these things are bad in themselves. Achievements matter. Taking care of how you present yourself matters. Sharing your life with people matters. But when any of these become the *foundation* of who you are—when they become the answer to "who am I?"—you're building your house on sand. Because all of these things can be taken away. All of them can change. All of them can leave you feeling like you don't know yourself anymore.

---

So what's the alternative? What if I told you that you don't have to *build* your identity? What if it was already given to you?

Here's what I mean. What if who you are isn't something you have to figure out from scratch? What if there's something deeper going on—something that was true about you before you ever picked up a phone, before you ever got a grade, before you ever knew what you wanted to be when you grew up?

What if your identity isn't something you earn? What if it's something you discover?

There's this idea that shows up in a lot of places—maybe you've heard it before—that you were made for something. That you're not an accident. That there's a story you're part of, and your life has meaning and purpose that goes beyond your grades, your followers, or how you look in a photo.

I know that can sound like a cliché. But here's why it matters: if your worth is based on what you *do*, then your worth is always conditional. But if your worth is based on something deeper—something that was given to you, not earned—then you can relax. You can take risks. You can fail. Because your identity isn't on the line.

You are not your GPA. You are not your follower count. You are not the version of yourself that you curate for other people. You are a person with inherent worth—worth that doesn't fluctuate based on how well you're performing.

That's the foundation. And from that foundation, you can actually start to figure out what you're *for*. Not in a stressful "what's my purpose?" way, but in a "what do I care about? What am I good at? What do I want to contribute?" way.

Purpose isn't usually a lightning bolt. It's usually quiet. It's the thing you care about when no one's watching. It's the thing you'd do even if you didn't get paid. It's the way you're wired. And when you stop trying to be everyone else, you actually have space to notice what makes you *you*.

---

So here's my question for you: What if you spent a week not trying to prove yourself? What if you took a break from the performance?

I want to give you three things you can actually do this week—not to become a better version of yourself in the way the world means it, but to actually get quiet enough to remember who you are.

**First, try a social media fast.** Just 24 hours. See what happens when you're not performing. When you're not curating. When you're just existing. Notice what rises up. What do you think about? What do you miss? What do you *not* miss?

**Second, ask yourself a question.** Not "what do I want to be?"—that's too big. Ask: "What do I care about when no one's watching?" What's the thing that matters to you that you don't talk about? That's probably a clue to who you actually are.

**Third, do one thing that scares you this week.** Something that puts you outside the version of yourself you've already built. Because the real you—the deeper you—can't be discovered by staying safe. Sometimes you have to step out to find out who you are.

Here's the truth: you are more than your achievements. You are more than your appearance. You are more than your feed. There's something in you that's already whole, already valuable, already worth something. Your job isn't to build that. Your job is to stop looking for it in all the wrong places and start living like you already have it.

That's where freedom is. That's where purpose starts. Not in the performance, but in the person you already are.

# Who Are You, Really?

Last Thursday, 9:47 p.m., my friend Jayla deleted three posts because they "only" hit 112 likes. She stared at the screen like it owed her money. Then she changed her bio three times—"plant girl / 4.2 GPA / she/her"—and still felt fake.

That's when we started talking about this.

Because here's what I've heard over and over from people your age: *I don't know who I am. I don't know what I'm supposed to be. And everyone else seems to have it together.*

So let's talk about it. Not in a "you're perfect just the way you are" kind of way—because honestly, that can feel hollow. But in an honest, let's-get-real way. About who you actually are. And why that matters.

---

## Building on Sand

Here's what I think is happening. Somewhere along the way, we started believing that identity is something you *build*. Like it's a project. You collect achievements, you curate an image, you perform a version of yourself that you hope people will like. And if you get enough of the right stuff—good grades, the right friends, the right look—then you'll finally feel like you know who you are.

But here's the thing about building your identity on achievements: there's always a bigger mountain. You get the grade, but there's another test. You make the team, but there's always a higher level. You get the followers, but there's always someone with more. It's exhausting. And it never actually ends.

Or maybe it's appearance. You spend hours on how you look, what you wear, how you present yourself. And for a while, it works—you feel confident, you feel seen. But then you see someone else, someone who seems to have what you want, and suddenly your own appearance doesn't feel like enough. The goalposts keep moving.

Or maybe it's TikTok. You post, you trend, you perform. And for a moment, you feel like yourself—the edited, filtered, carefully selected version of yourself. But then the views don't come in as fast, or someone says something, or you just feel hollow after scrolling for an hour. Because the version of you that lives on a screen isn't really *you*. It's a performance. And performing forever is exhausting.

Here's the hard truth: none of these things are bad in themselves. Achievements matter. Taking care of how you present yourself matters. Sharing your life with people matters. But when any of these become the *foundation* of who you are—when they become the answer to "who am I?"—you're building your house on Jell-O. Looks fun, wobbles the second you stand on it. Because all of these things can be taken away. All of them can change. All of them can leave you feeling like you don't know yourself anymore.

---

I think about my friend Marcus. He was the star of the JV soccer team—starter, captain, the whole identity. Then he tore his ACL junior year. And I watched him crash. Not just physically. He didn't know who he was anymore. He wasn't "soccer Marcus." He was just... Marcus. And he had no idea who that was.

It took him a year to figure it out. He started helping coach the younger kids, realized he actually loved teaching. Now he's thinking about sports medicine. But the hardest part wasn't the injury. It was realizing he'd been standing on something that could collapse the whole time.

---

## House on Bedrock

So what's the alternative? What if I told you that you don't have to *build* your identity? What if it was already given to you?

What if who you are isn't something you have to figure out from scratch? What if there's something deeper going on—something that was true about you before you ever picked up a phone, before you ever got a grade, before you ever knew what you wanted to be when you grew up?

What if your identity isn't something you earn? What if it's something you discover?

There's this idea that shows up in a lot of places—maybe you've heard it before—that you were made for something. That you're not an accident. That there's a story you're part of, and your life has meaning and purpose that goes beyond your grades, your followers, or how you look in a photo.

I know that can sound like a fortune cookie. But stick with me—there's something real here.

If your worth is based on what you *do*, then your worth is always conditional. You perform well, you're valuable. You fail, you're not. But if your worth is based on something deeper—something that was given to you, not earned—then you can relax. You can take risks. You can fail. Because your identity isn't on the line.

You are not your GPA. You are not your follower count. You ≠ ratio. You are not the version of yourself that you curate for other people. You are a person with inherent worth—worth that doesn't fluctuate based on how well you're performing.

It's the thing you'd do even if you didn't get paid. It's the way you're wired. And when you stop trying to be everyone else, you actually have space to notice what makes you *you*.

---
